DEAN STANLEY'S FUNERAL. ticWSBT3,MiSTIM ABBEY, JULY 25TR, 188 L ot this, not this, 0 Friend, thy funeral day Five long years since, for thee, that passed away, When she was borne from thee, thy 3oy and stay; And bowed and patient here we saw thee stand, The children she so loved in either hand, Thy home" unroofed," a stranger in thy land. Lost the dear presence of that perfect wife, Still to fulfil, alone, the double life. Alone to bear the burden and the strife,— Shed benedictions fronva smitten heart, Food to the hungered from thy dearth impart. Dying, still blessing, from thine own to part. Till now, at last, thy double task is done; The last fight fought, the victory fully won; Thou'rt gone from this small world beneath the sun. Gone to the vision of the Crucified, The Master loved so long, trusted and tried 4 Gone where the blest who enter in abide; Gone to the Mother City of the free, Where mercy with the Merciful shall be. The pure ireheart the face of God shall see. And in the many mansions fair and wide, Serene thou dwellest and art satisfied, Adoring now for ever by her side. —Author of "The Sclgeberg-Cotta Faintly," in" Goad Herds for October.

Hush_a_bye, baby, Grandmother sings ; Hither and thither the cradle swings. Purl and plain, and plain and purl, Be it for boy or be it for girl: Two and two is a neat device; Learn to shift the thread in a trice. Hush-a-bye, baby, Grandmother sings; Hither and thither the cradle swings. Inch by inch the long leg grows,_ Straight and narrow for fitting close; A very poor leg, is the saying well known, That cannot shape a leg of its own. Hush-a-bye, baby, Grandmother sings; Hither and thither the cradle swings. Count the stitches and halve them now, And one-half set in a single row, And back and forth, outside and in, Knit the heel on the single pin. Hush-a-bye, baby, Grandmother sings; Hither and thither the cradle swings. Knit it long, and narrow midway, To round it. and bind it off, as we say; Take up the hoops on either side And add a few more to make it. wide. Hush-a-bye, baby, Grandmother sings: Hither and thither the cradle swings. Now each side narrow, or slip and bind, To shape the instep as you will find; Then knit straight round till you near the tie; This is the way the foot must grow. Hush-a-bye, baby. Grand mother sings Hither and thither the cradle swings. Then narrow once more, and narrow away, Toeing it off, as knitters say; There is a stocking lit for an belt! Now knit the mate—fur he must have a pair. Hush-a-bye, baby, when you are grown Your feet may be worthy to climb a throne! HARRIET HCEIVSN KIMBALL.

As a young man named Leary, son of the president of the Knocknagree Land League, who had been engaged in saving the crops of a boycotted farmer, was returning home on Monday evening he was attacked by an armed and disguised party Gf about 40 persons. lie ran away, but when he was about 50 yards off one man fired a rifle. The bullet struck Leary in the hip, inflicting wounds from which he died on Tuesday. . _

Mr. Parnell attended a " Convention " of the Land League at Dungarvan on Wednesday, and repeated his ad- vice to the farmers not to avail themselves of the Land Act except under conditions which the Exective of the League shall dictate. Mr. F. H. O'Donnell, M.P., who has rarely spoken in public since the prorogation of Parliament, has bitterly denounced the "tyrants in Dublin Castle and Ha- warden," and declares that the Land League ist now the only Government in Ireland. The Dublin. Gazette contained, on Wednesday a list df all the persons in prison under the Pro- tection of Person and Property Act on the 3rd inst. There are 133 in all, of whom 34 are in Kilmainham, 40 in Galway, 37 in Limerick, 11 in Dundalk, and 11 in Naas prison. ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF A LANDLORD.

On Monday night, Mt. Arthur Sheen Bingham, of Doo- lough Lodge, Belmullet, in the Eiris district of county Mayo, was fired at when returning home in his croydon from marketing with his wife and servant girl. Mr. Bing- ham is the owner of a small estate. He has been boycotted for some time, and compelled to do his own marketing, pro- curing supplies from a distance. He has not carried fire- arms, and trusted merely to the rapidity With which he drives. One part of the road be had to pass was so steep as to necessitate a slackening of the pace, and this was the spot selected by the assassin, who fired at him with a revolver. The bullet missed Mr. Bingham, and passed through the arm of the servant girl. He at once jumped off the car, pursued the assassin across a field, and caught hold of the cloak which enveloped him. His face was blackened, and Mr. Bingham could not identify him. The man aban- doned the cloak and succeeded in effecting his escape. Mr. Bingham then returned to the croydon and drove rapidly to Belmullet, where he informed the police. No arrests have yet been made. The wound in the girl's arm is not dangerous.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

BARROW-IN-FURNESS, MONDAY.—There is still an upward tendency observable in the hematite pig-iron trade. The demand is well maintained from all quarters, and the output of the furnaces is all going into delivery to the extent of about 30,000 tons per week. Stocks are also being reduced. Prices are firmer, and 61s. ed. to 625. is asked for No. 1 Bessemer, with Clls. for average parcels at works, while No. 3 forge is qftoted at 595. per ton. The steel trade is very busy and new business is offering, especially on foreign account, while prices continue to show an upward movement. Shipbuilders are receiving new inquiries from all quarters, as also are enginneers. Iron ore and coal are in improved request. Shipping is fairly employed. LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAY:A healthier tone is apparent throughout the coal trade of this district, and with the com- mencement of the month there has been an advance in prices which, so far as round coals are concerned, has been pretty general all through Lancashire. Up to the present, however' the upward movement has been comparatively only limited in extent. In the Manchester district the advance has not gone beyond 101. per ton upon the delivery rate for coal supplied to household consumers, fuel delivered to works and the pit prices remaining without change. Frotn the West Lancashire collieries notices have as a rule beed- sent out announcing advances upon the pit prices ranging from ed. per ton upon the inferior sorts of round coal up to le. per ton upon the better qualities, and in other districts there has been a more or less similar upward movement. The average prices now being quoted for round coal at the pit mouth are about as under : Best coal, 9s. ed. per ton ; second qualities, 7s. to 7s. 6d.; and common round coals, be. 9d. to 6s. 3d. per ton. It is as yet too early to ascertain what effect this upward movement will have upon the de- mand. So far, although the exceptional briskness which characterised the demand last month has scarcely been maintained, all classes of round coal have been moving off freely at the advanced rates, and in many / cases there are still considerable arrears of on- executed orders yet to be worked off. Engine classes of fuel remain without alteration, any upward movement in these being checked by the increased produc- tion of slack and the large quantities of fuel thrown upon the market by the recent stoppage of the mills. There is, however, still a fairly steady demand, and prices are all well maintained, good burgy fetching 4s 3d. to 4s. 9d. and good slack 3s. 31. to 3s 9d. per ton at the pit mouth. In the iron trade although there is only a_comparatively limited amount of buying going on so far as consumers in this district are concerned, the market continues to move upwards, and makers are firm at their advanced rates. A moderate amount of business has been done in Lancashire pig iron both for foundry and forge purposes, at from 465. 6d. for forge, to 475. ed., less 2i per cent, for foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester ; and these are now the minimum prices quoted by local makers, whilst at these figures they still , decline to sell beyond the end of the year. For outside brands coming into this district higher prices generally are being asked, and some brands are now being altogether with- drawn from this market. Sales of Lincolnshire forge iron are

Lord Erskine declared in a large party, in which Lady E. ant Mr. S. were present, that "a wife was only a tin canister tisd to one's tail," upon which Saericlan presented Lady Eeskine with these lines:— Lord Erskine, 'at woman presuming to rail, Calls a wife "a ti,a canister tied to one's tail:" And fair Lady Anne, while the subject he carries on, Seems hurt at his Lordship's degrading comparison. AN Imola COSTITME.—The people of Itawa shave their hair back from the brow, tormd which they tie a band of beads with much tastefulnees and effect. They wear enor- mous cylinders of wood in the lobes of their ears, and copper pins sticking through their lips. Their dress consists almost entirely of a flap of skin behind. The absence of this would be considered highly imroper, although, to me, its Bole use appears to be as a protective from damp when sittieg on the wet ground.—Joseph Thomson, in Good Words. Tian FIRST, SECOND, AND TIIIRD PERSONS.—In a trial before Baron Martin, a witness was called who interlardod hie account of a conversation he had heard with so many "says I" and "says he," that he was hardly intelligible. The counsel, failing to make the witness comprehend the form in which he was wanted to make his statement, the Court took him in hand, with the following result —"My man, tell us exactly what passed." "Yes, my lord, certainly. I said that I would not have the pig." "Well, what was his answer?" "He said that he had been keeping the pig for me, and that he—" "No, no, he did not say that—he could not have said it. IFle spoke in the first person.' "No, I was the first person that spoke my lord." "I mean this— don't bring in the third person—repeat his exact words." "There w-as no third person my lord, only him and me." "Look here, my good fellow—he did not say be had been keeping the pig—he said, 'I have been keeping it.'" "I , assure you, my lord, there was no mention of your lordships name at all. We are on two different stories, my lord. There was no third person; and if anything had been said about your lordship, I must biave heard it" TEE CAMELLIA.—The history Of the camellia is not gene- -rally known. We take the following account of its origin ' from the Debats :—lt was in the month of December, 1739, tla a Maria Theresa entered the chamber of the melancholy King Ferdinand VI. of Spain, bearing in her hand a flower of immaculate whiteness which she presorted to her hus- band. "It is a beautiful flower, but a scentless One," he languidly remarked, taking it from her and placing it in a china vase. The Queen replied that it had been found in the Philippine Islands by a Jesuit missionary who had just returned home, bringing with him a tree a metre and a half In height, upon one branch of which were two snowy flizrvers. The missionary who had discovered it was named Carnelli, and the flower was christened after him camellia. Bat although introduced into Spain in 1739, the tree of Pare Camelli remained for a long time comparatively un- known. Marie Antoinette herself failed to obtain a root of the spotless white camellia to ornament her hothouses and gardens at Trianon; indeed, it was only towards 1799 that the flower brought over by the Jesuit missionary sixty years before became obtainable by any bat Royal personages in France. Fisn as FOOD—Pound for pound fish is fully as nutriti- ous as butchers' meat. It may not seem so satisfying, but that is because the sense of satisfaction which we experience In eating is the result of supplying the stomach with food and in no direct or immediate way related to the mourish- went of the organism as a whole. Very few of the solid substances we eat are digested, even so far as the stomach it concerned, in less than an hoar, and nutrition cannot com- mence until digestion has proceeded for some time. It fol- lows that the feeling of satisfaaion produced by solid food during a meal must be due to the appeasing of those crav- ings which are set up in the stomach rather than the supply Of the needs of the system. Inasmuch as butchers' meat is less easy of digestion than fish, and it gives the stomach more to do, it as easy to see why it seems, at the moment, more satisfying. Looking to the ultimate purposes of nutrition.fih is the better kind of food, it is more readily and comple; ely reduced in the stomach, and it nourishes the - organism more thoroughly, and with less physical incon- venience. than the flesh of warm-blooded animals. Entails are thought necessary for maintaining this exclusive privilege of the nobility to the great offices and honours of their country, and that order having usurped one unjust advantage over the rest of their fellow-Citizens lest their poverty should render it ridiculous, it is thought reasonalee that they should have another. It is evident from the foregoing that Adam Smith lived before his time, for notwithstanding the unsparing and well- founded denunciation given above, and which was written 100 years ago, the system of life estates exists to such an extent at the present time in the United Kingdom, that ac- cording to Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., more than 52,000,000 acres are settled on this plan. The nominal owners of these large estates, which constitute such a peculiar feature of the British Land System, are not the real or actual owners. Mr. Arnold writes" When the House of Lords was crowded prior to the most memorable division on the Irish Land Bill (i.e., in 1870), a friend who was with me, looked down upon the august assembly and whispered 'And these men own three-fourths of the United Kingdom.' 'Would to God they did,' I answered 'I doubt if there are a dozen men there who have an acre of land that they can call their own.' Their families, not they, are the owners of the king- dom. Years ago, in their hot youth, when they were neither statesmen nor practical agriculturiete as many of them are now, they signed away to their sons, and failing them, to a long line of brothers and cousins—even when they had not thought of marriage,—the freehold of their inheritance." Some reader to whom all this may be fresh will naturally ask how this is managed? In order to be strictly accurate we will take the evidence of Mr. Joshua Williams, Q.C., in his "Real and Personal Property," an acknowledged text book for all legal students. He shows that in families where the estates are kept up from one generation to another settlements are made every few years for this purpose; thus in the event of a marriage a life estate merely is given to the husband; the wife has an allowance for pin money during the marriage, and a rent charge or annuity by way of jointure for life, in case she ehould survive her husband. Subject to this jointure and to the payment of such sums as may be agreed upon for the portions of the daughters and younger sons of the marriage the eldest son who may be born of the marriage is made by the settlement tenant in tail. In case of his decease without issue, it is provided that the second son and then the third should in like manner be tenant in tail, and so on to the others, and in default of sons the estate is usually given to the daughters. By this means the estate is tied up till some tenant in tail attains the age of twenty-one years, when he is able, with the consent of the father, who is tenant for life, to bar the entail with all the remainders. Dominion is thus again acquired over-the property, which dominion is usually exercised in a re-settle- ment on the next generation, and thus the property is pre- served in the family. The same routine is adopted in creating an entailed estate under a will. Sometimes, however, the plan known as an estate in tail male is adopted, which cannot descend to any but males, and mile descendants of males, and cannot conse- quently belong to anyone who does not bear the surname of his ancestor, from whom he inherited. As an instance of this, there is now a baronet resident in the Midland Counties of England, the life tenant of a very large estate, who has I eight or nine daughters, but no eon; and the result is that on his death the whole property will go intact to a very distant relation, who, however, is the next life tenant under this wonderful arrangement, leaving this numerous .family of daughters without a farthing's worth of the property. The uninitiated may also very naturally ask—Why does the "tenant in tail," when, he comes of age, consent to a re-settlement or locking-up of the estate. An eminent legal authority, Lord St. Leonards, in a few words, not only describes how, it is done but why It is done. "Where there are younger children,tlielather is always anxious to have the estate re-settled on them and their issue in case of failure of issue of the first son. This he cannot accomplish without the concurrence of the son ; and as the son, upon his establishment in life in his father's lifetime, requires an immediate provision, the father generally secures to him a provision during their joint lives, ae a consideration for the re-settlement of the estate in remainder upon the youngest sons. Thus are estates quickly re-settled." Now, what is the position of the reputed owner of one of these large estates, settled as above described. It is quite possible, and in fact it is very common indeed, for these_ large estates to he heavily mortgaged. Re has, therefore,! to pay the mortgage interest out of the rents. His prede- cessor widow is entitled to a jointure of a considerable sum; per annum out of the rental. Sometimes there are a couple or more widows, as annuitants seem to have a faculty for longevity. In addition to these charges, by the settlement under which the present owner inherits, the I estate was charged with portions or annuities for his I younger brothers and sisters, the result being that his nominal rent roll of, say, £lO,OOO per annum, is whittled down to perhapa_a couple of thousands, with which he is to keep up a respectable appearance in the county, and occupy the family mansion, as it would be such a disgrace to let it. There is many a landowner reputed wealthy by those who are not in the secret, who has a hard struggle to make ends meet, in this mixture of poverty and gentility. But, no matter, not one square yard of land can be sold until pos- sibly an unborn heir attains majority. Lana so circumstanced cannot be said to have an owner —it is "no man's" land—or, as one writer has put it, there is one owner in the tomb and there may be another in the womb, and the man in possession is merely a stop-gap be- tween the deed and the unborn. It is obvious that a landowner so situated cannot improve his estate or assist his tenants by an abatement of rent in bad seasons, and the effect generally of such a state of things will be dealt with in subsequent articles. Moreover,_ in some cases, where the next heir is a nephew or cousin, or more distant relation, the owner of the estate is naturally averse to spend his income in effecting permanent im- provements, of which his successor, and not he, will reap the benefit. , There is, however, another question to be considered in eennection with these life estates, having special reference to good feeling.in families. From his very cradle the eldest son is known as the heir presumptive to the family estates. As Mr. John Bright said more than 20 years ago, speaking of a young Peer," He is one of those fortunate individuals I who are described as coming into the world with a silver spoon in their mouths '." or, to use the more polished and elab qate phraseology of the poet, it may be said of him— Fortune came smiling to his youth and wood It, And purpling greatness met his ripened years. When he is a boy, among his brothers and sisters he is pre- eminent ; he is the eldest son ; he will be " My Lord ;" this fine mansion, this beautiful park,these countless farms, this vast political influence will one day centre on tie's inno- cent boy. The servants know it, and pay him greater de- ference on account of it. Be grows up and goes to school and college; his future position is known; he has no great incitement to work hard, because whatever he does it is very difficult for him to improve his fortune in any way. When he leaves College he has a secure position ready made for him, and there seems to be no reason why he should follow ardently any of those occupations which make men great among their fellow-men. There have been exceptions, and striking exceptions, to the above, but the description is too unfortunately true of a great number of cases; and it is too true also that the effect of the system has been, as one writer has said, "to estab- lish in the centre of each family a magnificently fed and co'oured drone, the incarnation of wealth and social dignity, the visible end of human endeavour, a sort of great Final cause imminent in every family." It is obvious, too that the eldest son, so foreordained to position and wealth', must find himself in a very great rnea- su-e independent of his father, and this, together with the inequality between him and his brothers and sisters, weakens Paternal authority. Bourgault-Dacoudray, one of the professors at the Conservatoire of Paris, is a present making a tour through Brittany for the purpose of obtaining from the peasants as complete a collection as possible of Breton melodies. The German Emperor has recently conferred the great Prussian gold medal for art and science upon Mr. George Matthey, F.R.S., of the well-known firm of refiners in Hat- ton Garden, in recognition of his services in the interests of science. Mdlle. Skortsova, a Russian lady, having been Proposed by Prof. Magnan has been unanimously elected a membre associe of the Medico-Psychological S ciety of Paris. This lady has especially devoted herself to the treatment of nervous diseases. Mr. Darwin's new work will be published by Mr. Murray on October 10th. It is entitled "The Formation of Vege- table Mould through the Action of Worms, with Observa- tions on their Habits." It will appear in one volume, with woodcuts. Messrs. Blackwood and Sons have in the press the "Autobiography of Sir Archibald Alison," which furnishes a detailed memoir from boyhood down to within a few years of his death, and contains reminiscences of Scott, Jeffrey, Cockburn, Wilson, Lockhart, Telford, Moore, Campbell, Southey, and others. As people in the country villages have been unable to see the apertures in the wall letter-boxes after dark, Mr. Rea., the Post-office surveyor for the Eastern Counties district, has caused the apertures of the wall boxes in the neighbour- hood of Cambridge to be encircled with luminous paint. The experiment has been successful. ' No leas than ten observers are now engaged at the Obser- vatory of Paris in the completion of the catalogue of stars which was begun by Leverrier. The work is progressing at an unprecedented rate, not less than 70,000 observations having been tabulated, after having been duly reduced in a single year. Dr. Rudolph Ki.inig, of Paris, whose accoustical fame is world-wide, is about to publish in one volume, in the French language, his remarkable researches in accoustics, which have appeared at intervals in the Annalen der Physik and elsewhere during the last 15 years. The work will, we (Nature) understand, be liberally illustrated with drawings of the newer and more important pieces of appar- atus which Dr. Konig has invented. The Louvre is likely to be enriched by the acquisition of Babylonian antiquities from Tello, collected by M. de Sarzec while at Bussorah. Among the objects are several large statues in diorite, some covered with inscriptions of the Babylonian nionarch Gmdea of Zergul, rt.c. 2280, and one of an architect. Besides these are several remarkable cylinders and terra-cotta tablets. They have been valued at 130,000 f. TEE SEVERN TIIXNEL.—On Tuesday night the headings that are being driven under the Severn between Monmouth- shire and Gloucestershire for the Great Western Railway Tunnel, met midway under the river, having been so accu- rately planned that the lines were found to be only three inches out. The headings, which are over two miles long, have taken seven years in opening through. They are now seven feet high by seven wide, and have to be considerably enlarged. No BEES, NO BERRIES !—The common flowering currant is much frequented by bees as well as by other species of in-ects, and usually produces abundance of berries. The writer, last summer, carefully with muslin several of the newly opened blossoms of this bush. This had the effect of preventing any insect gaining access to these flowers, and it was observed that they continued fresh and bright long after all their unprotected neighbours had withered, and that whilst an abundant crop of berries was produced on all the exposed branches which had been visited by bees, not a single berry appeared on any of those from which insects had been excluded by the maslin.—Professor A. S. Wilson, In " Good Words," for October. An interesting exhibition of domestic industries and needlework is now open at Bada-Pesth, promoted by Count Eugen Zichy, and under the patronage of several ladies' associations. According to a correspondent of the Scotsman who frequently sends interesting letters from Hungary,about 40,000 objects have been contributed, including gorgeous rugs and curtains, coloured and golden embroideries, fancy work of every description painted porcelain and curious pottery, linen and lace, and ancient fabrics. Especially pro- minent are the Sclavonic-Hungarian, Roumanian, and Bul- garian rugs, the colours and patterns of which show a dis- tinctly Oriental character. These can be purchased for from £4 to £lO. They are woven by the women as domestic in- dustries. Attention is also drawn to the so-called "Service linen," which is light, transparent, and yet wonderfully durable. Fourteen different sorts are produced, and the price ranges from one franc to three francs per mkre. TIER Liter Mos..—Naturalists have for a long time been seeking after, and hoping to discover and pounce upon, a moa, one of the tribe of wingless birds. Their remains and skeletons have been found, a strange, vast, bulky bird. Mr. Wallis Mantell explored every possible cranny of New Zea- land in search of the creature and only heard of it in tra- dition. But in 1863 a camp Of gold seekers appears to have I been startled while sitting in the twilight round their log fire, as one of them exclaimed, "Look at that! What's that rises above us? There's some one there !" They looked, and beheld through the dusk a truly enormous bird. It teemed to be arrested by the glare of the camp fire; its heed was turned towards the light, and after a minute or two, it rose and stalked off. In height it appeared to be about seven feet, without reckoning the head or the neck. The next morning all the men set off in pursuit of their remarkable visitor. They were soon upon its track, and fol- lowed for a long way, but never found the creature itself; each footprint showed the mark of three claws, with, it is said, an interval of 12 inches between each—then a pad, and behind that the mark of a spur. A gentleman in New Zealand, as soon as he heard this report, offered £5OO for a moa, for such it was believed to be, dead or alive. Again the gold seekers started on their search for the wingless bird; they penetrated into the recesses of Melville Island, the region of the gigantic lizard, which is said to prey on men; but the object of their search they found not. —Sunday at

Home. TBLEPHONES AND LIGHTNIN6.—At the sitting of the Electrical Congress in Paris on Sunday, a discussion arose on the subject of the danger of telephones during discharges of lightning. M. Latigue and Professor Helmholtz stated their belief in the necessity of having some form of light- ning protector. Mr. Preece said that in the British Post. office it had been decided to discontinue the use of such , precautions—first, because the thin coil of w, the in- strument may be looked upon to a certain ea: sale- guard; secondly, because a damaged coil costq e, And is easily replaced; and thirdly, because a long el is tu'9 is used with the Gower-Bell telephone for listening with, ~nd this prevents the discharge from passing through the bo,ty. For these reasons the Post-office authorities believe that lightning protectors, though effective, are unnecessary. M. Bede expressed considerable surprise at this decision of the Post-office authorities. Professor Ayrton &pressed a belief that there are two kinds of lightning effects. The first is that of a violent, instantaneous shock; the second is that of a strong current sufficient to destroy an instrument. M. Wde stated that in the extensive system of wires under the Belgian Government, in the long time during which they had been at work, the ordinary lightning protectors had always been efficacious in protesting the instruments, and not a single case of the destruction of instruments by the currents spoken of by Professor Ayrten had ever occurred. It was unanimously agreed that it was desirable to state the dimensions of wires in millimetres and fraction of a milli- metre, in order to bring uniformity into the labours of dif- ferent nationalities. The third section has had long dis- cussions on the subject of photometry and standards of light. , It has been settled that for the present the different nations shall continue to use their own standards. A recommenda- -1 tion has bean made to appoint an International Commission to settle a standard of light.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN, M.P. REFUSED A VOTE FOR BIR- ,UNGITAIII.—At the Birmingham Revision Court, on Monday, the Conservatives objected to the retention on the voting list of the name of the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, President of the Board of Trade, who was rated as trustee for premises occupied as the Children's Huspital. The Con- servative agent urged that Mr. Chamberlain was not entitled to a vote, as he was neither the owner, the tenant, nor the occupier of the premises. The Liberal agent did not contest the objection, and as Mr. Chamberlain had no other qualification his name was struck off the voting list, the re- vising barrister (Mr. J. J. Heathsaint) expressing some sur- prise, and remarking that. he could not help it. It was announced that the notice of objectien was forwarded by post to Mr. Chamberlain's place of abode as described en the voting list, but was returned with-, the postal endorsement, "Not to be found." A remarkable scene was witnessed on Monday at an ex- traordinary meeting of the St. Pancras Board of Guardians. The Board had been summoned to consider the advisable- ness of memoralising the Home Secretary to release from , prison a woman named Annie Purchase, who had been sen- tenced by Mr. Hosack, a metropolitan police magistrate, to ' a month's imprisonment for stealing a suit of workhouse clothing. The sympathy of the public has been strongly 1 excited in favour of the poor woman, and it is as clear as anything can be that the sentence ought never to have been passed. It is alleged against Mr. Hosack that he refused peremptorily to allow the mother of Annie Purchase to give evidence, although, as it now appears, she could have shown that the prosecution was the result of a misunderstanding. Curiously enough, the two members of the Beard ol Guardians who expressed satisfaction with the sentence were a clergyman and a lady—the Rev. Mr. Sutton and Miss Davenport Hill. The reverend gentleman was hooted and hustled by a crowd of indignant ratepayers, and Miss Hill was warned that her tenure of (Ace would probably be cut short at the next election. There were two forcible sales for tithes made last week at Plumpton, a parish in Cumberland. The squire and church warden af the parish both refused to pay the tithe charge, on the ground of its being illegally taken completely away from their own parish. An oat stack, mowing machine, and two pigs were put up for sale, in the presence of over two hundred farmers, who, notwithstanding the busy harvesting time, assembled to mark their disapprobation of the action of the Bishop and Ecclesiastical Commissioners. The goods were bought in by friendly purchasers, and after some vigorous speeches a series of resolutions were passed unani. monsly, amid great cheering. . Most of these related to the circumstances which had given rise to the sale, but the last, two were as follow:—" That th, change in the price of cereals which has taken place since 1836 makes it unfair to farmers to have the septennial average struck on the basis then made." "That the £lBO,OOO a year assigned for the maintenance of the cathedral system is no longer required for that purpose, and should be appropriated to two of the other objects for which those endowments were originally given, viz, the education of the young and the relief of the poor." _

Talk is cheap, but a good example costs something. If the fruit on the extremity be saved it will make a larger and later variety. Hawick tup fair was held set Hawick last week. T here were sold by Messrs. INSECT INJURIES.,—MiSS Ormereo. who has so long laboured in the collection -trution of information on this subject, and who biei .—i„ceeded in an altogether unexampled way in enlist-I,w ,in bluing the labour of intelligent correspondenT-.i. .a. parts of the country, has just issued her annual circular asking for notes regarding methods of prevention of insect injury of which any ex- perience has been realised during the past season, in order that such methods may be fully reported in her next report. She includes all insects that are commonly injurious to a serious extent to our food crops, forest trees, and hardy fruit; and we gladly adopt the following sentence from her letters as our own:—" The most serious attack of the season has been that of the turnip fly (flea beetle), arid it would be of important benefit to the country at large if information was gathered together bearing on means found of practical service ln prevention or remedy of this scourge of the turnip crops." Information is asked for any time before the beginning of November. The address is Boaster Lodge, I near Isleworth. DR. The finished-iron trade continues active; good shipping inquiries are still coming in, and in the home demand an improvement •is apparent. Makers, who are mostly well sold for the present, are decidedly stiffer in their prices and for bars, delivered equal to Manchester, £8 10s. to £6 15s. per ton is now being asked. Local tool makers are receiving a good many foreign orders, and amongst loco- motive builders there is an increased volume of trade stirring for export, although still at low prices. The Ince Hall rolling mills have just been purchased from the liquidator of the estate for the sum of £12,500 by the Wigan Rolling Mills Company, who will now, in addition, restart their own works, which have been stopped for a considerable time I past.

Alderman BtIRGE-S;: Then you know nothing. Alderman HantasoN : Don't you know anythink ? Alderman Briarms : Tdo not. (Laughter.) Councillor MONKS said it was a shame to make this a personal matter, and it showed a want of courtesy on the part of Alderman Burgess. It was very unbecoming at any rate. The hospital expenditure was adding much to the rates of the Borough, and crippling other committees; take, for rnstance, the Paving and Sewerage Committee. He ob- jected to the time of the medical officer being taken up alto- gether with attention to the hospital. His duty was rather to seek out the causes which were producing this disease rather than to pay attention to the cure—(hear, hear,)—and it would be better econonay if they left the parents to nurse their children at home th,in at the hospital. Councillor JEANS Said Ile had much pleasure in seconding the resolution. It was quite exhilarating to see the member stand up and oppose his own committee. Ha had obst:sed

Councillor CROSFIELD Will you tell us where to stop? Alderman lioLmEs said the expense had been incurred, and they would have to pay for it; but to express his dis- approval of the expenditure incurred on hospital account' he felt disposed to second Councillor Monks' amendment. They were told at the outset that the hospital was to cost .£3OO or £4OO a year, but they had in the Sanitary Ccim- mittee's estimates two items amounting to £BlO, to which would have to be added £4OO, interest on the sinking fund, and instead of the hospital costing £5OO a year, the expen- diture would be £1,200 for the half-year. lie• believed that a large portion of this expenditure arose from the resolution passed a few months ago that persons c3uld go to the hos- pital free of charge, and that the charge should be paid out of the rates. If the inhabitants of Warrington found that they could have their children better treated in the hospital free. of charge, there was great risk of [their allowing them to remain longer than was absolutely necessary. The DEERTY MAYOR said he intended to support the minutes of the committee. There might come a time when some decisive steps of this kind might have to be taken, and if they crippled the committee and refused to support their recommendation, they wouldnot be able to purchase what was wanted until there was disease in the town and they were unable to check it. He was not sorry that the discussion had taken PI ice, because he felt that there were many per- sons taken to the hospital that would be qulta as well treated at home. (Hear, hear.)

Alderman BURGESS : You can't, I tell you. 1 can tell you you don't know what you are talking about. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor Monks, he proceeded, had made assertions he knew he could not substantiate. He challenged Coun- cillor Monks in the room and he had failed to substantiate them. Referring to Alderman Harrison's suggestion, he said they had only had summer experience of the tents as yet. In the hospital patients were received at any period of the year. The largest expenditure was on the administra- tive ward, which they would have even if they had only tents. They must also have had a mortuary, disinfecting stove, Sze., besides the tents. At smile future time he might have something to say about the cause of the disease. He might show there was a cause which W9B supposed to have produced the present condition of things, but it would not gratify Councillor Dixon very much if he were to refer to it, and as he had a great deal of consideration for that gentleman lie would not go into it. (Laughter.) He did not think the Committee had acted in an arbitrary manner in any case. During the whole of the year the Committee had had nothing to do with what was going on. The Medi- cal Officer had done all the work, and although there had been 159 patients this year, it was only necessary to apply for a magisterial order for removal in four cases. All the rest bad voluntarily gone into the Institution. The Medi- cal Officer believed it necessary that isolation should be carried out by removal, and if his application for removal was refused, he went about his business. He was grateful to Councillor Litton for his observations, but he thought he mistook the mission of the Medical Officer. It could not be to his interest to get people into the hospital. He had a yearly salary, and if be had not a single patient in it he would receive just the same amount of money. (Hear, hear.) Did they think Mr. Gornall was such a consummate ass as to desire to have 150 patients to attend to? (Loud laugh- ter.) Mr. Gornall did not want to work for nothing, but he tried conscientiously to discharge the duty he had under- taken. It reflected infinite credit on him that, whilst he was not paid an extra penny for all his labour, be did not grumble to undertake work which 19 out of every 20 would shirk.—[Councillor CROSFIELR : That is very true.]—He thought it would have beets very much better if Councllor Monks had not said some of the things he had said. The MAYOR: We have forgotten them.

, Alderman BURGESS: We may as well have it out plainly. In the profound speech of Mr. Jeans—in fact, so profound was it some of us began to think we were listening to a lawyer—(laughter)— The MAYOR: I hope we shall have no personal allusions Alderman BURGESS: The whole thing was personal from beginning to. end. ("No, no.") The MAYOR: This has been a very fair discussion so fir. Alderman BURGESS: I have not the slightest hL ction to it. Let us know where we are. If there are p, bandied about let us get at the bottom of them. I uaintair there is no ground for the assertions. I do not think it necessary to to disease the matter after what the Town Clerk

II has said; and the respect we owe to him requires of U 3 that we should take his g.uidanee. it is immaterial what courre we take. I know tiffs; no such resolution as the silly thing before us now—(laughter)—can override the Act of Parlia- ment. All the resolutions the Council c“uld adopt wr./,1 affect it in the slightest degree. Councilfor JEANS: That is quite true. Alderman BURGESS: Who said so? I am afraid it is wrong. (Laughter.) I say, sir, we should accept the guid- ance of the Town Clerk. Councillor Burros said that inasmuch as they had had the opinion of the Town Clerk that they could not act upon the-resolution, if passed, he was in a difficulty how to act. But there was such a strong feeling in the town against the forcible removal of patients to the infectious diseases hospi- tal that he considered any member perfectly justified in bringing the matter forward that night and Endeavouring to obtain its rectification. When they obtained that Act of Parliament It was understood that it was only to be carried out in extreme cases. It was intended to deal with the cases in back parts of the town, where they had no proper food, medical attendance, or isolation. They had now 60 patients in the hospital, who cost about £1 each per week, which amounted to about £3,000 a year. He should support the resolution whether it had any effect or not. Councillor MONKS supported the resolution because the Council had been forced into this position against its own wish. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing they could do— shut the hospital up altogether. Alderman BURGESS: Can you? . Councillor MONKS: I believe we can. Alderman BURGESS: I think not.

Couucillor MoNEs said as a matter of fact the Medical Officer went into court by their authority. He supposed it was with the authority of the committee, although no resolutions were passed by the committee giving such authority. [Alder- man BURGESS: Certainly not.] As this was a somewhat personal matter he did not wish to say much about it, but he contended very strongly that many cases were removed to the hospital that would be far better treated at home. Alderman HARRISON could not understand what good they would gain by the discussion. He bad the greatest sympathy with a great deal that Councillor Burgess had said, but they might ait there two hours for a perfectly use- less purpose.

1 be MAYOR said the Sanitary Committee went by the Act of Parliament, and it appeared to him thkt this resolution would have no effect. The Corporation gave to the Sanitary Committee power to give the Medical Officer authority to do what he liked. Did they think he carried his orders too far?

Alderman HARRISON would go furthers and suggest that the next course to take, as it appeared to him, would be to discharge the Medical Officer. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR: If the Council thinks he is not a proper man, get another. At the same time, I think we are bound to take the opinion of the Town Clerk as to the law of the question, and that is that the Sanitary Committee are acting according to law. Councillor GREENING would be pleased if Councillor Burgess could see his way to withdraw the resolution. He quite agreed with the spirit of it, but as the Town Clerk had ruled it would be inoperative, he would take that ruling.

Councillor WALLINGTON : I believe our Medical Officer is as competent as any other medical man to decide when a house is sufficiently isolated. (Hear, hear.) It seems a very easy thing to isolate these cases, but there are very few houses in Warrington where they can be isolated. The MAYOR: I think the question is thrashed out, and I hope we shall not have it again. Alderman BURGESS: Not in your mayoralty. (Laughter.) Councillor Drzox could not say whether the Town Clerk was right or wrong—(loud laughter)—but Mr. Johnson told him he would have liked his case taken to the Queen's Bench. He said the Town Clerk was wrong in his interpretation of the Act.
The MAYOR: It is a mere matter of opinion. Was he a lawyer? ... _
douncillor DIXON: No. He was a person who was taken before the magistrates, and in that case you could not remove.

Councillor Fitaxcontia thought it must be clearly seen that there was a grievance, and it would be done away with if the Chairman of the Committee and the Medical Officer would use a little more moderation. He knew of cases of fever that had actually been concealed from all medical mc •-r. Alderman Burgess had said that only four cases were tot gh t before.the magistrates, and that all the other patients w.• ,to the hospital voluntarily. He believed Alderman eas was convinced he was right in making the state- n but he had seen disgraceful scenes in the streets. ..n had almost fought in Church-street with the officials o' • Coporation before they would allow their children to be r. --ed. lliat did not much look like people sending'. Arily to the hospital. If more moderation was used the i)le would only be too glad to go to the hospital. L rman BurtaEss: That appears to be a charge against mys ; and I must, therefore, says wordpr two. Let this C,,ancil thoroughly understand, if it has 'not done so I before, that of the 150 cases that have gone into the hospital this year, none have appeared before the committee in any way or shape. The Cnairman of the gommittee has had no more to do with the removal sthan Councillor Jeans has, not a bit more.

, Councillor JEANS: Who has removed them? I Alderman BURGESS: What's drat to you! (Cries of "Oh, ob.") - 1 Councillor Naos : My word, but i hat's outrageous! Alderman BURGESS: I may say I mean it to be! I am not going to be questioned by Mr. Jeans! The MAYOR: That is rather too warm. Alderman BURGESS: Never mind! I say the Chairman of Ike Committee bad nothing whatever to do with the re- moval of a single case to the hospital, nor has any member of the committee. It is a duty that appertains entirely to the Medical Officer of Health, who has to discharge that duty in a moderate, straightforward and proper manner, and if you think he has done what you, cowardly as you are, suggest that he has done . (Cries of "Oh, ch.") Alderman HOLMES : Really, Mr. Mayor, this is too bad. (Hear, hear, and " Chair, chair.") . Alderman BURGESS: Never mind. The MAYOR: Mr. Burgess, I must say that kind of lan- guage is much to be deprecated. Alderman BURGESS: It may be; but never mind, I mean to have my say out here. lam not going to write in news- papers, I can tell you ! Dismiss that oteoxious gentleman; take upon yourselves to do it, and then see what you have done for yourselves and your town. DO- you think you can, by your noble will, dismiss a gentleman who has done no wrong? You will have to show that he has done wrong before you will have justification for his dismissal. Take and dismiss him. If you have not the manliness to support your opinions, leave the man in the proper discharge of his , ditty. I think he has discharged his duty in an efficient 1 and moderate manner, and while you make these accusations there is not a man among you can prove any one of the assertions. (Hear, hear.) I tell you again that your Medical Officer is very much too good for you. Alderman Hommts : I hope Mr. Burgess will withdraw this resolution, because it would be absurd of the Council to go in favour of the resolution after the Town Clerk has so explicitly stated •it would be entirely inoperative. I hope the Council will not get into the same difficulty they got Into some eighteen months ago, when the Sanitary Com- mittee, with Alderman Burgess at their head, jaroposed a resolution, and forced it through the Council, but they found it was illegal and afterwards came to the Council and passed a resolation to rescind it.
The MAYOR ! I think after what the Town Clerk has told Mr. Councillor Burgess it would be advisable for him to withdraw the resolution.

Councillor BURGESS said he felt it was really necessary in 1 the present state of things that an expression of opinion should be given by the Council. He did not wish to ques- tion the Town Clerk's decision, although he had spoken to four or five lawyers who held different opinions. The ques- tion was—were they compelled to remove these cases or were they not? If not, he wanted to instruct whoever took proceed- ings that in certain cases they should not be taken. The resolution was then put when there voted for it:— Councillors Monks, Caldwell, Brown, Whittle, Francomb, , Jeans, Burgess, Woolfall, Dixon, and Sutton • and against it Aldermen Burgess and Holmes, Councill'or Wallington I and the Mayor. •

FINANCE OOMNFITEN.-THE BATES.

-- This committee recommended that the total estimated ex- penditure of £4,082 Os. 3d. on the borough rate account for the half-year commencing the 29th September, and on tie improvement rate account of £9,814 ss. ld , and on the general sewers rate at.count of £957 9s. 2d. for the same period, be approved. The minutes were approved. Alderman HOLMES moved that the estimate for the borough rate, amounting to the sum of £4,082 Os. 3d., as re- commended to the Council by the Finance Committee, be confirmed, and that the Mayor issue warrants to the over- seers of the townships of Warrington, Latchford, and Thel- wall forthe payment within thirty days of the respective proportions to be contributed by each of the said townships; that the estimate for an improvement rate, as recommended, be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee make an improvement rate accordingly at one shilling and ninepence in the pound; that the estimate for the sewer rate, as re- commended, be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee make a sewers rate accordingly at twopence in the pound. The motions were seconded and carried. RE-ARRANGEMENT OF VOTER'S LISTS. _

The MAYOR proposed the following resolution:—'That the Council, as the Local Authority under the Parliamentary and Municipal Registration Act, 1878, do direct that in copying and printing divisions 1 and 2 for the parliament. ary register, and divisions 1 and 3 for the burgess roll of any revised list made out in divisions under the said Act, the two divisions in each set shall be combined and be arranged according to convenience for use in parts for poll. ing districts or wards, and where the polling districts and wards are not conterminous in such manner that the parts may be conveniently put together, to serve either as Polling districts or ward lists, and the names of the wards and polling districts shall be distinguished bv a number accord. ing to the parts, and be arranged so that One print or edition of division Imay be available for both sets." He said they had formerly three books; the first hook contained the burs gess list and also the:aprliamentary list within the borough. The second list contained the parliamentary voters outside the borough but in the parliamentary district. The third was a list of all women voters on the burgess roll. It was thought that by putting them in two parts they would gave about half the printing, whilst the lists would be more con- venient for reference.
The DEPUTY Meson seconded the motion, which tr ts carried.

COST OF THE nEvisow. The following resolution, moved by Alderman KEAN, and seconded by Councillor Surrox, was carried unanimously: —" That the Council hereby allows the account of expenses amounting £lO7 Sc. 11d., chargeable in connection with the revising and printing of the lists of parliamentary voters, and hereby certifies to the Town Clerk as required by the 6th Viet., c. 18, s. 55, that the total sum allowed by this Council in respect of the said expenses is £lO7 Ss. 11d. And further that the sum to be paid by and as the contri- bution of each of the several townships within the borough towards defraying the same ia as follows :—Warrington, £B6 Bs.; Latchford, £lO 14s. 10d.; Thelwall, is. id."
