div.head: 1 REMOVAL OP INFECTIOUS CASES.
div.p: 1 REMOVAL OP INFECTIOUS CASES.

WARN DISCUSSION. At a meeting of the Sanitary Committee, held on the 2nd September, the Medical Officer reported that further accommodation was required in the hospital to meet the daily occurring cases of ecarlet fever, and the committee resolved that a suitable eight bed tent be purchased trona Messrs. Pigott Brothers, of London, and that all necessary fittings and furniture be provided. On the 7th September it was recommended that Mr. Alfred Edmundson Greenhalgh • Robinson, R.C.V.S., be appointed a veterinary inspector under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, and 'that he be paid 10s. 6d for each professional examination, • and £2 2s. per day for his attendance and services at the half yearly fairs. A second hospital tent to hold 12 beds, manufactured by Messrs. Pigott Brothers, was also recom- mended to be purchased on the 14th September. The estimate of expenditure, amounting the £4,712 10s., for the half yearcommencing 29th September, was recommended for approval. ; Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes„, said they had had, he was sorry to say, a very considerable increase of scarlet fever. Perhaps it I would be improper to say that they were never fairly with- out it in Warrington, but the returns of the hospital showed that in January there were eleven patients, suffering I from scarlet fever and two from typhoid ; in February, four from scarlet and one from enteric fever; March, three ' scarlet fever; April, three; May, six; Jane, 12; July, 15; August, 36 ; September, 62. As would be observed from the minutes, the attention of the committee had been called to the insufficient accommodation at the hospital by the Medical Officer, who properly required the committee to give him extended accommodation to treat the patients that were being sent in. When the first application was sent in they bad 28 beds, and the number of the patients that this number was supposed to hold; but inasmuch as the patients were entirely young children, they came to the conclusion, under the advice and guidance cf the Medical Officer, that the hospital would accommodate.a larger number, and at the same time afford them sufficient room for their treatment and recovery. Again the accommondation became insuffi- dent, the wards being full. The thing that commended itself to the judgment of the committee was an hospital tent, and whilst there were only one or two members of the committee who doubted as to how far the public of War- rington would be satisfied with the treatment of cases in a tent, the experience acquired of tent treatment and accom- modation perfectly satisfied the committee that nothing could be better than that desatiption of treatment. On Friday evening, or on Saturday, the order was sent 'to London, and on Monday morning it was erected. The promptitude with which they could make such an addition was extraordinary. That tent was also filled, and a second was ordered, which was now in use. It was satisfactory to know that as they must have increased accommodation so rapidly, that they could get it at so smalls price. The cost of a tent with accommodation for 10 patients with nurses and everything included was £9l, and for an outlay of £lBO they had accommodation for about 60 patients in the hospital. Whilst they had this epidemic prevail- ing, the town was in a very healthy condition—(hear, hear)—and the death-rate for the nine months ending 30th September was only 19.2 per thousand per annum. He should be glad when he could report the epidemic had sub- sided. There was a tendency to abatement, and at this period of the year its exiinction was expected. The com- mittee, he thought, could not have acted other limn they had done, and they believed their action would meet with the approval of the CounciL Councillor CROSFIELD seconded the motion. Councillor MONrKS moved as an amendment, that the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be confirmed with the exception of the resolutions authorising the purchase of additional tent accommodation, and the recommendation that the sum of £2lO be expended on tents, cots, dm. He felt it a somewhat painful position to be at variance with his colleagues in a matter of such importance as this; but he had a right to express his' feelings in reference to the hospital extension. He also considered it best to raise the question and see what the feeling of the Council was upon it. He had been met on the committee with the statement of the chairman that the committee had the report of Dr. Ballard to carry out, and that he felt it his duty to carry it out whatever the cost might be, if he had satisfied the com- mittee and the Medical Officer that farther accommodation was required. He (the speaker) differed entirely. He thought the chairman quite right in advocating the adoption of an infectious diseases hospital. Certain plans were brought be- fore the Council and approved. To that extent • the com- mittee would be right in using the accommodation then afforded, but if any further extension of the hospital were required, the Council should be consulted. He further objected to the hospital extension on the ground that it was not necessary; the hospital accommodation they had eas quite sufficient for all the purposes of the borough. He l did not approve of the attempt to force every case, that was reported as being fever, into the hospital. (Hear, hear.) He o expressp inion—r iagshf rightof did not see why the Medical Officer should impesebis Opinion—for after all it was neither more nor less than his thine atemadatotef rthoef ftahmisflysofrot,raesfefangaminesmber against the of his own family in his own house if he were willing to make sufficient Isolation. (Hear, hear.) That sufficient isolation could be provided he was quite satisfied. He had it on the testimony of the Medical Officer himself. When Mr. Wareing hired an empty house in which were placed no one but the grandmother of the child and the child itself, the statement was made that no isolation was possible short of sending the patients to the hospital. The other night the Medical Officer reported a case offfever in Mr. Francomb's. family as not being removed, stating that Mr. Francon* had engaged an empty colt ge for a nurse and ths child, which he considered sufficiently isolated. That disposed for ever in his mind that isolation was not possible outside the hospital, and he was satisfied that where the parents, who had the undoubted right to control their own household, were prepared to incur the expense and make arrangements that theii family may have a separate room, that that was sufficient isolation. Alderman BURGESS: Do you think, Mr. Mayor, this is in accordance with the minutes or anything connected with the proceedings of the Council? Is there anything in these minutes which leads to a discussion like this? If it came on the resolution which appears at the end of the proceedings I could understand the remarks Made by , Mr. Monks. I contend that they are entirely out of place, and do not refer in the slightest degree to the question before us, and I ask you to exercise your ordin- ary prerogative. The MAYOR said Mr. Monks was arguing to show whether the items he objected to were necessary or not. (Hear, hear.) He could not see but what Mr. Monks was perfectly in order. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS: I want to know what this has to do with what we are listening to. He is attempting to prove his case by what he is saying, but he is travelling into a matter entirely foreign. The MAYOR: I think he will have to draw his remarks to a close. Alderman Timms said Mr. Monks was trying to prove that the eight-bed tent now on the ground was unnecessary. Councillor MONKS: I am entirely in your hands, Mr. , Mayor. The MAYOR: I don't know whether you have anything further to say. Alderman HARRISON:Are the tents on the ground? Alderman BURGESS: They are on the ground and full of ti pa ate.. The MAYOR: Mr. Monks has a perfect right to show why he objects. Alderman BURGESS: But let him show why, Councillor MONKS: I am sorry to be interrupted in this way. I have heard what Alderman Burgess had to say on the committee, and in a matter of this sort I consider that Alderman Burgess has as much right to his opinion as 1 I hue to mine. (Hear, hear.) Nothing more, nothing less. But if I differ from Alderman Burgess, I am not going to be put down by Alderman Burgess or anyone else. (Hear, hear.) I contend that as a member of that committee I have a right to give expression to my view. (Rear, hear). The MAYOR: Certainly, if you are in ordet. (Hear, hear). I shall stop you if you are not in order. ' Councillor MONKS: If you will tell me th,at I am not in order-- • Alderman BURGESS: I shall not hesitate to call the atEention of the Council if I think I am being unfairly treated. Councillor MONKS I object to the extension, because I think it is saddling the Corporation with a responsibility they ought not to accept, and which it was never intended they should accept. The thing runs smoothly enough so long as we have such officials as we have; but members of the committee know that that has not always been the case. I dread the consequence of having 59 or 60 patients in the Hospital under conditions that if I chose I could explain to this Council, and which would put us as members in in awkward position. Alderman BURGESS: I think— The MAYOR: I think you are wandering from the subject, and looking into the future. You are speaking of a case which has not yet arisen. If you will speak to the amend- ment that is all you have to do. Councillor MONKS: I contend I am doing so. Alderman BURGESS. Mr. Monks has now insinuated a something which it i * 8 necessary he- should thoroughly I (Hear, t something which .ear.) He has hinted a I know to be outset. untrue. I do not hesitate to say so at the Councillor MONK It is well known to members of the Committee that e two of the officials for had to dismiss more than one or or conduct which has been very unsatis- factory. I don't Burgess to explainca care to say more, and I will leave Alderman n' e about knows all aut it. Alderman littntassb. (Laughter.) I must • I don't know anything about it. not a word of truth inaatYhaa that statement far as I am concerned there is Councillor MONKS: weiratement. (Oh, oh.) know as much as I do. , I don't hesitate to say that you

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOI3ER 8, 1881
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOI3ER 8, 1881

that minutes of committees were passed without discussson, and had seal the chairman .of the Sanitary Ctimmittee put down a Member of tie committee by saying that he would not allow that member to ask questions in the Council ;and if he had anything to say he should attend the committee meetings. It was quite proper that the proceedings oi com- mittees should be discussed; they were simply delegates of the Council. With regard to the hospital, he contended that the power of the Corporation had been exercised in a moat outrageously bard manner as regarded the feeling of parents and the children who had been removed. During the four years the hospital had been in existence there had been 302 patients removed there, of whom 45 had died. That ap- peared to him wgreat proportion'of deaths. Councillor SurroN remarked that all the expense of the tents had already been incurred, and, consequently he did not see what good this discussion could do. (Hear, hear.) There was no need to test the feelings of the Council (which Mr. Monks stated was his object,) because it was apparent to everyone what their opinion of compulsory removal was. It sin:rived what a great mistake was made by Councillor Monks and several other members, in walking from the chamber when the question was previously brought forward, instead of showing their approval or disapproval of the resolution. It in a great measure gave the Sanitary 'Committee to understand that the Council were perfectly agreeable to carry out the law, that was, compulsory removal to the hospital. He did not think they ought to carry on this discussion any further, and he agreed with Alderman Burgess thus far :—that there was nothing in the minutes which permitted them to go into the question of the removal of patients to the hospital. It was simply a question whether the tents and cotsshould have been obtained. But they were obtained, and Councillor Monks, as a member of the Sanitary Committee was bound to support the resolution. (Cries of 'No, no.") Councillor MONKS: No, not at all. I opposed it on the Committee. , Councillor StrrroN asked how he would get over the difficulty. _ . _
Councillor MONKS: They have no right to get nom until confirmed by the Council. Councillor Surrox: Then you are to blame as well as other members of the Committee. _ _ _ _

Councillor 'Arrow said he went through the hospital on Friday and he was very pleased with what he saw. (Hear, hear.) Everything was done in a workman-like manner; the patients were being well cared for and well treated,' and everything seemed to be working in a very satisfactory man- ner. The two tents were a grand addition to the whole establishment. One tent was being used by the convalescent patients, and the other was being erected also for their ac- commodation. That was a most admirable movement. The tents seemed to be most comfortable, useful things, and in his opinion, when understood they would not find it neces- sary to compel people to go there, but it would be difficult to prevent them. (Laughter.) The whole matter required great forbearance on the part of the doctor. (Hear, hear.) He had an idea that the doctor was very off-handed in his manner, and if he made up his mind to go nothing would be able to stop him. But if he would exercise fair discretion, and think of the charge of maintaining the sick children be was sending there—(hear, hear)—or if he had to pay a trifle out of his own pocket, he would be more lenient with them. (Laughter.) He supported the minutes of the Committee. Councillor CROSFIELD: I think Councillor Monks is weak in his argument. (Laughter.) It is not for him or any other member of the Council to say how far fever is to go in the town, and where it is to stop. When the Difeetioue Diseases Hospital was built it was not laid down by the Council what number of patients were to go there. We in the hands of Providence, and we do not know but whar there may be 500 patients to-morrow. I want to ask Celle,. cillor Monks if we are to allow infectious tees to go rampaging through the town because we are not to go to the expense of an extra Let. It is a question of life and money. It is a question of whether the lives of the inhabitants of Warrington are worth the cost of £lBO for two tents. Councillor Sorrow: And £1 a week to keep each patient. Councillor CROSFIELD: Whatever cost the patients miy be besides. It is a question of money against life. If Coun- cillor Monks is consistent, he ought to have stated all this to the Council when it was proposed to build a hospital. The motion to build a hospital woe sanctioned, I believe, unani- mously by this Council. [Alderman BURGESS : It was.] —lt is not in the power of this or any other Council- to say how far fever shall go or where it shall stop. We are indebted to our Medical Officer of Health that heAticks as he does to his duty. There are many medical officers in this kingdom who would shirk the responsibility of such a number of patients. (Hear, hear.) But, to Mr. Gernall's credit be it said, he shirks no labour and no duty, and does not think of himself when he seeks to have patients removed to the hospital. If he were a selfish man and looked to his own comfort he would let a lot of cases go by. But he does his duty, and because he does so is be to be blamed by the Council? I trust the Council have more sense and humanity than to stop at the expendi- ture of a paltry sum of £lBO for two additicnal tents, when it is necessary in a case of this sort. Counciller WALLINGTON did not see how the Committee could have acted in any other way than they had. It seemed to him they were bound by Act of Parliament to isolate these cases. When the hospital was not large enough of course the Committee were bound to take other steps to supply the want; and, so far from finding fault with them for doing this, he thought they ought to be praised for being so energetic. If the Act of Parliament did not bind them to the course- now adopted then they might consider whether it was proper to pursue it or not; but so long as they were bound by the Act of Parliament they were doing their duty creditably. Re was sorry to see the expenses were large, but when it could not be Avoided they were obliged to submit to it. Councillor FRANCoaIs said as his name had been men- tioned in connection with the fever hospital he wished to say a few words Unfortunately, he had a little boy taken ill, and he at once sent to the regular medical attendant who said it was fever, and must be reported that night. He (Mr. Francomb) said, "Very well, I am quite willing." At the time, fortunately, they had an empty house, in which they pot the child the same night, and a nurse along with it. Although that took place something like three weeks ago yet they had never been near the child, arid the isolation had been most perfect. He did, perhaps, more than he should ,have done had he not been' a member of the Council, and he wanted to clear Mr. Gornall, or any member of .the Sanitary Committee, from blame in 'favouring him. (Hear, hear.) He had very much altered his opinion since his child had been taken ill. He had heard it said that children in the hospital as soon as they were convalescent ran about, and enjoyed themselves, and he had found that a terrible thing in his case. He had seen the little fellow at the window, and bad felt that he and his nurse.were consigned to a frightful case of imprisonment for a month or six weeks. H it were more understood there would be less talk, and also less bitter feel- ing in the town and opposition to the fever hospital than at present. This time last year he was as determined as any- body against it. It seemed to him to be dashing to pieces the most sacred rights of man, to think that tbe town officials should go and force from a mother her child. He believed the mother, was the proper person to look after the child, whether elle hain the cottage of the workingman oi in the palace of his Royal Highness the Prinoe of Wales. Last year he did not so much object to the hospital as to the expense. He than thought when a -poor man, getting, perhaps, les. or 18s. per week, was charged something like 16s. for his child when suffering from fever, it was too much; and he made it his business to go from house to i house n the evening, and found that it was so. He found 'enormous letters from the Town Clerk—letters that perhaps would not frighten any member of the Council, but they were in enormous envelopes, such as lawyers and town clerks were fond of using, and when one happened to get into the hands of a workingman he had a terrible dread of it. (Laughter.) He found also in another case that the attendant at the fever hospital had actually sent, on a post- card, a demand for so much money. He mentioned that to Alderman Burgess, who at once said it must have been an error; and he did not doubt he chastised the maa for doing it. (Laughter.) Alderman KEAN: Are these cases before us? Alderman HARRISON: Oh, dear, no. The MAYOR: Councillor Francomb, I was just going to ask, are you supporting the minutes or the amendment? Councillor Faawcoms: I think, Mr. Mayor, my speech Is a kind of mixture. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: That has been my opinion since you com- menced speaking. (Laughter.) I think myself that it will be as well to allow every gentleman latitude on this ques- tion, and let it be thrashed out to-night. It will save time hereafter, and, with your permission, I will allow Councillor Francomb to proceed. .
Councillor r Suwon : It will save time if he will keep to the minutes. We shall have another discussion on the matter directly.

Councillor FneNcomn : I will close at once. (Laughter.) Councillor Dixon. said a fortnight ago a medical gentleman assured him that he knew where there-wal a family of seven or eight children with the fever in the house • but in con- sequence of the action of the Sanitary Committee they were not reported, neither would they have any medical atten- dant He had found very few people indeed, from one end of the town to the other, who approved of the action of the Committee, and he hoped that the Council would sup. port the amendment, and put a restriction on the doings of the Sanitary Committee.

Alderman KEAN remarked that the purchase of the tents was a step in the right direction if they had not the proper means of getting ieolation. Alderman lienuisoN felt be had no alternative but to support the committee. They had built the hosp:tal, got Ithe whole thing into working condition, and in order the more effectually to accommodate the people that were already there these tents had been provided. He did not see how the Council could with any fairness attempt to pass the amendment. The tents had been purchased, and, he pre- sumed, paid for; and if the Council passed the amendment it would create a state of confusion. Judging from the laudatory way in which Alderman Burgess spoke of the tents, and the facility with which they could be obtained and put into working order, it appeared to him a mistake they ever built a hospital at all. Epidemics were of a very fitful and uncertain chart-toter; and. it was a pity the Coun- cil did not begin with providing temporary accommodation, such as these tents. If they had done that simply, and taken a piece of land for the purpose, it would have answered the purpose and have saved the Council enormous expense. But the Council had incurred it, their income was mortgaged for the payment and support of it; and he could see no wisdom in Councillor Monks' amendment on that ground and that alone. If the amendment were passed it would be perfectly inoperative. Somebody would have to pay for the tents and cots. (Hear, hear.) He hoped Councillor Monks would let the minutes pass; and when Councillor Burgess introduced his motion Councillor Monks could fire off his artillery and discuss the merits of the question in such a way as he hoped would settle thc dispute for ever. He supported the minutes.

Alderman THEwLis said the expenditure of the Sanitary Committee had been prodigious, and he was only sorry they could not go into the Longford Depot question. He should support the amendment. Councillor PLATT could not quite understand what Coon. cillor Monks meant in bring forward his amendment. He suid he thought the Council did the right thing in establish- ing the hospital, and that he did right in supporting it in the first place; and in the next breath said he did not think the Corporation ought to accept the responsibility of controlling infectious disease within the borough. But, the Council had accepted the responsibijity, and, having done so, be did not think they should draw back. They were in a position to endeavour to control infectious disease, and they would be doing very wrong in limiting the action of the committee in doing the best they could to make the hospital effectual for the purpose for which it was established. The hospital was built to check the spread of disease throughout the Borough. and to say that they should only admit a certain number of patients would be giving the disease full scope to spread desolation throughout the town. The Council could not stop at any certain point. They were bound to do theb utmost to isolate every case which could not be io operly isolated at home. He did not think it was necessary to send every case to the hospital. But these cases occurred mostly in the poor parts of the town, where, if one case was allowed to remain without isolation, the disease was very likely to spread through the district. He did not see that. if cases had been removed to the hospital unnecessarily, it would lead to the spread of the disease ; but, on the con- trary, if the error had been anywhere it had been in the other direction. If isolation had been more stringent they would not have found themselves in the position they were now in.

Councillor PERCIVAL thought that if the Council had joined the committee and (lone its utmost in the cause of isolation and seat children to the hospital, it would have prevented in a great measure this epidemic. He thought the committee ought to be supported. Councillor BURGESS said his opinion upon the subject of the Ipital was well known. It was the best way to meet the matter in a straightforward way, say what they thought, and vote for what they thought. If it was necessary that tents and csts should be provided the committee were justi- fied in providing that accommodation ; and if they could not provide it in the hospital they were quite right to pro- vide it outside. But he slh.nid not vote at all upon the gnat- titin because he might seem to express approval of the manner in which the hospital had been carried on for some time. _

Councillor GREENING regretted that the tents were requisite, but he could not help saying that the way in which cases had been liken to the hospital had been very objectionable, and in many cases sufficient isolation could have been obtained outside. He had had a case of scarlet fever in his own house and had isolated the case entirely. Whether the expense incurred had been right or wrong they could not do less than pay it. Councillor CALDWELL said the question had been argued in good humour on both sides, but he certainly could not vote against the minutes; because the Council would then stultify themselves. It was a case of compulsion ; the thing was done; and he could not see it in any other light. Councillor MONKS: I have been asked to withdraw the amendment. Will you allow me to say that— The MAYOR Are you going to withdraw? Councillor MONKS: I am going to give reasons why I cannot withdraw it. .1 opposed this matter on the Sanitary Committee ; and I had my vote recorded. I wish this matter to be fairly looked at. We have no right to spend money till it has been confirmed by the Council. The MAYOR: You cannot go any further. Councillor lltioluts : Very well. The MAYOR said It was his opinion that the committee had been working by Act of Parliament; they had carried it out in the way in which they read the Act. Some people said they had carried it out too rigourously and others that they had not. There was another matter which had caused some little irritation in the minds of members of the Council, and that was with reference to the hospital being declared free. The speakers appeared to regret that the charges were taken off, but they could net conduct a largo hospital free to rich and poor, without great expense. He had always thought it was a great mistake to take off the whole of the charges. (Hear, hear.) There was one blot on Councillor Monks' amendment, and that was that the tents had been bought and the patients were in them. He did not say in his amendment how he would provide for the patients. Councillor MONKS: I contend that they ought not to have been ordered : that they had no-- The MAYOR: How can you get out of the difficulty? The thing is done. I certainly under the circumstances must support the minutes. Alderman BURGESS (who, on rising, was met with a cry 1 of " Cut it short"), said he did netlike to be told every time ' he rose to " Cut it short." He was not in the habit of making long speeches. (Laughter.) One thing was very satisfactory to his mind, and that was no one had found the slightest fault with the tents provided. No one had said they had not afforded sufficient accommodation, That being the case, he would leave the Council to determine the matttir themselves. The committee had an epidemic upon them, and had not the means of isolation. The hospital was full, and they provided in a prompt and efficient manner the ac- commodation required. If the members of the Council would declare that there should be no accommodation be- yond 28 beds, an 1 that rather than extend the accommoda- tion fever should spread from one end of the town to the other—if the Council were prepared at anybody's bidding to take such a responsibility as that let them do so. He would not attempt to prevent them. Ae to the hospital being free, it was not by any action on the part of the committee that that was brought about. He opposed its being made free, and he could net help thinking that it was an unlawful pro- ceeding. No one bad a right to put his band into his pocket and make him maintain his child in food and medicine. All eases of infection were reported by some medical gentleman In the kwn to the Town Clerk, and the Town Clerk sent on the report to the Medical Officer. Now he was told many of the patients sent to the hospital should not go there. If Mr. Charles White certified to the Medical Officer that in such a house there was a case of fever or smallpox, was it not in accordance with the Act of Parliament and common sense that the Medical Officer, having satisfied himself that the representation was correct, should in the discharge of his duty get that case removed to the hospital ? He took upon himself a huge responsibility if he neglected to take the necessary measures for removal. With reference to the epidemic ; they had 28 beds, and he wanted to know if the Council supposed that, with the wards full, their responsi- bility ceased ? He said it did not, and that they were not only morally but legally responsible to provide further ac- commodation. If the committee bad not taken measures to provide further accommodation someone else would have taken those measures, and very soon too. They could not at this time determine whether the accommodation should only be to a certain extent, and whether with the hospital completely full they should not have more. Councillor MONKS: Yes, you can.

Alderman BuncEss Ouis, friends the reporters will take care that the public know something about them. I won't say one word to add to the heat that has arisen. If we have done the evil things Councillor Monks suggests we have let them be made known. If we have not done them—l tell you again we have not, and that he cannot prove them—let that also be made known; and let the public know that Mr. Monks cannot substantiate his charge. Councillor MONKS: If Alderman Burgess will say dis- tinctly to the Council that he knows nothing oi the circum- stances under which previous matrons were dismissed I will withdraw the remark so far as it concerns himself,

Alderman BURGESS: I really don't understand what Coun- cillor Monks refers to. (Laughter.) The resolution and amendment were then put to the vote, which resulted as follows :—For the amendment: Alderman Homes and Councillors Monks, Whittle, Dixon, Woolfall, and Jeans-6. Against: The Mayor, Aldermen Burgess, Thewlis, Harrison, and Kean, and Councillors Greening, Litton, Caldwell, Fairclough. Crosfield, Gresnall, Sutton, Platt, Wallington, Brown; and Percival-16. The motion for the confirmation of the minutes of the committee was then pet and carried.

COUNCILLOR BURGESS'S MOTION. Councillor BURGESS moved. "That it be an inetruction from this Council to the Town Clerk that np proceedings shall be taken under the provisions of the Warrington Cor- poration Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, to compel removal to the Infectious Diseases Hospital when it is certi- fied by two legally qualified medical practitioners that the sick persons are sufficiently isolated; and that if 'the Town Clerk advise that he cannot adopt this course under the present law steps be taken to procure an amendment of the Act of Parliament." He said he remembered when he moved a similar resolution to the first part of the present one, the Town Clerk said he thought that when the Medical Officer of Health reported that a case of fever was' not pro- perly isolated the Corporation had no option ; that it was compelled whatever ether doctors might say, to take the case and try to ol.rain a magisterial order if removal could not be effected withmit it. Ile would not question the Town Clerk's opinion on a legal queetion, but the whole question of the discretion of the Council to apply for an order depended on the word "may." He quoted extracts from the Act to show that where the word "may " was used, the power was optional, and where no option was meant the word " shall" was used. The magistrates had acted on the plain literal meaning of the Act of Parliament, and it seemed clear that it was for the Corporation to determine whether it woe desirable to require and to endeavour to compel the removal of all cases. If the Council instructed the Town Clerk under what circumstances he should or should not take action, it would be his duty to act upon those instructions ; and if it were true that the Act of Parliament made the pro- ceedings obligatory, then the Act must be altered, and the sooner the better. When a case of infectious disease could not be properly treated at home' it was right in the interest of the patient, of the friends of the patient, and of the public, that advantage should be taken of the excellent accommodation which had been provided with much care and with great expense at the fever hospital. But it is a scandal and a shame that attempts should be made to drag sick people from their homes without necessity. And when, in the judgment of two doctors, the patient is pro- perly isolated, and can be properly treated at home, the ne- cessity for removal did not exist. It was utterly unrea- sonable in cases of this kind to allow the opinion of one doctor, be he Medical Officer or anyone else, to override the deliberate judgment of two other men equally qualified in every respect to give an opinion. Looking at the Act as he viewed it, the magistrates had the power to refuse to order removal, and he was glad to say they had more than once exercised that power. And if the magistrates were not compelled to grant the order, the Corporation was not compelled to ask them to grant it. When it was proved that people suffering from infectious diseases could be attended to at home without injury to themselves, and without harm to their neighbours, he could not see why the Corporation should put the sick people and their friends to the expense and annoyance of appearing at the police court. When people had sickness in the house they had anxiety enough, and they should take no course which would make. their sufferings greater. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON seconded the proposition, subject to the opinion of the Town Clerk that it would be operative if passed. The TOWN CLERK: I must say I cannot see how it could be operative. The wording of the resolution itself to me is purely mistaken. It says "that it be an instruction from this Council to the Town Clerk that no proceedings shall be taken." I have no power to take proceedings without the direction of this Council. If you pass the resolution, every case that al ises where the Medical Officer certifies, all I could do would be to request the Mayor to call you together to say whether proceedings should be taken. I have no power in the matter. Councillor BURGESS asked who took proceedings P The Corporation was not obliged to take them and the resolution said in certain circumstances they should not be taken. He wanted to know whether in a case like that the Council could not tell the Town Clerk he was not to take pro- ceedings. -
The Towsr CLERK: You can tell me, but I shall do nothing.... _

Councillor Mornts: He asks you who takes proceedings. The TOWN CLERK: The Medical Officer of Health. Councillor BURGESS: It does not say the Medical Officer of Health shall take proceedings at all. The TowN CLERK: The powers are delegated by the Council to the Sanitary Committee to carry out the Act of Parliament, and the Sanitary Committee do so. Councillor BuRGESS : The Town Clerk takes proceedings at the police court, and all legal proceedings, I take it. Alderman HOLMES: There must be somebody at the back of him.
Councillor &moms: This Council is at the back of the Town Clerk. We give him instructions, and I say he must act upon them. That is all we want to do.

The TOWN CLERK : I could not act upon such instructions as those mentioned in the resolution for the simple reason that lam asked, if the medical officer of health gives me a certificate I shall be bound to bring it before the committee to know what I should do with it after you have passed that resolution. It is all 'very well for you to say that two medical men may certify that the case is properly isolated; hut the Corporation, on the other hand, may have three medical men to Certify that it is not properly isolated, and although you may pass such a resolutity as this the Act of Parliament itself says the Corporation may cause cases to be removed. It is well known and well understood— I although I don't wish to lay the slightest stress upon this— where the word may is used a duty is imposed upon persons where the necessity arises of doing an act which they are authorised to do. If you "may " provide a hospital and an epidemic occurs you are bound to provide a hospital, or a mandamus may be obtained to compel you to provide that hospital, and in the same way where the word may is used in cases which should be removed, you can compel a child to be removed. But I put it on the simple ground that the Act of Parliament says you must do a certain thing as a Cor- poration. You exercise your functions through certain officials. The resolution of Councillor Burgess can in no way, take away the powers conferred by Act of Parliament, and any single ratepaper may call upon you to exercise those powers, although you may have passed the resolution just read. If you pass the resolution, as far as lam in- dividually concerned, if a certificate is given to me all I can do is to send it to the Sanitary Committee. Councillor BURGESS: It seems to me that the Town Clerk after all would act upon these instructions. We are the Corporation, and we have certain discretionary powers con- ferred upon us by Act of Parliament, and we may say how they may be acted upon in this resolution. If the Act of Parliament renders it necessary for us to take these proceed- ings, then the last part will come into play. The Town. CLERK r This is exactly where you make the mistake. You do not lay how the powers shall be acted upon, but how they shall not be acted upon if a gentleman gives a certificate that a certain state of circumstances can-, not arise. Then I say you cannot do that. It is taking away powers conferred upon you. Councillor BURGESS: Would the Town Clerk give us an idea what resolution we should pass P We intend this sort of thing shall not go on.
Alderman BURGESS: We don't intend any resolution to be passed, and we intend this sort of thing to stop directly....

Councillor JEANS, in seconding the motion, said it was well.known that the arbitrary powers conferred by the Act of Parliament had been exercised in a manner which had thoroughly roused public indignation in Warrington. Aid. Burgess said that in only four cases had compulsory powers been applied for, and that the rest of the patients had gone voluntarily. This was a statement he begged to deny. To his certain knowledge two children were taken. They were sent for at ten o'clock at night and taken from home against the wish of the parents, from a house where they could hare been isolated. The result was the children never returned home, but died in the hospital. It was most outrageous that young children should be compulsorily removed without an expression of opinion from the Council. They were the Corporation, and it was right they should give expression to tbeir opinion, and say in what way the act should be carried out. They did not want an alteration in the Act. What they wanted was that the powers conferred by it should be carried out with discretion. They did not want an Act to vest discretion in their officers. If they had not officers with discretion let them change them. He had not a word to say against Mr. Gor,,all personally, but there was a strong feeling in the town that the powers given in the Act were carried out in an arbitrary manner. Alderman BURGESS: Nonsense. Councillor JEANS, in supporting Mr. Monk's amendment. did so with a view to having a discussion on the subject, as they ought not to have discussion stiffied in the way it had been.

The MAYOR: I don't think you are in order in that last expression of yours in reference to discussion being stifled. I think every member will admit it has gone to very great length to-night. Councillor JEANS: I quite admit that. The intention was to si.itle it, but we prevented that.

FOOTBALL.

_ NORTRWICH IST V. RUNCORN 21PD TEAM.—These clubs met at Runcorn on Saturday afternoon, when a well. contested game was witnessed by a large number of specta- tors. Runcorn having won the toss, Forster started the ball for Northwich, which was well returned, when some play ensued in neutral ground, and Runcorn carried the ball into the Northwich territory, but only a touchdown resulted. North wich dropping out and following well up compelled Runcorn to touch down. The ball being again put into play, the Runcorn forwards worked the ball up to Northwich ground, when Joule ran in and obtained the first try, the place being entrusted to Sherlock, but being rather a diffi- cult one, he failed to put it across the bar. On the drop out, Northwich scored a dead ball, when half time was called. On play being resumed, Mason set the ball in motion for Runcorn, and some good scrimmaging was witnessed; when the ball got loose Speakman got possession, passed to Waulkey, who by a dodgy run got well up into Northwich ground, when Dennison ran in and obtained a second try, which Sherlock converted into a goal. Northwich on start- ing the ball followed up well, and some fast and loose play ensued, when Capper get a good run, but was soon collared; the ball got forced again on Northwich ground, when a maul took place, resulting in favour of Runcorn, when Sherlock again placed it across the bar. The ball being set rolling again, some tight play on both sides took place, and North* wich playing up well forced the ball into the Runcorn ground, but the ball went into touch in goal. On the drop out Runcorn worked the ball well back, and from a line up, Sherlock ran in and gained the fourth try for Runcorn, which the same player converted into a goal. On the leather being again started, the Northwich forward took the ball into the Runcorn goal, which was, however, kicked into touch in goal. On the drop out, and being near call of time, Runcorn men took the ball right up to the Northwich goal line, when Hankinson got possession of the leather and nicely placed it across the line; the place kick, however, failed. Time being called, left Runcorn the victors by three goals, two tries, and three touchdowns, to Northwich one touch- down, two touches in goal, and a dead ball. The following were the teams :—Northwich: Full back, A. Burgess; three- quarter backs, F. Thompson and W. N. Capper; half-backs, Bates and Chandler; forwards, Forster, Thompson, Marsh, Carter, Wainwright, Dutton, Garton, Barlow, Deakin, and substitute. Runcorn: Full back, Stubbs; three-quarter backs, Sherlock, Waulkey, and Hankinson; balf-backs, W. Pownall and Speakman; forwards, Roberts, Page,. Joule, Riley, Dennison, Mason (captain), Dunlavand, Gittons, and Wright. For Runcorn Waulkey, Sherlock, Speakman, and Pownall did good service, as did Capper, Thompson, and Forster for the visitors.

RUNCORN v. CREWE.—This match was played at Crewe on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors. The weather was very fine, there was a fair number of spectators present, and a start was made about a quarter past four Crewe kicked off, and a scrimmage was formed in the Run- corn twenty-five. Riley relieved the lines and the ball wa3 quickly taken to the Crewe quarters, where several good scrimmages took place. Runcorn nowpressed their opponents behind the goal line, and Andrews availed himself at a mis- take by Garside, and se:mred a try, which Rate converted into a goal. After each side had touched down twice, half time was called. Bate restarted the ball, which was returned to Joule' who retaliated with a long punt. Tophill now obtained possession and gained considerable ground; but was brought down by H. Hughes, who kept a strict watch over his movements. Wright, Lewis, Cox, and Hoffland were the mainstays of the forwards, and dribbled the ball to the Crewe territory, when Tophill was again to the fore. Riley, however, prevented him from going far by carrying him into touch. Cowap, who played well all the game, took the ball out of danger and sent it to Roach, who ran it back again. After a good attempt to get behind by Larkin, the Crewe team succeeded in driving the ball to the Runcorn citadel, and Hickton ran in, Crutchley kicking a neat goal. Andrews, aided by Gatley, was instrumental in obtaining another try, but the place kick, close against the touch line, did not produce the desired result. On time being called, a very pleasant and well contested game ended as follows. Runcorn one goal, one try, three touches down. Crewe, one goal, four touches down. Players, Runcorn—J. Pownall, back; H. Hughes, T. Roach, W. Larkin, three quarter; H. Andrews, W. Riley, half; F. Bate (captain), F. Joule, W. Wright, W. Cox, J. Hoffland, J. Lewis, J. Gatley, C. Pownall, W. Hughes, forward; Crewe— Harvey, back; 131akeley, Garside, three quarter; Tophill (captain), Cowap, half; Howard, Butt, Hickton, Hitchen, Crutchley, Parsons, Lindup, Holden, Davies, Liptrot.

Then; too, we anticipate that free expression of the opinion of tenant farmers in all parts of the country will be elicited Upon the provisions of the Bill. Members of Parlia • latent, between now and the meeting of Parliament, will have opportunities of finding out what their con- stituents, who are farmers, think of the scheme. Its deficiencies, if any, will be pointed out. Landlords, likewise, will wloissien, will talk about it, and will not be slow in what parts of it are most objectionable to them. div.head: Ri 111 th °b.
div.p: Ri 111 th °b.
AT LEEDS.

The reception accorded to the Premier at Leeds yesterday was most enthusiastic. Eighty-six address s were presented to the right hen. gentleman (who was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone) from the Leeds Corporation, Liberal Clubs, in the presence of above 10,000 persons. Mr. Gladstone, in responding to them, said the addresses, so far as they had ken read, introduced a variety of topics, from which he could only make a selection, and with the selection he could not fully deal on the present occasion. But there were two sentiments in the addresses in respect to which be desired to comment. The first was entirely personal ; the second had reference to his foreign policy. Having referred to the policy of the country in the days of Peel, the right bon. gentleman said he gave enormous weight to two principles, the first, that every foreign coun- try should be credited with the same good motives as our- selves until they showed the contrary ; and, secondly, that every Power, great or small, was entitled to exactly the same rights and the same privileges., These were the dis- tinctive principles of the Conservative party together with the Liberals in the days of Peel, as they were principles of the Liberal party now. That which we called the "policy of peace," which is now so often the mark of ridicule and scoffing in the Tory meetings of to-day—the policy of peace was as sedulously pursued by Liberals now as ever it was in the days of Peel. Mr. Gladstone was afterwards entertained at a grand banquet, and subsequently a torchlight proces- sion, in which nearly 3,000 persons carried torches, took place.

div.p: LThIM.

—... ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT LYMM. The anniversary services in Canned ion with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lyrnm, were preached. on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Rev. W. Rowe, of Chester. At both services the chapel was crowded, and the collections on behalf of the trust fund amounted to upwards of £B. REVISION COURT AT LYIWM: EECITIDTG SCENE.—Mr. W. Langford Ffonlkes, revising barrister for Mid-Cheshire, held a revision court at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, on Saturday morning last, for the townships of Agden, Bollington, High Legh, Ly am, Millington, Partington, Thelwall, and War- burton. The Liberals were represented by Mr. Patterson, and the Conservatives by Mr. Lance Bentley. Shortly after the opening of the court, the reutine of the business was greatly disturbed by the advent of a tall, burly fellow, I who as soon 39 he pot his head through the door, volun- teered the information that he was "Dick Rowbotham, of I Agden." Having taken a seat on the end of a sofa, " Dick " I commenced to talk in a manner that indicated he had had , something more than his breakfast that morning, and after I he had expressed, with considerable vigour, his conviction I that "something would have to be done for the farmers," it , I was decided to hear his case. Mr. Rowbotham, it transpired, I had appeared in response to an objection that had been served upon him by the Liberals, and when he had replied to a question by Mr. Patterson as to whether he had occupied , his house the whole of the last 12 months, the Liberal re- presentative put the delicate question "Had he been in- solvent ?" This was more than "Dick Rowbotham, of / Agden," could stand, and be excitedly repeated " Never! assuming at the same time a most threatening attitu le. Although the room was rather small for such a purpose, ' everyone present expected to witness a pugilistic encounter, and indeed so near did the massive fists of the Agden butcher , approach Mr. Patterson's face that the Revising Barrister , began to make anxious enquiry for the police constable, ! who, while "bound by the Act of Parliament to be present," I was nowhere to be seen. The anxiety of the Revising 1 Barrister increased with the excitement of Mr. Bowbothatr, I who loudly anathematised the Liberal agent, and exhibited I a great desire to lay violent hands on that gentleman. He, however, managed to get behind the table, and thus evade the burly butcher he had so unintentionally annoyed; and after Mr. Rowbotham had been assured his vote was all right. he was eventually got out of the room by the Lymm over- seer and Mr. Bentley. The gentlemen in the room after- I wards indulged in a hearty laugh at this unexpected and I exciting occurrence, and Mr. Bentley remarked that Mr, i Rowbotham was the most spirited claimant he had seen. I The remainder of the business was of an uninteresting I character. In the afternoon Mr. Ffoulkes held a court at Ithe Barry Arms, Grappenhall, but the proceedings were (1- ', 1 void of public interest.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A MOULDER AT Wamtmurog. —Mr. C. E. Driffield, held an inquest at the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-stree`, on Thursday, on the body of James ' Roberts, 64 years of age.—Edward Taylor, eon of the de- ceased, said he was a file cutter, residing at 1, Eldon-street. His father was a brass moulder, and had a shop in Hopwood- street. About eight o'clock en the night of the 6th Sep- tember, he was told that his father was on fire in his work- shop. He quickly proceeded there, and as he was entering a man named William Taylor, placed his father in his arms. He carried him home, and immediately afterwards conveyed him to the Infirmary. The deceased was badly burnt about the armlet', and down one leg from the knee. The molten iron had run into his shoes. Witness thought his father had been stepping from the top of the furnace where he had placed the crucible, upsetting the metal upon himself Wm. Taylor said when he heard of the accident he ran to the shop, and forced open the door which was locked. Deceased was laid on the floor.—Mary Alice Cooper, the matron at the Infirmary, said one foot was totally burnt, and the other leg was considerably injured. If deceased had lived the foot would have required amputation. The ex- planation deceased gave to her was that he was carrying some molten metal, when his foot slipped and overturned it upon himself. A verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned.

SAX> SITICIDZ AT WARRINGTON. —An inquiry Wha held at the Unicorn Inn, on Thursday, before Mr. C. E. Driffield, touching the death of Thomas Boardman (29), of 53, Pinner's-brow.—Eliztheth Boardman said deceased was her husband and had been employed as a warehouserd'an at Mr. Howson's, tine asd spirit merchant. On Tuesday afternoon, her hushawl went home about half-past four, aid as it was an unusual time, she asked his reason. lie said his employer did not knew he had done s.r. He then went upstairs, and she followed, asking "Are you going back to your %i (irk?" and he replied "No, I am going to bed," at the same time pulling off his coat. He requested her te leave the room. She did so, and heard him fasten the doer. Directly afterwards, and before she had descended the s•epri, she heard the report of a gun, and gave the alarm. The father of the deceased broke open the door and entered the room. Her husband lay on the door and appeared to be dead. There was a wound in his side. She had not seen him take anything upstairs, and he mentioned nothing of his intentions, lie had had a gun in the room about a week, and was in the habit of shooting in the morning. When he took the gun home he warned her that it was loaded, hut Bald that he would draw the charge. She was sure be had never done so. In reply to the Coroner, Witness said her husband had carried on a provision shop in addition to his ordinary business. The shop business had been going wrong for some time, but he had not known it until a few days before his death. He was very much troubled, and got excited at the least thing.—At this point witness was taken from II e room in a fainting condition' and was not again examined. —George Boardman, of the Wheat Sheaf, Vrford-lane, said the deceased was his son. He saw his son on 'Monday night, when he acted in his usual manner, and be did not see him again until Tuesday afternoon- 11,4 was then tont for by the wife of deceased who said "the gun has gone off." He burst open the bedroom door and found deceased laid by tho side of the bed dead. He was shot if) the life breast and death must have been instantaneous. Deceastd had threatened to take his life years a:eo, and he had taken a gun away from him once. He was very fiery temperer', and would have his own way. The business had been goit,g wrong, and the wife, who managed it, laid never told him. —Dr. Bride said he saw deceased about a quarter pas five on Tuesday. He had been dead about a touter of an hour. There was a large wound on the cheat. The grin must have been placed near the apex of the heart, which was shat- tered, the shot also haying penetrated the lung. The sixth rib was fractured in two places. The wound was aboat :••• [inch in diameter.—The jury returned a verdict of mitted suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 8, 1881.

A case heard at the St. Helens police court on Friday will give tradesmen an idea of what they have to expect if they give credit to working people to the extent of £2O. Ann Collins and Catherine Seery had been allowed to obtain goods from Mrs. Michael McGee to the amount of £2O, and because the latter thought it was time the money was paid, and therefore asked her customers to be goo. enough to pay off the debt, Mrs. Collins and Mrs. Seery became some- what indignant, and waxing warm at the idea ef being called upon to pay they commenced a series of annoyances, and eventually made use of threatening language to Mrs. McGee, and assailed her with a quantity of mud. I have heard of many expedients adopted by debtors for paying their debts, but this is certainly a novel one. The magistrates, however, did not coincide with it, and therefore ordered the defen- dants to be hound over to keep the peace for three months. The report submitted by the Medical Officer of Health to the Prescot Local B)ard this week. shows that scarlet fever, which some time ago seemed almost dying away, has again assumed very formidable proportions, there being no less than twelve deaths during the past month. fhe deaths numbered 22 as against 17 in the corresponding period last year, and the death-rate was 4113 per 1,000 as compared with 04 last year. This is really an important matter which ought to have the serious attention not only of the sanitary authorities, but of every resident within the district of the Board. The Medical Officer states that the sanitary condi- tion of Prescot is much more satisfactory than it has ever been, and yet we have this enormous death-rate. We are told that "the propagation of the fever is due entirely to the general amount of intercourse between infected persens and their friends. If the conclusion at which the Medical Officer has arrived be a correct one, and I have no re Isom to doubt it, it plainly points to the great necessity which exists for the perfect isolation of every case of fever, and it is to be hoped that steps will be taken at once to effect this so as to prevent the continued spread of the divase. WIDNES SCIENCE ANT) ART CLassEs.—The names of all students must be sent in to Mr. Morrison, the secretary, be- fore the end of the month.

CATTLE DISEASE IN RUNCORN DlSTRlCT.—Yestgrday a meeting of the sub-committee under the Contagious Animals' Act, for the Runcorn district, was held at the Town Hall, Mr. S. B. Chadwick presiding, when Bartington and Great Budworth were declared to be free from swine fever. SIGNOR LEOTARD Bosco AT RIINCORN.—Those who have paid any attention to the art of conjuring will be pleased to hear that Signor Leotard Bosco, whom, we understand, is the son of the Bosco who at one time occupied such a high position as a conjuror, commences an engagement at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday, for one week. The en- tertainer is accompanied by a band of 12 performers, and a very strong company. In addition to the other attractions, presents will be distributed.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The first annual harvest thanksgiving service was held in the new church of St. Ambrose, on Wednesday. The chancel and font were artistically decorated with fruit, flowers and corn. The decorations, which were of a very tasteful' character, were entirely carried out by the St. Am- brose Sunday school teachers and a few friends. The dona- tions of fruit and flowers were greatly in excess of similar gifts last year. The service was read by the Rev. S. A. Spooner, and the lessons by the Rev. B. B. Prescott, vicar of Latchford, who also preached the sermon. There was a crowded congregation, and the offertory amounted to £4 155. NEW CHURCH FOR GREENWAY-ROAD, a speech at an entertainment given in the National School, Runcorn on Thursday, the Rev. Canon Barclay referred to the large increase of popuLition on the south side of the Bridgewater Canal and the inadequate accommodation which the Newtown Mission Church afforded. To meet the spiritual requirements it was proposed to erect a new church in Greenway-road. Besides the cost of the erection they would require an endowment of some £2OO per annum to- wards the stipend of the minister. He must confess that he Clid not like bazaars; but he thought they were a necessary evil, and only to be resorted to when they had secured all subscriptions and donations possible.

• HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT WIDNES.—By desire, the harvest thanksgiving service, entitled " The Giver and His Gifts," was given in the Oakland-street Wes- leyan Methodist Sunday school, Widnes, on Wednesday evening. The teachers had made the roo.n very attractive with ferns, flowers, fruit, mottoes, and banners. Mr. Joseph Robinson presided ; Mr. W. Whitby acted as conductor ; the J. H. Cummings gave the connective readings; Mr. A. Jackson presided at the harmonium, and Mr. F. Harper accompanied,on the corn. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. H. Cummings, the Chairman, and Messrs. T. Whitby and R. Keyworth. During the rroceedings it was stated that a strenuous effort was being made by the congre- gation worshipping at the place to clear off the debt of £lO on the old building. They hoped in a short time to erect a new and commodious building for the rapidly increasing congregation.

TIM PINK DOMINO COMPANY AT RIINCORN.— On Thursday night, Mr. Henry S. Dacre's Pink Dominoes Com- pany, who are now in their fourth year's tour, appeared at the Public Hall, Runcorn, to a good audience, who, judging ' from their frequent applause, were highly gratified with ' the performance. Unfortunately, during the evening, Mr. I Deere fell ill, and was not able to take his part as Joekin Tubbs, "the dear old gentleman with a weakness," which was very fairly filled by Mr. Ward, considering the brief ; time he had for preparation. The cast was as follows : Charles Greythorne, Mr. W. Manning; Sir Percy Wagstaff, Mr. F. Ilibbert ; Harry Greenlanes, Mr. C. Groldsworthy Brisket, Mr. Harry Rivers; first waiter at Cremorne, Mr. E. Ward ; Lady Maggie Wagstaff, Miss Jenny Beauville ; Sophia, Miss Clara Cavendish ; Rebecca, Miss Carrie Lee Stoyle ; Mrs. Joskin Tubbs, Miss Jane Grey ; Miss Barron, Miss L. Gordon. Miss Beauville, as Lady Wagstaff; Miss Cavendish, as Sophia; and Miss Stoyle, as Rebecca, proved admirable exponents of the characters. Mr. Manning took the part of the Manchester manufacturer with a deep interest in Surat cotton, to perfection and Mr. Ward, as the first waiter at Cremorne, was worthy of all praise. Last evening "Truth " was put upon the boards, and to-night (Saturday) " Pink Dominoes will be repeated. It is not I often that Runcornians have the opportunity of seeing such a capital company, and we should advise them to avail , themselves of the opportunity. Warburton, of Arley, applying for .a certificate of occupa- tion of a new house at Appleton respecting which proceed- ings had been taken; and the Inspector was directed to ascertain from Mr. Warburton if he was willing to have a sample of the water supply submitted for analysis.—The Inspector presented an application from Mr. Gibson, of Warrington, to connect the drainage of a new house at Stockton Quay with the main sewer. The Inspector stated that he had communicated with the engineer and had re- ceived his reply, which was read.—lt was resolved that the I Inspector confer with Mr. Gibson as to the intended mode ! of dealing with the storm and surface water. Mr. Randle presided, and a discussion followed, in which Messrs. J. D. Jones and F. J. Norman took part. RUNCORN Si. JOHN'S CALVINISTIC METHODIST CHAPEL. —On Saturday night, Miss McLatchie delivered a very interesting discourse at this place of worship, on "I am the resurrection and the life." The fair sermoniser's style is very simple but extremely graphic, and she still retains a great measure of the popularity which she won in the town years ago. FUNERAL OF A RuNcoax GENTLEMAN—On Monday afternoon, the mortal remains of Mr. John Humphreys, late of Bridge-street, were interred at the Parish Church, by the Rev. Evan Williams, pastor of St. John's Presbyterian Church. Deceased, whose death was caused through apoplexy, was much respected in the town, and the funeral was attended by several tradesmen and friends, and many of the shops along the route were closed as a mark of respect. Deceased expired at his own residence on the previous Thursday night, at half-past nine, and as he bad been out of the house on the same day, it was very unexpected. He was attended by Drs. Robinson and McDougall. This is the first funeral which has been conducted at the Parish Church burial ground since the passing of the Act of 1880. REVISING BARRISTER'S COURT AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. H. Butler, revising barrister, held a court for the townships included in the Widnes parliamentary polling district, in the Police Court, that town, on Tuesday. Mr. G. H. 1",,we11, secretary of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association- with whom was Mr. T. P. Major, appeared for the Liberals, whose agent (Mr. H. B. Shores) was also in attendance. The property claims made on behalf of the Liberals numbered 70, the occupation claims were 102, and the objections about 90. Mr. Swift, sour., accompanied by Mr. J.O. Swift, junr" represented the Conservatives, whose local agent, Mr. I'. A. Bullough, with Mr. John Hampson, sub-agent of the Liver- pool Conservative Association, were also in attendance. The Conservative new claims numbered 19, and they also made 20 claims on the £l2 list, and about 90 objections. The Liberal agent objected to Dr. O'Keeffe's claim for a vote on account of leasehold land and buildings in Lugsdale-road, which he had owned for five or six years, under a lease for an unexpired term of 999 years.—ln reply to Mr. Swift the applicant said he got his lease from the trustees of the late Mr. Rowlands, who obtained it from Messrs. Hutchinson's. The claim was allowed.—Dr. O'Keeffe : Will you allow the expenses? The Revising Barrister said he could not is this was the first time of proving.—Dr. O'Keeffe remarked that he attended a revision court some four years ago, and though it was the first time of establishing his claim, he was allowed a guinea.—The Revising Barrister : We have taken your case out of turn in order to oblige you.—D/. OKeeffe : I should be still more obliged if you would allow me costs. (Laughter).—The Revising Barrister intimated that he could not do so.—The Conservatives objected to the vote of the Rev. Father Clarke, in the case of freehold land and buildings in Hutchinson•street.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, Father Clarke said he held the property for Dr. O'Reilly, Catholic Bishop of Liverpool. —The Revising Barrister : Are you liable to be sent away by the Bishop at any time ? Father Clarke : Yes —The Revising Barrister disallowed the vote.—Mr. Powell said the Rev. Father Clarke was on another list, so that his disqualification would not affect him very much.--This terminated the proceedings, which were of a very tame description, and lasted from ten in the morn- ing to four in the afternoon. Certainly the result obtained is fairly creditable to our party, but in view of the large num- ber of claims and reclaims made, we find some difficulty in understanding how it was that the Conservative claims, in which the applicants paid .£l6 per veer, were allowed, whilst a number of Liberal claims, in which the claimants paid £l6 18s., were disallowed. It did not seem to us that the repre- sentative of the Liberals placed this point with sefficient prominence before the Revising Barrister. CONGREGATIONAL TEIANICsGIVING SERVICE AT RUN. CORN—On Sunday evening a harvest thanksgiving service was held at the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, the preacher being the Rev. T. D. Thomas, who preached from the text, " Let both grow together until the harvest : and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles and burn them : but gather the wheat into my barn." The preacher drew some very apposite lessons from the text, and said that the fields with their fruits were constantly fur- nishing Christ with subjects wherefrom he gave his hearers instructive lessons. He drew his illustrations not alone from the fallow field, but also from the meadow clothed in ver- dure. The parable of the sower was an illustration of the reception accorded to the word of God ; and tha field in which the wheat and tares grew together an illustration of the mingled results that attended the Gospel, though not at- tributable to the Gospel. The first point that called for their attention Was that there was a possibility of growing in both good and evil. This was suggested by the words, " Let both grow together ;" and they found illustrations of the fact in all directions. Side by side with trees bearing precious fruit were others yielding no fruit at all, or only that which was poisonous; in the same field with the rich and golden corn, they might see the poppy, the thistle, and the dock ; in the same forest they might find animals which were easily domesticated and made of service to man, and others that were absolutely untameable ; in the same ocean, yielding the most wholesome food, might he found fish, whose only work appeared to be to live upon one of the great supplies of human beings ; in the same town, in the same church, and in the same family, there were found growing up together men of sterling worth and brighter soul with men of disreputable character and blighting it,- fluence. These characters, so opposite in their tendencies, and so diverse in their principles, thrived together, some— times the evil outliving the good. The principle of genera- tion was just as strong in the evil as in the good; children of unrighteous parents with no outside influence must of necessity lee evil. What sad and serious reflections this fact ought to occasion! Think of thousands of degraded fathers and mothers who had almost, if not entirely, cut off all re- ligious influence and associations. Their prison annals told them that the same families supplied for generation after generation their gaols with their worst criminals. But the good and the evil were capable of growth, because there was is possibility of ome conquering the other. The good frequently conquered the evil and won them over to the side of virtue, and he rejoiced to know that every year those conquests were becoming more and more extensive. But alas ! the con- quests on the other side were far too frequent. They had sometimes occasion to lament for those who had been drawn away from positions of great honour in the church. Evil- doers were only in the world on sufferance. From the text they would observe that the word "let" applied only to the tares. The wheat did not require such permission. It was only by permission of the husbandman that the tares were allowed to grow. "He would thoroughly purge His floor, and gather His wheat into the garner; but he will burn the c'haff with unquenchable fire." There was nothing tyrannical in this. It was as natural as the law of natural selection. Every creature chose its mate from among its own species, and the passage meant nothing less than the choosing of His companions by Almighty God. If Esther was beautiful, then no one could blame Ahasuerus for making her his Queen ; and if the grod were the really beautiful in character, the really noble in life, no one could blame the Most High for choosing them to dwell with Him in His many mansions. Unless they considered the circum- stances under which the separation took place they could not realise its awful meaning. They might live together on the earth, but what would they do in the day of generation ? The degree of separation was immeasurable, and they had seen something like it this world. There Was the case of James Abram Garfield, the late President of tire United States, and Charles Guiteau, his assassin. They were nur- tured by the Same Sail ; they enjoyed the benefits of the s-ane political inetitutione, yet see how immeasurably they are separated. It might be said that the whole Christian worl4l watched with clasped hands and bonded knees around the bed of the dying President, and when the news came that he had breathed his last whole nations wept and mourned for him; and it might safely be said that never was a king carried to his grave amid honours so universal And great. But what about Guiteau ? His memory was execraqsl almost more than that of any man since the worl4 began. Hundreds of men were thirsting for his life to-day, as hounds thirsted for the blond of the beast; ard the w I ole world ould hail with delight the day when he should PVC in 4 upon the gallows. There were many of them on the wrong road, but while there Was yet time he asked them to turn hick while it was to-day, for to-morrow the great set) iristron might have taken place and their souls irretrieraoly lost. RUNCORN AND THE TWO AGRICULTURAL SOCIETIES.— On 'Thursday morning, an adjourned meeting of ratepayers was held at the Commissioners' Board-room, Runcorn, for the purpose of considering the advisability of inviting either the Cheshire or the Tarporley Agricultural Society to hold their next annual exhibition at Runcorn. There was a very spare attendance, although the proceedings were not started until considerably after the time announced—eleven o'clock. Dr. Stez'e, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. Thos. Norman, W. F. Salkeld, W. Fisher, C. E. Linaker, W. li. Linaker M. Barker, William Brookes, E. A. Chorlton, F. A. Lake, T. H. Hitchen, Peter Smith, S. Spann, Joseph Williams and James Kirkham. The Chairman having referred to the object of the gathering, said it appeared, from the fact of there being so poor an attendance numerically, that they had not the general support of the inhabitants in the matter, and the proposal to invite either of the shows to visit Runcorn would have to drop.—Mr. S:eward said a good many people had told him that morning that they were not aware that a meet- ing was to be held on the subject.—The Chairman, in reply, remarked that 150 circulars had been sent out, but the meet- ing had not been advertised. He believed there was a general feeling in the town against inviting the Cheshire Agricultural Society to visit Runcorn, because of the fact that they declined to come last year, when strongly invited. —Mr. Norman said they must consider whether the holding of a show in the town would benefit it in a pecuniary sense. —Mr. W. H. Linaker had seen several farmers who had ex- pressed a willingness to take part in the show if it were held in Runcorn.—Mr. Salkeld said twelve months was a long period to look forward, and people were apt to become luke- warm when an object was so far off. He thought that if a meeting were held nearer the time of the holding of the show, it would receive greater support. He would move, as had been suggested by Mr. W. H. Linaker, that a committee of twelve gentlemen should be formed to consider the matter and call a further meeting at a more convenient time, when they could decide upon the course which should be pursued.— Mr. /Sorman seconded the proposition, which was carried.— The following gentlemen were appointed on the committee: Dr. Steele, Messrs. John Brundrit, S. B. Chadwic'r, P. Bris- coe, Thomas Norman, W. Fisher, Henry Linaker, J. Harri- son, P. Percival,R. Holland, W. Baker, and W. Wilkinson.— After a vote of thanks had been passed to Dr. ,Steele for pre- I siding, on the motion of Mr. Briscoe; seconded by Mr. Fisher, the proceedings terminated.

In the Liverpool Revision Court, on Thursday, a woman was struck off the register because of her receipt of Parochial relief. She was not a pauper in the ordinary acceptance of the term, but her daughter was in an indus- trial school, and the parish authorities contributed a shil- ling a week towards her maintenance. The Liberal agent contendtd that this payment did not constitute parochial relief, and that the vote was therefore good, but the re- vising barrister took a contrary view and disallowed the vote.

MIDDLRIVICH ALEXANDRA. CRICKET Cum—This club met on Saturday last at the Magnet Coffee-house, to cele- brate the close of the season. A supper was provided for the occasion. The accounts for the past season were brought forward and verified, and a vote of thanks was passed to the secretaries (Messrs. Sproston and Lendop) for the highly consistent manner in which they had conducted the business of the club.

Fourth Battalion the King's (Liverpool Begiment): Captain Charles Louis Atterbury Farmar retires under the provisions of clause 173, army circulars, 1881, also is granted the honorary rank of major, and is permitted to wear the prescribed uniform on his retirement; Robert Merton Mana, gentleman, to be lieutenant. Thirel Battalion the Cheshire Regiment : Captain and Honorary Major William Vigar 'Fox retires under the provisions of clause 173, army circulars, 1881, also is permitted to retain his rank, and to wear the prescribed uniform on his retirement ; Quarter- master Edward Charles Hicks has been placed on a retired allowance, also is granted the honorary rank of c iptain, and is permitted to wear the prescribed uniform on his retire- ment. Fourth Battalion the Cheshire Regiment : Captain Thomas Unett Brocklehurst retires under the provisions of clause 182, army circular, 1831.—Militia Medical Depart- ment.—Surgeon-Nlajor Thomas Starkey Smith, Third Bat- talion Prince of Wales' Volunteels (South Lancashire Re- giment), resigns his commission.

SCHOOL FEES FROM POORS RATE IN LANCASHIRE.- A return just issued shows the sums distributed by the Poor Law Guardians in the shape of school fees, for the education of the out-door pauper children in public elemen- tary schools, during the year ending Lady Day, 1881. In 1881 the charges amounted to £33,045, against £31,916 in 1880, £2,464 in 1879, £21,546 in 1878, and, £16,650 in 1877. In Lancashire in 1881 the c)st was £4,313, agiinst £1,903 in 1880, £2,464 in 1879, and £1,910 in 1878.
