PRINCE OF WALES THEATRE, WARRINGTON. 0 Monday evening, the drama "Astray from the flock," by Mr. Alfred Beddoe, was placed upon the boards at this theatre for the first time. There was a crowded house. The piece is in four acts, the first scene being laid at a rural vil lags in Warwickshire. Alice Walker, a village maiden, is betrothed to Joshua Steer, the parish clerk, but through the connivance and machinations of Henry Greenwood, who is at enmity with Steer, she is brought in contact with Horace Bridgewater, a rich brewer's son. They fall in love, and an elopement is planned. Bridgewater, however, lacks the means to carry out the scheme, not having received an expected remittance from his father. Greenwood promises to obtain the requisite sum. He enters the rectory, where the dead body of the rector lies, breaks open the box where his gold was secured and craftily fixed the theft on Steer, who is obliged to leave the village. Three years elapse, Alice is the wife of Horace, and Steer from a good thrifty young man is converted into a misanthrope and a miser. Horace has not dared to inform his stern, unyielding father of his marriage, and his wife lives apart front him, with her child, in sumptuous apartments. His visits become brief and less frequent, and Alice learns from the brewer's hous2- keeper, Sally Harcourt, that he is betrothed, and is shortly to be marrLd, to an heiress. She deter mines to proclaim her- self to his father, and with her child in her arms starts on the journey on foot, through blinding wind and snow. Her strength fails her and she sinks down in the snow, before the hut of her rejected but constant lover Steer, in whose arms she dies brqueathing to his care her child. In the last act the chili has grown into a I andsome young girl, and Bridge- water, stricken with remorse, claims, her as his daughter. She spurns hire, saying Steer has been her true father. The Piece is a most fascinating one‘and was most tastefully put upon the stage. Miss Fairfax, in the double part of wife and daughter, takes her part most excellently, and without that excess of action which is so common. The part of Horace Bridgewater: was faithfully portrayed by Mr. J. 11. Ashley, and Mr. George Claremont, as Joshua Steer, is de- serving of great credit. As the crafty, scheming rogue Greenwood, Mr. 11. Cullenford took his part so well that the audience failed to separate Iris part from his acting, and hissed him. Mr. Alfred Buldoe's eccentricities as an Irish servant were most amusing ; not less so were the actions of the energetic and stong-tninded housekeeper, Sally Harcourt, represented by Miss Tilly Poole.

Facrs FOR "FAIR" TRADVIS.—Facts are generally reputed to be stubborn things, and those which Mr. T. P. Whittaker reproduces in the Nineteenth Century may well stand alonside Mr. Ecroyd's fallacies and fiction. This country, as Mr. Whittaker reminds us, has had some experi- ence of Protection and its effects. Those were terrible times —not very long ago either—when every commercial and agricultural interest was " protected." In the year 1842, in Glasgow, 12,000 people were on the relief funds; in Accring- ton, out of a population of 9,000, only 100 were fully em- ployed; in Marsden, near Burnley, half the people were on the rates, which were 12s. in the pound. In.the same year, the factory inspectors reported that 10 per 'tent, of the cotton mills and 12 per cent. of the woolen mills in York- shire and Lancashire were standing idle, and that of the rest only one-fourth were working full time. In Stockport the poor-rate was 10. s. in the pound, and 3,000 houses were unoccupied, while half the factories were shut up. Leeds had 30,000 and Sheffield 20,000 people on the rates. In Bolton the Poor Protection Society had nearly 7,000 appli- cants for relief. In 1816 rates at Hinckley, in Leicester- shire, were 525. in the pound! In the following year, in a porsetshire parish, 409 persons, out of a total population of 575, were in receipt of relief. while at Ely, the one-fourth, who were not paupers, had to keep the other three-fourths who were. This was in the days of the Corn Laws. In 1829 the workhouses wire so crowded that people had often to sleep five or six in a bed. Corn was 945. 9d. per quarter in 1817. 675. 101. in 1820, and 435. 4,1. in 1822. The price fixed by law for imported corn was 803. a quarter, at a time Iwhen farmers were ruined by thousands, and when a news- paper published in an agricultural county advertised 120 sales of stock in one day. In 1829, in Huddersfield, over 13,000 persons were in a state ot seini-starvation. County ;Irentlemen going up to London Carried aunties of the failure if rents all over the country, and the prospect of general ruin. Guizot says of the period 1836-40 that " disorder and crime, as well as nursery, increased with awful rapidity ; nearly half the houses were tenantless, the prisons over- flowed, infants died in their mothers' arms; fathers deserted their wives and families, striving to forget those whom they could no longer maintain." The worst of recent times were prosperity and plenty compared with the "coed old Tory days."

div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.

This Board met yesterday, by adjournment, to consider a proposal to purchase a plot of land in Duke's-field, at a cost of about £BOO. Dr. Steele occupied the chair.—The CHAIRMAN referred to the fact that Mr. Philip Speakman had objected at the meeting on Monday, to the minutes of the Highway Committee recommending the compulsory purchase of the plot of land—Mr. Handley moved the adop- tion of the recommendation of the committee. Dr. McDouGALL seconded the motion, and said that for a con- siderable time there had been a disposition to Boycott any proposition at that Board which had for its object the pro- motion of the best interests of the masses. He then gave a history of the negotiations which lind taken place during the last eighteen months with the Bridge-2 water Trustees, and others to carry out a scheme for dealing with the land referred to, and in which a builder of the name of Statham was interested. The land was known as Duke's Field, and abutted upon an old road- way leading to the Bridgewater docks, which was very much used by the people of Runcorn, and especially hy the working classes, The committee at first appeared to be animated by no other desire than that there should be a fair roadway to the only part of Runcorn which provided for the public anything approaching to pure air. At the last meet- ing of the committee he and others took objection to the action of a previous meeting at which Mr. StaLhatli'd plans I had been passed, and he received no other explanation as to why the course at first agreed upon had been deviated from than a statement to the effect that the Law Clerk bad said that the Manchester solicitor engaged for Mr. Statham would not state the exact amount of his costs, and, under such circumstances, he could not advise the Board to pro. coed with the matter. (Interruption by Mr. Shaw.) Really he must appeal to the Chairman in reference to the conduct tif Mr. Shaw, as it had become nearly a matter of impos- sibility for any member to make a statement at that Board without having to stiffer interruption from that gentleman. (I.iughter ) tJr could net c oiceive of any gretter niqilty ti in to attempt to limit tire an- spice of the community. They were sutrounded by a pertect amphitheatre of alkali works. (Laughter.) If the road in qiiestion, which led , to the river, was blocked up, there was no other means of exit unless the people went to Helsby, the Cheshire hills, or the Isle of Man. It was to the eiertal credit of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. that under no circumstances had they attempted to curtail the liberties of the Runcorn people in going to Duke's-field or the dock. The thoroughfare between Heath-road and Greenwity-road had cost the Commissioneis between £3OO and £4OO, and he thought that they would he quite justified in paying a fair amount for the land required in Duke's- field, for the purpose of holding it in trust for the rate- payers.—Mr. NORMAN considered it would be a very serious matter to Biddle the town with something like £BOO for all time; and he could not see his way to vote for the proposal. —Mr. SHAW ridiculed Dr McDougall's ideas as to the neces- sity of air space in the neighbourhood referred to. If there was any spot in the world where there was free air space it was the one in question. Only a short time ago the Com- missioners were very anxious to curtail the expenditure, and went so far as to alter the rate owing to the dulness of trade, yet there were gentlemen on that Board who solemnly proposed to vote for an expendiiure of MO, when there was no engineer would say that the land was neeeed in order to provide sacs.—'lr. MEADowcnorr thought that the gentleman who had caused the members to be brought together-specially that morning, in order to discuss the sub- ject before them, had shown a want of respect in not giving a proper explanation about it..—[Dr. 11.1cDonostt : Hear, hear.]—He had on previous occasions strongly supported Dr. McDougall's contention upon the matter, but things had since occurred which modified his views, and caused him to hesitate before incurriag so large an expenditure. In all fairness, Mr. Shaw ought to have given utterance to the opinions he had expressed that morning, at previous meet- ings when the question had been under discussion.—Mr. Mr. SHAW protested against Mr. Meadowcoft's re- mark, on the ground that in former discussions about the plot of land the Board had never gone further than to propose that £4O should be spent upon the proposal.-Mr.MEanowenot^r. asked whether the formation of parks or boulevards, were Matters which were al ways decided upon the question of air space.—Mr. Straw said the question would have been entirely altered if it been proposed to buy the land for the purpose of establishing a park.—Mr. MEADowenorr considered the arguments of Mr. Shaw had been entirely refuted.-Mr. SHAW : I must object.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT replied that it was quite open to Mr. Shaw to object, but the fact remained unaltered. He had thought it necessary to mike these observations, though he should not support the the motien—[mfr. SHAW: Oh, oh ! and laughter,]—as there were now upon it about £2OO value in erections, and a large amount of unused material. If they resorted to the Board's compulsory powers, there would be the expense of arbitration.— Mr. P.SPFAIBIAN: I think it is a matter of regret that the committee appointed to go into this matter have not done so more energetically.—Dr. lilp.Douciatt: I must protest against such a remark—(laughter)—about a committee who have done all they possibly could.-.-Mr. P. SPEA.KmAs said that if the Proposal were c trried out it would entail an ex- penditure of £lOOO, and CHISC such an uprising as had never been seen in the town before.—Mr. LAKE was of opinion it would be a great pity that the portion of the town referred to should be entirely spoiled. He moved an amendment "That so much of the land be purchased as would make the thoroughfare the width of 36 feet.' That would be show one-third of £BOO, and so reduce the amount thrown upon the rates.—Mr. FISHER seconded Mr. Lake's proposal--Ti.• Cruiamirr thought that it WAS a pity the Iteinster-tetrac property should be depreciated by the erection of property similar to that now being put up, the property owners avin. the people who ought to deal with the matter. It would h. a pity to saddle the ratepayers with an expenditure of £BOO and it would likewise be unwise to pay compensation te Mr. Statham in order that the road might he widened.—Mi HANDLEY said one of the most important duties of a govern• ing body was to see that a town was laid out and hod, is proper manner. The coach road had always been Ii her; upon as being one of the pretty outlets of Rune irn, end le was of opinion they were not stepping the ordinary pith of their duty in trying to presery There voted for Mr. Lake's amendment:—Messrs. rile Dougall, Lake, and Handley (3). Against :—Messrs. Steele, Norman, Williams, J. Speakman, Briscoe, Shaw, and J. J Speakman (7). The amendment was therefore declared lost. Mr. Meadowcroft left the room during the voting The original proposition was then put and lost by a larg( majority, only Messrs McDougall and Handley voting for it.

div.head: DARING ROBBERY OF JEWILLEHN
div.p: DARING ROBBERY OF JEWILLEHN

AT IIUYTON. Early on Friday night last one of the most daring and impudent robberies that has occurred in this district foi some time took place at Huyton, when a gentleman's resi- dence was entered by the bedroom window, and upwards o £7O worth of jnvellery stolen. In Graham's-road, in thf North Park, in addition to other houses, there are two at- tached houses, one of which is occupied by Mr. William Reynolds, a cotton merchant, of Liverpool, while the othel is at present unoccupied. It appears that on the night in question, between eight and ten o'clock, the empty house was entered, an entrance being effected by means of the cellar window, the sash of which had been bored and the latch forced back. The thief then seems to have proceeded upstairs, opened the front room window, and by means of a water pipe between the two houses, succeeded in getting on to the top of the bay-window of Mr. Reynolds' house, and thence into the bedroom. A wardrobe was opened (the key having been left in the lock) and a box containing a large quantity of jewellery taken away. The jewellery consisted of a lady's gold Geneva half-hunting watch, and silver albert guard attached, with three or four coins, and a champagne- bottle shaped silver pencil case, a gold diamond ring, heart. shaped, with diamond set in ; a gold diamond ring, set with five diamond atones; pair of gold acorn ear-rings; pair of gold interlinked ear-rings ; pair of gold ear-rings, long- shaped ; two pairs of coral ear-rings: gold locket, oval shaped, set with pearls and emeralds, with gold locket at- tached; gold Italian seal ; and a gold pernil case. The rob- bery was discovered about ten o'clock, but information was not given to the police, it is at tted, until nearly art hour afterwards, and of course the thief had ample epportuniti,s of making off 71th his plunder in the meantime. The police, as yet, have no clue to the perpetrator, but it is the opinion of many persons in the locality that the robbery was com- mitted by 83111 C one COnVereAnt with the premises,as nothiwz in the bedroom, with the exception of the jewellery, was ill any way interfered with.

HAIIVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT Si. HELENS PARISH CHURCH.—oe Thursday night, a harvest thanks- giving servic3 was held in the Parish Church, when the Rev. W. 11. Marsden, of Southport, delivered a sermon to a crowded congregation. The church was beautifully deco- rated with flowers, oats, fruits, and banners. The commu- nion table bore three silver plates of apples and grapes, and glasses of beautiful flowers. Entering the communion at each end of tho rails were sheaves of corn with bands of flowers around them. • On the wall immediately over tin communion table were beautiful devices worked in cereals, mosses, and flowers. The reading desk in front of the com- munion was also beautified with a floral arrangement, and the reading desk.in front of the pulpit was similarly deco- rated, except that tbe latter was mote profusely . covered with oats. The pulpit, of cou-se, wa's the principal object of attraction, its decoration necessitating a great amount of time and labour. On the top of the pulpit externally there was a border of green leaves, over which hung apples atealises u tlanctes tphfefipvuelpoirt six inches. On each of the eight pu flowers prettily arranged were placed in a triangular pocket, and up each corner of the panel were cereal arrangements. Immediately below the panels, cape flowers were set in a moss ground of four or five inches broad, and below this lining a hinge of oats. The font was nice adorned with an arram;ement of moss and flowers, a beautiful bouquet rest- ing in the basin. On the front of the south side of the . gallery were the words of scripture, " Ile shall eat in ' plenty, and prAist) the 1...0,d over all with the tirst friths on the west side on the line uf the clock, " I will magnify Him with thanksgiving ;" and on the north side, " Thou satisfiest the desire of every living thing." In front of the communion tat.le were several hot-house plants, contributed by Colonel Gamble, Mr H. S. Hall, Mr. Varley, and Mrs. C. Bishop. The window sills bore flowers and vegetables.

div.head: MR. THOS. BEASLEY'S BANKRUPTuY
div.p: MR. THOS. BEASLEY'S BANKRUPTuY

The case of Mr. Thomas Beasley, solicitor, of Widnes. a bankrupt, again came on for hearing at the Liverpool Bank- ruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Perronet Thompson, judge. Mr. Henry Gregory appeared on behalf of the credi- tors, and said the bankrupt had been several times before the court for his public examination, and even now the accounts were not sufficiently completed to enable the trustee to make a report. A meeting took place at the trustee's office on Wednesday, when the bankrupt gave an assurance that, through his friends, be would probably be in a position shortly to make an offer to the creditors. He (Mr. Gregory) felt, under these circumstances, the best thing to do would be to ask for an adjournment of the public examination sTe die, so that these repeated applications would be obviated. Mr. Segal, barrister. who appeared for other creditors, quite approved of this course. Mr. Copeinan, who represented the bankrupt, said Mr, Beasley was perfectly ready to answer any further qnei.rions. lii litmour agreed to an adjourn- ment sine die.

LEC:URE BY THE REV. PRII,II' RAINS, AT ST. HELENS. On Monday evening a lecture was given in the Assembry Room of the Town Hall, by the Rev. Philip Heins, of Wigan, on "Land-marks in the History of Human Pro- gress." The proceeds of the lecture, which are small, on account of the poor attendance, will be devoted to the funds in aid of the proposed new Wesleyan Chapel and schools at Nutgrove. The chair was occupied by Dr. McNicoll, and there were also on the platform the Revs. M. Walmsley, W. G. Pascoe, W. C. Tayler, and J. Brown.—The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheers, said that if it was well to be zealously affected in a good cause, then he was sure that the youftg spirits that dwell in the region of Nutgrove, who were present and who were not present, deserved their commenda- tion and praise for the pertinacity with which they carried on the work of raising funds for their contemplated new chapel and schools. They had had discouragements, but they did not seem to be made of that stuff which bends be- fore disaster. He. was sorry to find not so full a meeting as they had relied upon, but that was due to a rival meeting in the shape of a concert at the Volunteer Hall. When there were two rivals in the field and one appealed to the under- standing and the other to the emotions—music, he knew which would win the day. (Laughter.) Nutgrove was at Thatto Heath, but the people at Nutgrove did not like the name of Thatto Heath, nor should he if he lived there. (Laughter.) It was a little bright spot on Thatto Heath, but who liked to dwell on a heath? Nutgrove had some- thing poetical about it; and it had something very agree- able about it. Well, they had tried all means to raise the money, and as they could not do it by direct taxation they did it by indirect taxation, and appealed to the public by lectures. As they could not live on an aurora borealis suc- cess let them hope that they would have the permanent sun of prosperity to shine upon them for ever in the chapel and schools of this and future generations. As the object was good so the means were good; and whilst having a good subst tntial lecture and contributing to their cause, the Nut- grove people were contributing to their instruction and grati- fication. So that they were quite even wfth the public. (Laughter.) If they asked a shilling or two they got more than their money's worth. The Lecturer's name was well- known, although his presence had not been largely known amongst them.—The LECTURER said the lecture would not be a political one. Such a design as giving a history of human progress would be presumptuous, and he would only give a few landmarks. Anything like a complete history of mankind on earth, he believed, had never been written, and perhaps never would be written. All they could venture to do was to grope about as with a dark lantern and endeavour to decipher the meaning of what they could get, and at the very best only with purblind eyes. It had been stated that our system knew no development. The earth, described pre- cisely the same orbit when there was no man on earth ; the seasons were precisely the same; the planets, sun, 10030, and stars were no better now than they were millions of years ago. So far as the world of matter was concerned, it had stood still, and the world of spirits alone was moving on. Even this latter statement could be received only with reservation. When they spoke of the history of mankind they meant an account of man since the flood.. With the exception of the narrative of the B'ble they knew nothing of the early history of man. Tot thousand as ego there was a civilised race existing in Anit tic, as diecovery of bones near the Nli.siosiptii had shown.fli re mast have been a civilieed and a highly rdaa ded r tc- on the continent of Americ t. Our chtnnoloey was woefully defee'lve. We I knew that in the beginning tied created the lieevens and ' the etrth, hilt we were net in!ortned when CI Ii e,lna.ng was or how it cAne about. A; edaishop Usher, Mii we acknow- ledged as an authority, had fixed the 1,-„leLing of the I 'amid 4,004 years before the Christian ea, v.' list another had said it was 5,411 anterior to the coming of the Messiah, showing a difference of 1,407 years. Calendars differed, , .and as they were entitled to equal, respect there was no doubt they were all equally wrong. All would admit that man was capable of development. The Chinese were much in the same state now as they were. What that was good or noble ever came from the children of the sun, where reigned perpetual midsummer, or from the children of the Poles? They had known r o progress. Fifteen hundred years after *Grecian and Roman literature Christopher Columbus discovered the great tropical regions of the Western Continent, and Washington Irving described the , natives as being stricken with awe at the appearance of the Europeans and their ships ; they made signs of adoration and then fled to the woods thinking that Columbus and his ' crew were inhabitants of the skies. The existence of those I islanders was like a pleasant dream, their fields without labour furnishing them with food. This had been their ! contln thousands of years before, because they had had ' ne :n.e-course with the rest of mankind. America now con- .scivilieed and an intellectual race of men. Human ' progroes in Asia and Africa was not only stationary but re- tro.irmie. They gemmed to have been more prosperous than th y are now. In Europe and the United States they had beep progressive, and bad outstripped the elder brothers of the-East. How was this? The lecturer went on to say that it was owing to our geographical position, the superi- ority of the people mentioned above, arisiug from that graceful inclination which our mother earth makes to that I grand luminary the sun. He took this as the first land mark in the civilisation of the European portion of the human race. Man was a creature capable of improvement and pro- gress. All animals were vet y much the same as they were ages ago. The ligh'e of civilisation were extinguished dur- ing tbat7.period which is called the Dark Ages, bat individual man never slept, except in the case of Rip Van Winkle, so IS to forget all that he ever learnt. Tbe Chaldeans ap- oe.ne 1 to be a people who made the first rapid improve- meets and the Land of the Pharaohs was a civilised country when Greece was in her swaddling clothes. Herodot us, 500 years before Christ, told us that the arts of civilisation flourished in Egypt. there were astronomers, geometricians, architects' mathematicians, chemists, mechanics of the ' highest order, even as great or greater than those that exist among ourselves. An extraordinary chemical process was known in F.gypt, but ultimately the particular shades pro- duced by the process were lost: and after the secret had been pronounced irrecoverable for three thousand years the process was discovered by a gentleman in litistol. (Ap- plause ) The Eg.yptians, the lecturer went on to say, were deficient in poetry and eloquence, and the Hebrews were the most ancient poets known but with this exception, they were children when the Egyptians were full-grown I men. To Cadmus, the phoenician, we were indebted for in- troducing into Greece all alphabet of 16 letters, which was ultimately increased,this being 1490 yearsbefore Christ. The lecturer, proceeding, said that the Illiad was a faithful representation of men and women belonging to the Heroic Age, and as such it served as an epoch in the history of human progress. Many trivial circumstances served as important epochs in history by which time was reckoned such as the Olympian Races. The founding of Rome by Romilus presented another significant landmark or point in the history of human progress, for after this chronology be- came comparatively clear. The first public library was founded in Athens, 500 years before Christ. Greece was a lover of the beautiful, and it was extraordinary that such a I power of intellect should have existed then. Her chief glory was that she was the teacher of mankind. There lied been, said the lecturer, great poets, historians, philosophers, sculptors, painter', and logicians, since the golden age of Grecian literature ; but they had all been inheritors and itnitttors of Greece. She exhibited all the wisdom, philoso- phy, poetry, and erudition, in the very first bloom of youth as it were; but this occurred only once in the history of mankind, and it was this that made the enduring power of Grecian manner, and all the Grecian influences, a most ex- traordinary phenomenon in the history of the human mind The Romans, with their admirable government and military 0'37, and jurisprudence, conquered the Greeks, but in literature became copver of a people they never equalled. The captive cynic Diogenes said, r can govern men ;- therefore sell me to some one who is in want of a master:' It was just so with the Greeks: they became master of their conquerors. After all, if the Romans had not been in existence we should never have been taught that reverence for law which in England is liberte's safeguard. Of course, he considered Christianity as a landmark in the bietory of human progress, but it was destined to be greater than it is in MI: it succeeded to Pagan philosophy, and beyond every attempt of Greece or Rome. We had to thank Christianity for the abolition of the gladiatorial shows. and for the abolition of the herrers to which prisoners of war were subjected. There was now respect paid to women, and they had the greatest reason to he indebted to Christianity for the position they now occupy. If we searched the history of Rome or Greece we should never find that they erected a hospital for the ameli- oration of human staff !ging. The history of the world showed that civilisation was tending westward. After speaking of the treatment to which some who had made landmarks in the human race were subjected, and the violent deaths of others, he went on 03 speak of soldiery, remarking that a Christian cenald net enter the profession of a soldier of his own free will. The sehoolmAster was, however, abroad, aud he. beli..ved the time would come wben the questions between nations would be settled in a more humane and Christian-like fasltion.

On the motion of the Rev. J. 13Bovnl, seconded by the Rev.W. G. Pascon, a vote of thanks VMS accorded to the lecturer; and a similar compliment was paid to the chair- man, on the motion of the Rev. J. M. WLIZISLET, seconded by Rev. W. C. TATUM.

conveyed to Galway Gaol. The warrant charges him firing with intent to kill. The reply of the Goy - fusing an inquiry into the conduct of the police during late rioting at Lilaerick was read by the Mayor at the sessions yestetday. His Worship said that if necessary he would wait on every member of Parliament in Ire- land to insist on the inquiry being held. He would call a monster meeting to condemn the action of the Government. He dared the Government at its peril to proclaim that meeting.

The Triumvirate of the Transvaal have sent a telegraphic despatch to Mr. Glatisone, in which they set out the objec- tionable clauses in the Newcastle Convention. They declare that the Convention ig contrary to the Sand River Treaty of 1852, and is in many respects an open breach of the peace agreement entered into by Sr Evelyn Wood, on behalf of the Queen, and the Boer leaders, who, trusting that the princi- ples then laid down would be executed, laid down their arms. The Volksraad request that articles 2 and 18 be so altered that the Suzerain shall Lave no right to the conduct of foreign affairs, but only a control. They add that tlte peace agreement was that the Boers should have complete self-government, whereaus they stand articles 3, 13, and 26 are a breach of the solemn treaty. The demand that the Suzerain shall have no right of approval of the Transvaal laws. The Resident, they say, being a foreigner, cannot be a trustee of property belonging to the citizens; that it is infra. dig. far the President to be a member of any cotmnis- sion ; that although willing to pay their debts the Voiks- raad want proofs and vouchers, which have not yet been given ; that article 8, as to "commandeering," should dis- appear; and that al ticles 15, 16, 26, and 27 are superfluous and only calculated to offend. The movement of troops towards the coast has been stopped. ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION OF MR. ULADSTONE

RUNQ.VRN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. 'The monthly roteting was held on Monday. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Messrs. Lyon, Williams, P. 'Speakman, Briscoe, Shaw, Handley, Lake, Fisher, 3. X. Speakman, Linalor (law clerk), Brookes (sec- etari), and Barker (surveyor).

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT .-REMARKABLY LOW DEATH RATE. Dr. Mounuz presented his report, which showed that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month numbered 11, representing a death rate•of a fraction less than nine per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths four were due to disease of the nervous system and two to Mesenteric disease. Cancer, gangrene, diarrhcea, hemorr- hage, and senile decay accounted for one each. Four in- quests were held, making the total deaths 13. He had attended three cases of scarlet fever on the canal bank during the past month, and given the nuisance inspector instructions as to what steps be should take to suppress the outbreak. The result was satisfactory, as each of the per- sons was convalescent, and no additional cases had been reported. The death rate was the lowest he had ever known since he had been appointed to the office of medical officer, about 161- years ago. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE -MR. STATHAM'S MATTER-THE NEW GLYCERINE WORKS.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee showed that Mr. Thomas Norman had been appointed chair- man. The committee recommended that the surveyor should serve a notice upon Mr. J. lligby, requesting him not to pro- ceed with the washhouses at the rear of his property in Perry- street and Prescot-terrace. That the surveyor should invite tenders for team labour ; that the construction of Percival- lane and Ashridge-street be deferred for six months. That a sub-committee consisting of Messrs. Handley, Norman, Taylor, Lake, Fisher, and P. Speakman be appointed to con- sider the best means of ventilatiag the sewer in Moughland's- road. That a sub-committee be formed, consisting of Messrs. P. Speakman, Norman, Handley, McDougall, Lake, and Fisher to consider the desirability of applying for a pro- visional order for the alteration of the boundaries of the district and other purposes. That the tender of Mr. H. Sefton to do the team labour for 12 months be accepted. That the surveyor require plane of the glycerine works on the Sprinch to be submitted. That with reference to the report of the subcommittee on the ventilation of Moughland's-road sewer, it be recommended that a 10in, ventilating shaft be fixed to the sewer near to the Cemetery Lodge. With reference to report of the sub-committee on Waterloo Bridge, it was re- commended that competitive plans be obtained, and the same be referred back for consideration. That notice be given to the Bridgewater Trustees, and Mr. Statham, that the Com- missioners intend exercising the powers vested in them for the compulsory purchase of the land in Duke's Field upon which Mr. Statham is erecting eleven houses, and that the Law Clerk be empowered to take the necessary steps for carrying it into effect. Mr. HANDLEY proposed, and Mr. FISHER seconded the motion for the adoption of the minutes. Mr. PHILIP SPEAKMAN said he had to object to that portion of the minutes dealing with Mr. Statharn's matter. The CLERK said that if the minute was objected to, it could not be discussed at that meeting, but only atone held within six days from that date. Mr. SHAW objected to the minute of the committee proposing to ask the proprietor of the new glycerine works for a plan of the manufactory, as it had not been customary to adopt such a course in the case of works previously erected. As long as the manufactories were put up in a manner satisfactory to the surveyor, it was sufficient. The CHAIRMAN considered Mr. Shaw's objection a good one, in one sense, but he reminded him that in this particular case the works were new. Mr. HANDLEY remarked that at the last meeting of the committee it was reported that though the erection of the glycerine manufactory was being pro- ceeded with, no plans had been. submitted. The action which the committee had taken was not dictated by any desire to pry into the secrets of any process adopted by the manufacturer, but simply to have an assurance that the buildings were being erected in a manner which would not at any time cause any danger to life or limb. The committee were also bound to see that the smoke nuisance was kept within reasonable limits. Mr. PHILIP SPEAKMAN considered this merely another in- stance of the plan so often adopted by that Board of locking the door of the stable after the horse had been stolen. It had been known for months that the manufactory in ques- tion was to be erected, and surely the proper course would have been for the Commissioners to have taken action before the proprietor had commenced to put up the building.—Mr. LYON thought it very undesirable that the Board should in- terfere in this case, as submitting plans would, probably, lay open some secret connected with the manufacture.— Mr. SHAW: Which many people are anxious to get to know. (Laughter.) I will move that the minute 'in question be sent back to the committee for re-consideration.—Dr. Mc- DOUGALL thought it very strange that the representatives of various works in the town should take such' a strong and extraordinary objection as they had done in this case. It was quite possible there might be sewage of an objection- able character passed into the town sewers from the works. What was sauce for the goose was sauce for the gander. There ought to be some supervision of the works in the course of construction, even if it were only for the sake of protecting the lives and limbs of the ratepayers. He should be very sorry to do anything which would seem to be like Prying into any secrets in connection with the works. Widnes had been referred to in the discussion, but he main- tained that they did such extraordinary things at that town that the authorities there were really no guide. (Laughter.) —The amendment was then put and carried, six out of those present voting in favour of it.—On the proposition of Mr. SPEAKMAN, seconded by Mr. SHAW, it was resolved that the whole subject of Mr. Rigby's property be referred back to the Highway and Sanitary Committee.

THE NEW HOSPITAL. The committee's minutes stated that the Surveyor had been instructed to prepare detailed plans of the proposed hospital.—Mr. HANDLEY moved the adoption of the minutes and remarked that the committee intended to bring the full scheme in connection with the hospital before the next Board meeting.
IMPORTANT ACTION AGAINST HAWKERS. PROTECTION V. FREE TRADE.

The General Purposes Committee recommended the ap- pointment of Dr. McDougall as chairman, And that with reference to a petition received from 94 shopkeepers, it be recommended that notices be published to the effect that, on and after 3rd October, the provisions of section 13 of the Markets and Fairs Clauses Acts, 1847, would be enforced by prosecuting all persons actiim in contravention thereof. -WHERE ISCALEDONIAN SOCIETY? Sir,—' have read with profound interest two letters which I have appeared in your contemporaries of last week relative' to the St. lielens " Caledonian Society." I have many times wondered what had. become of it, as it is no very good sign when We hear so little of their doings, because when a so- ciety is in a healthy c indition they generally make a great I fuss, and are not the least bashful of letting the public know how they stand tinancially, and with regard to num- bers, but alas, this so-called " Caledonian Society" seems to have ; neither called a meeting of its members lately, nor given any financial statement since it was first instituti.d.. Now there must be a want of energy somewhere, either on the part of the committee or its secretary ; but surely soine ens belonging to the society will give the desired informa- tion, and restore confid-nce in the minds of its members. I am perfectly sure that if more energy were exercised on the part of the committee no society in St. Helens would he more prosperous or prove a greater credit to the Scotch population of St. Helens and neighbourhood. I myself could induce many of my Scotch acquaintances to become members, provided the committee could be induced to lower their annual subscription to one half its present amount, as the poorer class of working Scotchmen find it too much for them, especi tlly when they have families to maintain. always thought that their secretary was a regular Living- stone, and would go tnrough tire and water to elevate the condition of his Scottish brethren, and more especially the I less fortunate for whose benefit it was especially founded. I well remember a Scotch friend a mine saying to me "We have made a good choice of secretary; he is a tine young Scotchman. I remember him since he was a wee laddie in kilts, and he hails free the seine neighbourhood as the great African pioneer (David Livingstone), and I sin sure he will hunt every Scotchman ia the neighbourhood. He is the right man in the right place." Now I hope that our young friend will not let such a valuable cause die out for the want of effort —Yours truly, LOCHINVAR. St. Helens, October sth, 188 L

THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES aoserrAL. Sir,—Unlike Alderman Burmss I do sometimes write to the papers, and to put a fitaish'ing touch to the proceedings of the Town Council on Tuesday last, I now again indulge in the propensity. You are doubtless aware that the com- pulsory power of removals is vested in the Corporation, and the power of the Corporation in this respect is delegatt.d by the Council to the Sanitary Committee. This delegation of power, however, does not limit the Council's power, and all acts of the committee are subject to the approval and ratifi- cation of the Council. What I wish to point out to your readers is the following extraordinary state of circumstances. Alderman Burgess said on Tuesday evening as follows Let this C.,unc I thoroughly understand, if it has not done beforo, that of the 150 cases that have been received into the hospital this year, none have appeared before the committee in any shape or form. The chairman of the committee has had no more to do with the removals than Councillor Jeans has." I can vouch for the fact that the Council has not caused any of the removals, inasmuch, as the resolution of the Council passed in September, 1880. requiring all cases of Infectious disease to be removed to the hospital, was rescinded in February last. Alder man Burgess vouches for the fact that not one of the 150 removals has been brought before the Sanitary Committee, and that he has had nothing to do with the rein rvalA, and this is consistent with the fact that not one single case has been reported to, or brought under the notice of, the Council in any way. When asked "Who has removed them ?" he replies, What is that to you ?" I leave the inhabitants of Warrington to answer that question, feeling satisfied myself with the expression of opinion given by the Council. After Alderman Burgess's dis- avowal of the whole proceedings on the part of himself and the Sanitary Committee, the only inference that can be drawn, is, that the functions and power of the Corporation have, with the tacit assent of the Sanitary Coinmitee, been usurped by the Corporation officials. It is quite true that the Council cannot by any resolution repeal their Act of Parliament, or do away with any power which the law has vested in them, but it is competent for the Council, as the governing body, to lay down any general rule for the guidance of their officials, and it is the duty of the Sanitary Committee and the officials to obey the orders of the Council. The will of the Council in this matter has at length been expressed, and it is to be hoped that we shall hear of no more abuse of power.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, WM. DAMPIER JEANS.

MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE, &C. Sir,—! hope Mr. Peers his not been taking the flattering unction to his soul during the past fortnight that he has controversially annihilated me. Absence in London, and not the consciousness of defeat, has prevented me giving his letter my earlier attention, and I will now offer a few com- ments thereon. The principal objects he seems to have had in view in writing it are, first:to make the public acquainted with the interesting fact that he is a great reader both of elassical and "blood and thunder" literature, though, judg- ing by the aptness with which he quoted some choice work entitled "The bloody coal sack," and the peculiar refine- ment and delicacy of his style, I should imagine the "blood and thunder" species to be his chief favourites; secondly, the very praiseworthy endeavour to overwhelm me, no mat- ter by what means, with ridicule; and thirdly, finding, I suppose, that my arguments were unanswerable, he has thought to obscure the real issue by a multitude of scriptural quotations paragraphs of proverbs which hardly bespeak the wisdom of a Solomon, rhetorical anathemas that are full of sound and fury, but unfortunately contain little that is more substantial and edifying than sound and fury, and wholesale abuse both of persons and principles; and under cover of the cloud of dust which he has thus raised he is trying to make good his escape. No doubt your readers will estimate Mr. Peers's letters at their true worth and will refuse to be blinded by his sophistries, They will see that in spite of the rain of his abuse, and the wind of his unrighteous indigna- tion, and the floods of his egotistical and valueless verbosity, the argumentative house which I built has not fallen, butre- mains perfectly firm, for it was founded upon a rock. Here my case is, quite sound. Our limited monarchical system is a strong bend of loyalty and consequently of union in an empire, upon the continued existence of which depend, not only England's greatness, but the welfare of many millions of our degraded fellow subjects in other climes. Is that no- , thing ? Our limited monarchical system imparts a per- manence to our institutions which in republican states is altogether lacking; while other countries are deluged with anarchy, the 'spent spray of the revolutionary wave" alone reaches our shores. Is that nothing? All grades of society and all interests in the country are represented in it. The working classes in a democracy have by virtue of members supreme power and their voice being, on your correspon- dent's own admission, sometimes rather the opposite of divine; while a self-seeking demagogue can play upon the ignorance of many of them and get them to vote just as he pleases. I contend that the riglA of the rich are not secure in their hands, and, at any rate until the popular voice becomes more reliable, more just, and more patriotic, it is very necessary to have a check upon it. That check is furnished by our limited monarchical system. Is that nothing? Noble institutions are patronised by that system, ecl at is lent to great and important national gather- ings by it, its members work hard for the good of the coun- try, it tends to ensure the unity and efficiency of the army, under it England has risen to the highest position which any nation ever occupied, and though she is ever looked upou as the truest horns of liberty beneath the sun, through- out her realms there is a great gulf fixed between liberty and licence. Are these nothing? Are we prepared to des- troy our monarchical system and with it these great benefits which it confers? And are we ready to run the risk of a terrible civil war which might extend far beyond our shores in our aspirations after a republic? For this is more than a mere possibility, and I cannot allow Mr. Peers to argue ' that because he is an " unchivalric soul" everyone else is ' the same. His is not the only mental organization extant, and if he would not fight for a system he loved others would. He may try to laugh sentiment and chivalry out of existence, bat he will never succeed. True there was no rebellion when the Reform Bill was passed, and a step was taken to- wards perfecting our constitutional system. When a step is taken towards destroying that system by the endeavour to abolish monarchy an integral part of it, the case may be rather different, I fancy. Well, in changing our system of government we forfeit all the advantages I have named, . and we are most probably plunged into a bloody revolution. And when we have changed it—if that be possible—in what are we the gainers? Why, we may, perhaps, be each two- pence three farthings per anm the richer. To quote Mr. Peers, "Is the game worth the candle ?" And even the two- pence three farthings is doubtful, for our new republic might plunge us into such difficulties as would involve an increase instead of a reduction in taxation. More than this. Not only might we miss the twopence three farthings, but we might, as a result of the new republic have, as France as had, eight revolutions in tee next ninety years; or we might sink to the level of the United States, which with all its vaunted freedom was a slave-holding country for 30 years after this ill-ruled England, which loved liberty so much that it turned the jubilee singers from its hotels because they bad black skins and sent their' over to our slavish land to be entertained right royally by the Queen and the noblest of her subjects, the machinery of whosa politics is, to quote one of the most eminent of living Americans, "turned by the hand of Satan," and where a noble-minded president has only to set his face against a most glaring abuse to be as- sassinated. I would speak with no disrespect of America. I wish her all success, and I am most happy to see how closely we are drawing together; but I cannot close my eyes to the evils which exist in what is called by way of eminence "the great republic," and I also would quote a proverb and tell Mr. Peers and his fellow demo- crats to " look before they leap," and to be careful lest they jump "out of the frying pan into the fire." There is my case "in a nntshell," as Mr. Peers so prettily remarks. The abolition of our limited monarchical system would involve the sacrifice of many most important benefits that result from it: to abolish it a bloody revolution might be necessary; and when it was abolished, though Mr. Peers might possibly be twopence three farthings per annum the richer, the chances are that we should be much worse governed than we are at present, should be less truly free than our limited monarchical system makes us, and should be in perpetual danger of revolution (vide the cases of the United States and France). Therefore, I contend that under present circumstances it would be the reverse of prudent to endeavourform of osfubstitute a republican for our limited monar- chical I government; and, for my part, I am quite prepared to pay the twopence three farthings, which that system renders necessary. lam sorry that amount pr a r much upon the mind of Mr. Peers; but really, if b will look at the matter calmly and without bias, and f. m a patriotic rather than from -a penerions point of view, I be

MR. ANNETT AND THE RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. Sir,—l believe any impartial and merely casual reader of Mr. Jelin Simpson's speech made at the last meeting of the School Board, and reported in your issue of Ist inst., will con- clude that it was uttered during a fit of temporary intoxication brought on by vexation and spite through defeat, and that consequently, like all persons suffixing from this malady, he was for the time being seen (salvos ntentis. To a man who is an absolute ruler in more than one establish- ment in this little town, defeat by a commoner, such as my- self, must of necessity be mortifying and galling in the extreme. Yet I never for one moment thought that Mr. John Simpson would have so far forgotten himself as to allow his feelings to obtain entire mastery over his judg- ment and cause him to utter statements that are, in the face of facts, simply monstrous. Mr. Simpson charges me, in ad- dition to supreme ability in the perversion or facts, and Ifalsifications of statements (which I assume can be readily expressed by the plain and expressive old English word "lying," and of course a second assumptien follows) with a want of honour and Christian courtesy. In thinking over Mr. Simpson's various moves since he began to take so deep an interest in me. I don't think the public can consider him a fit person to act as judge of these 2u tlities, for what do we find ? In your issue of June 4th, he figured prominently in preferring a charge of severity against me, utterly without a cause; he then tried intimidation as a means to secure his ends, for be buttonholed Her Majesty's Inspector in a rail- way carriage during a slim t journey to Chester, made an ex parte sta:ement, and drew from him the remark" Mr. Annett will lose his certificate if he continues to ref use the returns." Armed with.this authority he rushed off to one of the managers of my school, so anxious is he to curb my " cantankerous" nature—and thus, as is his wont, have un- disputed sway again—and urged upon hint the necessity of an Immediate interview with me. Like a man of true Christian courtesy, the said manager hastened to me and repeated Mr. Simpson's utterances, not omitting to point out the enormity of my offence and the severe punishment I was liable to according to Mr. Simpson's notion; he even urged me to go and thank Mr. Simpson for the interest he was taking on my behalf. I need not say that I did not act on this advice, as I felt convinced that the rattling of the machinery and railway carriage wheel's had carved Mr. Shampson to misunderstand the inspector's remarks. Mr. Simson's next ;act was to second a motion moved by Mr. Norman, "That the decision of the department be asked on the matter," and after receiving one adverse to himself, he in a fit of anger, apparently bordering on desperation, falls back on the state- ment that my previous letter was a tissue of falsehoods— gentlemanly without doubt. But stop! He can't let the matter rest even here, for I perceive that he intends writing himself to the department, and in the same breath advocates inditing a letter to the managers of these school.r, making certain enquiries. Ah ! why did he not do this at first? Then he would have set an example of "Christian cour- tesy," for I can assure Mr. Simpson that it was owing to the lack of "Christian courtesy" on his part, and the spirit of persecution (I can call his high handed actions and bitter remarks by no other name), that characterised his every movement in this case that caused me t) fight the battle through, being confident of success. And now, sir, I must throw myself upon your clemency, and ask you to bear with me whilst I, as briefly as possible, comment upon my previous "falsification of facts." In the first place, Mr. Simpson again strokes the officer down the back by stating that my remarks reeoecting the said officer were "false," " without foundation," and so forth, and that the letter to the depart- ment was an amendment upon my letter to the Board (by the way, I have never pen ed any letter to that body; there- fore that that Mr. Simpson criticised existed only in his imagination). Well, sir, it is evident Mr. Simpson and his party believe their officer. My managers believe me and my assistant. Surely no one will deny that my supporters are not as honourable, truthful, and sensible as are the repre- sentatives of the ratepayers. I still assert that the statement that I complained of was made, and maintain that Mr. Simpson has not been able to prove that it was not, except by the mouth of the individual charged with the utterance of the remark, which in a court of justice would not be accepted as sufficient evidence. In reference to the letter to the department, and Mr. Simpson's remarks thereon : He is chagrined at the numerous complaints therein contained over and above those made to the officer. But I would remind Mr. Simpson that the officer is not paid wages to carry messages, or to be the mouthpiece of the Board to the teachers, or of teachers to the Board. In fact, I would not condescend at any time to give an officer of a School Beard all my reasons for not obliging such a body. Mr. Simpson's subsequent remarks on the officer's work conclude that my statements could not be substantiated. Perhaps his mind will be dis- abused of this by the figures I append. He next accuses me of failing to do my duty previously to May last. I have looked through my letter of agreement and can find no mention of absentee visitation required from me, neither does the said letter contain any mention of Mr. Simpson's 1 name and does not even bear his autograph. Hence, how 1 I can he know what I agreed to do when I took charge of these schools? But before going further permit me to say that Mr. Simpson has driven me in self-defence to ask a question respecting a professional brother. I much regret this, as I deprecate introducing an outsider into "a discussion of this nature, and snore particularly in the present instance, as Mr. South), is a martyr to a bodily infirmity that has caused him to live outside the town in order that he may be able to gain strength and vigour to carry on the work of his school. The words that compel me to question Mr. Soulby's actions are : "It was a very strange thing that the master of a school should admit that he so far failed in his duty as not to visit absentees systematically. It was part of the master's duty to do so. I take it that he considers it part of his head maeter's duty to do this visitation work to thel same extent that it is mine. Seeing then that his head master now resides out of town will Mr. Simpson be good lenough to inform the public through you, sir, when and at what hours Mr. Soulby makes his weekly visits ? I willingly admit that the Board's instructions to teachers printed in the absentee books are in the words used by Mr. Simpson. I take it, though, that these instructions are for the benefit, guidance, and use of teachers actually in the Board's service, inasmuch as the Education Department has ruled that a "local authority " has no power to order or demand from any teacher in a voluntary school information respecting absentees. Now, sir, fore few facts and statistics. It is an indisputable fact that the attendance officer visited my school on May 261 h—side the local papers of June 4th. It is also equally indisputable that returns were refused at this visit. It may not, however,. be generally known that , the officer called on Thursday, June 2nd, and owing to my courtesy, I cannot say whether it was "Christian" or no abstracted the information I declined to give, from the registers. Very well, I take it that up to the end of week ending June 3rd we were under the distinguished patronage of the School Board officer, and that after that time all connection ceased, seeing that no returns have been made to the Board since that date. This being so, we quite naturally, rightly, and justly sent to the Educa- tion Department the attendance up to the time that the School Board threw us off; and I assert again—it was no slip of the pen; perhaps the clerk intends this for sarcasm —the average for week ending June 3rd was 1848. The figures 1941, quoted by the clerk, were for the week ending May 13th, i.e., four weeks before the officer's last visit. You will observe, sir, that in four weeks there was a falling off of 10, which certainly tends to prove my CABO against the Board. Seeing this declension in the attendance, I awoke to the fact that it was time somebody bestirred themselves ; and, as a result, we secured an average of 195, 196, and 203 respectively for the three weeks ending June 24th, thus proving the accuracy of t ahf koe re figs ge as r et the met ao duty the ye sDop fee pea ca hr paidt et sn e an; e . r mostvTaha et clerk—by members, andth e , , .wpapya, r lieen tI my —calls attention to the average attendance twelve months irajfnt os,ut rosl yittrmhhl;eey2iwttr 12th, 1880, nlBstwBtoosahis2e Schooliet:h: aawloagnuebodikiuwn:r infant al.:nen:at °Ntuhforoestreh ' mistresshi weeknci gigahi odnafr' drafting tfenhttrdihaeni gingssego .17'31.01 should have thought that men of business, and a clerk well up in logic and forensic argument would have asked what caused the sudden fluctuations in the attendance-1921 to aiarldesri2unellniaottt. 231.7, and back again to 192 4—before naming the fact pub- licly, and claiming it as the result of their work. Besides, sir, do net these figures again prove my case to the Depart- ment? for if the attendance were 231 and then drops to 192, 194, 201, 189, and so on, is it not an evidence of negligence on the part of the Board and its officer? The last state- ment to which I will call attention is that made by the clerk, where he says—" I may mention that the average attendance has steadily fallen off since the complaint was made by Mr. Annett, and the statement has prove groundless." In the words of Mr. Simpson h S'r Ls to pson were know ? " And in proof that the clerk and Mr. 1 to each at at sea in the various statements they attemp ted " e hbe. prove, I send the following statistics : Aver age attendance. To argue that such figures are signs of a dee_mnse in neimi attendance may be the privilege of a r•-•,_ ~.ari who has enjoyed the luxury of an university ed'.43... , Ltola but lam compelled to stabs that. in public ettfnentavy schools we should be bhged o "'that they. are indicative of progress and olicremet ?.. pi.7ct onotaslori, sir, seeing that facts are on my \ side, ,Incl that I have neither fabricated statements nor falsi- I fled facts:, and that Mr. John Simpson, as the mouthpiece of the rita.jority of the Board, and after matare consideration, has, in his wisdom, seen fit to arraign me as a liar and a slanderer, I call upon him, as he appears to put himself forward as a champion of " honour " and "Christian cour- tesy," to make Inc an apology in the same public manner as he brought the charges against me. I fear, sir, that I have trespassed too much on your valuable space, but. as you appear to have carried out in sztenso Mr. John Snapson's wishes, I respectfully request you to extend to me a similar favour.—' remain, sir, yours respectfully, T. 11. ANNETT. Holy Trinity School, Runcorn, October 3rd, 1881.

NEWTON AND EIELESTOWN. 1 NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. : The monthly meeting of this Board was held at Newton- le-Willows, on Monday. Present: Mr. F. Gooch (in the I chair), Messrs. Winstanley, Emmett, Wood, Forster, J. E. Worsley (law deck), and R. Brierley (surveyor.) HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. , At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sani- tary Committee, held on the 19th ult., the surveyor reported his interview and correspondence with Mr. Worthington respecting provision for an archway in Suez-street. It was ordered that the surveyor make the best arrangement he can to secure an archway for traffic to pass under if practicable, and that Mr. Gooch and Mr. Winstanley be a committee to see Mr. Worthington, if found to be necessary.—Dr. Wat- kins attended to confer with the committee upon the spread of scarlet fever in the district which was of a mild, but in- fectious character, and of the means of ascertaining the ex- tent of the disease. The Surveyor submitted tenders he had received for High-streetnand Crow-lane outlet sewer, and 1 it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Unsworth be accapted. • ' Plans for additional premises for Mr. F. Sanderson, Earle- street, and an amended plan for Mr. J. Unsworth's house in i Foundry-street were approved. Plans for bakehouse and , alterations at the rear of Mr. Dawson's premises in Bridge- street for Mr.• S. Bethel], and for four cottages in Crow-lane L for Mr. A. Ball, were 6isapproved for amendments to the 3 byelaws. . On the motion of Mr. EatafErr, seconded by Mr. FORNIER i the minutes were confirmed. --

GAS AND WATER SUPPLY. At a meeting of the Gas ard Water Committee, held on the 19th September, tenders for the purchase of gas tar and ammonical liquor were read, and it was resolved that the tender of Messrs. Meadows and Son, of Rainhill, be accepted for a term of three years, according to the conditions approved by the committee. An application was read from Mr. Aveline, secretary to the new Baptist Chapel, Crown-st, for a supply of gas and water thereto; and it was ordered that the mains be extended in Market-street and from thence along Crown-street, on the chapel trustees undertaking to pay the Commissioners 10 per cent. on the outlay in Crown- street until the street is built up. It'etas ordered that four of Bray's 80-candle lamps be obtained and fixed in the following places: at junction of High-street and Church- street. junction of High-street, Ashton-road, and Crow-lane, junction of Queen-street, Bridge-street, and Market-street, and junction of Market-street, Legh-street, and Oxford-st.; and that suitable lamp pillars and brackets be erected for their purpose atAhose places. A letter was read from Mr. F. Webb, of Crewe, dated 6th inst., stating that an addi- tional well and pumping plant were being put down at Park- side, to prevent the stoppage of water supply in case of accident. A letter was read from Mr. E. Ice, Market-st., asking for an abatement of the charges for water for domes- tic purposes on his adjoining shop, used only as lock-up premises; and it was resolved that inasmuch as the charges are based upon the assessable value of the premises, the committee, in justification to other consumers, cannot see their way to alter the basis of the charges.—Mr. WINSTA.N- LEY moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. EMMETT seconded the motion—Mr. WINSTANLEY suggested that one of the large lamps should be placed at the bottom of Earle- street.—Mr. EMMETT asked whether any alteration had been made in the pressure of gas within the last month.—The SURVEYOR said the pressure was taken off early in the spring.—The CHAIRMAN said there was a very bad light in VVargrave Church on Sunday night; he could scarcely see. —The Surveyor was instructed to attend to the matter, and ascertain the pressure of gas in other towns. SCARLET FEVER OUTBREAK. The following" letter was read from Mr. W. H. Brook, town clerk of Warrington :—" Dear sir,—The attention c f the Sanitary Committee has been called to the report of the proceedings of your committee on Monday last, and lam instructed to inform you that certain statements then made are incorrect, inasmuch as no application has been made to us for the reception of your patients, and it is not a fact that there is no accommodation in the hospital for them."— Mr. WINSTANLEY said it was a fact that einee the conversa- tion occurred they had got a tent from London, and put it up; and it was also a fact that they had not sufficient accommodation, as they had got another since. He was told this week in Warrington, by persons connected with the Institution, that they had not accommodation now for the number of patients.—The CHAIRMAN: We have got a letter from the Town Clerk stating that they have accammoda- tion, and I do not think it is our-place to contradict them here. It is time enough for us to find fault when any appli- cation of ours is refused. The Chairman then read the following letter from the Newton Relief Committee:—" The following resolution was proposed and carried unanimously —lt having been brought to the notice of the Relief Com- mittee by 'the district medical officer that scarlet fever extensively prevails in Earlestown and neighbourhood, it is desirable that, in addition to the measures already adopted by the Commissioners, a further investigation should be instituted by means of a house-to-house visitation. It is earnestly recommended by the Relief Committee that the Sanitary Authority should at once organise a complete system of inspection!' The Chairman said their sanitary officers had taken every means in their power to ascertain where these cases were, and had done their best to meet them. He did not see what a house-to-house visitation could do. They had no power to go into any person's house.—Mr. WINSTANLEY: Yes.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that the Law Clerk said they had not.—Mr. WINSTANLEY said if they had not that power it was a perfect farce to have a Sanitary Committee.—The LAW CLERK: You have no compulsory powers for removal.—Mr. WINSTANLEY said he was not talking about removals, but a house-to-house visitation to see that proper measures were taken for disinfection and isolation. He explained that he had no intention of asking the committee to go into houses and take people out compulsorily. He knew the Commissioners had not sufficient power to do so, but in the course of his duty as a guardian a great number of cases had come before him that he believed ought to have been taken notice of by the Sanitary Committee or their officers. He wanted the Sanitary Committee to adopt such an organisation that they would know when there was an such epidemic ssteps sor t aakneyntlal anything were elrike n em the fewveerliaarendof the people and the preservation of the rates. If isolation and disinfection were neglected it Was at a very heavy cost. ea necessaryepidemic for ic There was no provision at all, in his opinion, to meet these cases. The removal of persons in an advanced state of fever to Warrington was manslaughter or next door to it, and he believed it was their duty—a duty which was press- ing upon them very strongly at the present moment—to make provision for the cases within that township. They could do it at a low expenditure.
