PARISH CHURCH-. The in-gathering of the harvest was teiebratea OD. Sunday last at several episcopal churches in WaVringt-Ve and neigh- bourhood. At the Parish Church ti t tft stival was most successful. In the morning and afteetton large congrega- tions attended the services; and in the evening the sacred edifice was filled in every part, large numbers of persons being accommodated with seats placed in the aisles. The noble structure had been specially decorated for the occa- sion, but the ornamentation was confined chiefly to the chancel, which was exquisitely embellished. Much atten- tion had been devoted to the pulpit, which, owing to its composition, presents great difficulties to the decorator, but these had been surmounted by Miss Allen, who had succeeded in imparting to it a most attractive appearance. The top of the pulpit was adorned with beautiful lily leaves, relieved with sprigs of brilliant gladiola and bunches of grapes. Ears of corn were disposed, with pretty effect, above the panels in the body of the pulpit ; in the centre were arranged neat little bouquets; the short pillars le ere entwined with oats, and the bottom was fringed with oats, set off like the top, with lily leaves, gladioli, and other flowers. At the base of the pulpit was a collection of varie- gated geraniums from the rectory garden. The prayer desk was tastef ally fringed with cerials, mosses, and ferns; and its appearance was enhanced by the judicious disposition of pendants of the fuschia, gladiola, grapes, Sze. This was the work of Miss Dooley. Close by the prayer desk was a splendid collection of vegetables, presented by Mr. Isaac Warburton, of Poulton, and Mr. B. L. Pierpoint, Horse- market-street. Misses Robinson and Chrinaes had neatly ornamented the clergy stalls with fringes of cerials, bordered with ivy leaves and berries; and the choir stalls had been I treated in a similar manner by the Misses Burgess and Macf trquhar, the border in this case consisting of dahlias, I ' geraniums, and gladioli. On either side the chancel steps were placed some choice ferns. The chancel seats were embellished with splendid purple and yellow dahlias; while the chancel windows were decorated with miniature sheaves of wheat, wreaths of oats, and borders of dahlias. Wreaths of the vine' suspending bunches of grapes, hung from the gas standards inside the communion rails, and the standards I were also entwined with wheat and adorned with peaches, collections of vegetables king placed at the foot of each. Between the gas standards were Borne magnificent gladioli, seen to great advantage, with a background of ferns, and surrounded with apples, melons, Sm. Miniature sheaves of wheat were placed in the east window, beneath which were the words, "The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness there- of." Below this was some trellis work, ornamented with cerials, by the students of the training college; and on either side were wreaths of vine. The windows on the south aide of the church had been nicely decorated with mosses, &es by Miss Boyle; and the font was embellished with mosses, maidenhair and other ferns, studded with white lilies, by Miss Longden (the rector's granddaughter). On the north gallery was the text, "He reserveth unto us the , appointed weeks of harvest," executed on a white ground in Roman letters with illuminated capitals; and on the south gallery the text, "The folds shall be full of sheep; the fields also shall stand so thick with corn that they shall laugh and sing." Besides the above-named, the following ladies also assisted with the decorations :—Mrs. Quekett, Miss Ilesketh, Mrs. Tauranac, and Mrs. Moeres. The fruits and ferns used in the decorations had been presented by Mrs. Jones, of the Elms, Daresbury, Mrs. John Crostield, Walton Lea, and Mrs. Peter Whitley, of Wilderspool. At the morning service the first lesson was read by the Rev. J. Willcocks, and the second lesson by the Rev. M. Stephenson, and the prayers by the Rev. J. 11. Davis. The sermon was preached by the Rev. W. G. Longden, M.A., vicar of South Norwood, Surrey, frotn Ist Theseelonians, v. 18, In everything give thanks : for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." The Rev. H. C. Stubbs, principal of the training college, peached in the afternoon. In the evening the Ist lesson was read by the Rev. F. W. Cory, and the second lesson by the Rector, and the prayers by the Rev. W. G. Longden. The sermon was preached by the Rev. T. P. Williamson, M.A., vicar of Thel wall, who took for his text Romans, 2nd chapter, latter part of 4th verse, "The good ness of God leadeth thee to repentance." He said that one- year more had rolled away, one more hearvest hid been gathered in, and once again they had met together in God's house to give thanks unto Him. Very meet, very right, nay, surely their bounden duty it was that these harvest festivals should be held, and that they should be held almost 'so universally was a cheering, and he hoped, a good sign in times when good signs were sorely lacking. Was it not strange that there should be no special feast ap- pointed by the Church to celebrate the occasion, and that [ the whole matter should be left to the discretion of the clergyman to fix the day and make arrangements according to his own will and pleasure? For se, indeed, it practically was; but in these days they could not complain of the apathy of either the clergy or the laity in this matter, aml for that they thanked God. It was a good sign; but this I was not always so, as these thanksgiving services were of recent growth. He could remember, and no doubt most of them could, when such a thing was rarely or never heard of, when any rejoicing that there was at harvest was in no wise " rejoicing in the Lord." The whole affair was a mere matter of feasting and merry-making. And yet from the beginning it was not so, and that a religious duty should have been so degraded was a sad legacy to them from that dreary time when the Church of England slept. That such a festival was in accordance with the mind of God was easily seen by reference to the church of the earlier dispensa- tion, whose fasts and festivals were appointed by God Him- self. At the Feast of Penticost they bearded the first-fruits, the earliest sheaf, being brought to the sanctuary and solemnly waved before the Lord. At the Feast of Taber- nacles all the males appeared before the Lord to return thanks to Him for the fruits of the earth. And the Church, not unmindful of this God-given precedent, had also two holy services, which specially brought before her children the holy associations which belonged to the harvest—but, alas! these were almost wholly lost to the Church of Eng- land—the service of supplication upon the Rogation days, and the service of thanksgiving on Lammas thy. The former, held on the three days before Ascension day, oc- curred at that critical time of spring when the young, the tender growth, was in greatest danger from storm and frost, and then it was that for three days prayers and supplica- tions were offered to God, beseeching Him to preserve to their use the kindly fruits of the earth, so that in due season they might enjoy them. From the calendar they would find these holy days still survived, and however much in past times they had been neglected, and though the services were now much shorn of their beauty and impressiveness, still there was an ever-increasing number of parishes in which they 'were duly observed. The great regret was that the observance was not universal. Harvest was a call to repentance, but who regarded it as such? From the Queen on the throne down to the poorest of her subjects all were sharers in the blessings of harvest, all were effected by it, all were dependent upon it; but of all these millions of people how many saw the goodness of God in the harvest? How many heard the call to repent- ance? He asked all those who believed in God Almighty to believe that He it was and not blind chance that ordereth the affairs of this world. Might not the prayerless and un- thankful way in which they sowed, might not the thankless way in which they reaped, have earned the poor and partial harvests they had of late years suffered under? Might it not be by this laying on of His hand that God was seeking to ir.duce them to recognise more clearly and really the goodness and mercy which had followed them all the days of their life, to which they might have perhaps been hither- to too blind ? In the harvest of 1881 they clearly saw-the goodness of God. God, not unmindful of his promise that seed time and harvest should not fail, gave to the children of His great family their daily bread, and this should fill tHhiemi r withh r t ewpi et lir; acnekffourl npeassst asni nd,scaanuds e stihmemmet ofor t npr pest iunton. I gratitude. The harvest of 1881 was far from being an abundant one, and in this, too, the thoughtful Christian dis- broug;ldt,tntiiNanotaviangtant cerned the goodness of -God seeking to lead him to repent- ance. It was a warning, perhaps, of what might be ; a threat of greater trouble in the future ; it was a call to them to look into their hearts, and to see what wickedness might he lurking there, and see what they could amend in themselves, as Christians, as Churchmen, as members of society, as citizens of the kingdom. National wickedness ldssdwtspvooototaiuniiimsr-tnfedenhtteth:arrhgiaeeartaonthrstcrditaaidel byftueweiusalngitte:muiureeontarr iraisaatrin,dlts nomeagsdui't hts'i ahgdrtt tifhhies ontt baheottt neotieehindui naniesnnesanr tuagehewnensaeidysain;fsnetytseexr virusiateetgehl interests brought national punishment, as certainly as individual sin [ individualpsgn icaoarocroet according solli ttdoyr eth a nation." Thus it was that the righteousness of the evil when he said that the hand of God was pressing us suffered with it. The body corporate was touched on a griev- ous national sins which cried to Heaven for vengeance they greater griefs to come. Let them think of the drunkenness that desecrated the land, of the unbridled lustthat defiled it, of the lawlessness that was rampant, the little respect paid to human life, how the pistol and knife were resorts! to on the slightest provocation, of the immoralities that were eating the heart out of honest trade, and above all of the dark clouds of deadly infidelity which were creep- ing up and threatening to over-shadow all the land. Did not such sins as these deserve greater punishment than had yet befallen them? Were they not enough to provoke the most righteous God to anger? A day of humiliation scented all but necessary. Could they not see, in the present condition of society and the existing modes of life, that which would enable them to account in some measure for the depressed condition of agriculture? The large farmers would tell them that they found it hard to make the engue and buckle meet, and small farmers were barely earning a livelihood, while of course the evil fell heaviest on the labouring classes. Hundreds of farms were to let, and thou- sands of acres were going to waste for want of the care of the tillers of the soil. The reasons for this sad state of things were multifarious and complicated, and were not to be- cussed in a sermon even were the pulpit the proper place i such a discussion. He wished, however, to bring befw them an evil which seemed to him to have fastened itself like some malignant cancer upon society, and was gradually eating its way into all classes and undermining the efforts which might perhaps have been more availing. "Tire old order changeth giving place to the new." There were those who wottle tell them that the old was better, and exhort them to continue in the old paths. But they could not even if they would. They lived in a world of progress • in times of -special and marvellous progress, and it was Plainly in- cumbent upon every man to improve as much as in him lay, wdbo ul theyf suffered ulrrtteffeehhipasto:eusysur

and tb- • ...ay should ever seek "to go from strength to strength." tAlt-, though habits and customs changed, principles abided. Our fathers had one thing which he feared was lacking now. It was a matter which raid the foundation of the extraor- dinary prosperity which England enjoyed. The very name of that virtue which thcy possessed sounds strsnge in Our ears. It was almost waxing obsolete. It was thrift. That quality was in ith Wise allied to parsimony or niggardliness. It was cotnpatiblb'with the truest liberality; and it was a quality by which many men and nations thrived. Look where they would it was hard to see any signs of thrift now- a-days. From the top of society down to the very bottom they saw signs, neither few nor insignificant, of increasing luxury, self-gratification, and self indulgence, and that was perhaps the most dangerous tendency of the age. No class seemed to be exempt. It had invaded the agricultural classes amongst others—speaking generally thrift was un- known amongst them, or at least unpractised—and this was in his opinion one of the many causes which had brought about the prevalent distress. He did not say farmers and farm labourers were worse than others, but he did not think they were any better. The accusation of unthriftiness was against them all, and the evil was so wide spread as to be almost universal. Let them lock for themselves, let them think for themselves, let any man, whether farmer or other- wise, ask himself how he lived compared with his father's or his grandfather's style of living, and he had little doubt the man would admit there was a change towards luxury. He did not say that if we had more to spend than our fathers we should not spend it, but he did say that much that we spent upon eating and drinking and bodily indulgence generally would, if we had been thrifty, have been saved against a rainy day. We should spend less upon our bodies and put more into the hank. Over much luxury \VAS the bane of the present day. The rich man was clothed in purple and tine linen and fared sumptuously every day ; " men of moderate income aped rich men in style, those of small income trod I upon the heels of those who were richer, and even the poor man must pretend, or at any rate live as if he were richer than he really was. And so on down the whole scale. Yet Lazarus lay at the door, for England, with all its wealth and all its boasted civilization, harboured an amount of abject and hopeless poverty almost unexampled, to the statesman an unsolved problem, to the State a danger, and to the nation shame and disgrace. Luxury proved the ruin of Nineveh, of Babylon, and of Greece. We should pray that our wealth, which should be our strength, may not prove England's undoing, that the enervating influence of luxury may not undermine her greatness, and cast her glory in the dust. The collections for the day amounted to .£4O 9s. 3d.

WARRINGToN COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS, WEDNESDAY—Before Mr. John Rylancls, Mr. Samuel Rigby, and Mr. Peter Stubs. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE—Win. Haygan, an innkeeper, was charged with having, on the 28th Sept., un- lawfully and cruelly illtreating a horse by working it in an unfit state.—P.S. Pattinson said that about half-past four o'clock on Wednesday, the 28th September, he was on duty on the main road near Hollins Green village, when his at- tention was drawn to the defendant, who was in charge of a roan horse and cart in a hay field. The cart was laden with hay, and the horse was so lame that it could scarcely walk. He examined it and found it was suffering from a very bad strain on the near foreleg, and the fetlock joint was very swollen and had been much blistered. It was also swollen at the knee.—Defendant said the horse w4,s five years old and he had asked the doctor if it would do it any harm to cart away a ton of hay, and he said no.—The Bench dis- missed the case on payment of costs. NUISANCES AT PENICETIL—Mr. Richard Ockleshaw' of Penketh, was summoned to show why an order should not be made upon him to abate the nuisance existing at his seven cottages, through the condition of the privies and ashpits.—lnspector Rawling said he visited the premises on the 21st July, as he had done on many previous occasions, and found the ashpits and closets in a foul and offensive condition.—Dr.Gornall said he had had these premises under his notice for some nine or ten years, and as far back as June 1874, he called the attention of the Rural Sanitary Authority to their offensive condition, warning them that sooner or later they would lead to the production of some form of fever. In April of this year, two deaths occurred from diphtheria and it was his opinion and the opinion of Drs. Smith and Sherratt that if the emanations from the privies were not the cause of the diphtheria, they induced such a de- pressed condition of life, that these children took the poison. He recommended that the Sanitary Authority should have the closets so constructed as not to be a nuisance and in- jurious to health. That recommendation was made in 1874, but no notice was taken of it. The same state of things existed to-day.—ln reply to Mr. Rylands, Dr. Gornall said the pail system would remedy the nuisance. He did not think they could be kept in a proper sanitary condition from their construction.—Mr. Ockleshaw said he objected to the pail system, and called a witness who stated the privies were dry, an', no complaints were made by the tenants. He emptied them about once every two months.—A. tenant named Wm. Nicholson mid the houses were healthy.—Mr. Rylands said th Bench vere bound to taJte notice of so strong a report as that of the Medical Officer, and the Bench made an order for the abatement of the nuisance.—Eight persons were summoned by the Rural Sanitary Authority for neglecting to empty the ashpits, dm., of their respective .houses. The cases were adjourned until next sessions to give them an opportunity of doing so. --410---. •

The members of the Olive' Branch Lodge of the Inde- pendent Order of Oddfellows, M.U.F.S., held their annual platform tea party and ball on Monday evening. About 200 persons Bwwapl 3:as. s sLov W. oad.lt poi tereihnnruePen:lypi platform pt frol fur. anHH. the Mayor (Alderman Fickmere), Bro. Boyle, P.F.G.'54., Bro. Notbury, G.M., and Secretary Smith. The CHAIRMAN, after a few introductory remarks, said the meeting had a two-fold object. The first was to assist the Olive Branch Lodge with their fund relative to their in- cidental expenses, and the second to give an opportunity to fernsccf and ct mae the its members and friends, their wives and sweethearts, to enjoy themsaves for a few hours. It was welf-known that the society was formed principally of workingmen, who con- tributed weekly from their earnings to a fund to relieve them in case of sickness or distress. When sickness laid them low and their spirits were failing, the band of fellowship was stretched forth to assist them in their heavy affliction, and during his long connection with the Order he had heard expressions of giateful satisfaction from those who were stricken down. It was a well-known maxim that they endeavoured to instil into the minds of everyone joining them three principal duties—their duty to God, to their neighbour, and to themselves. Their object was to make a man abetter man, a better husband, a better father, and so better member of society generally. How far they had suc- ceeded in that object was seen front the fact that in War- rington and neighbourhood they had something like 1,000 members, and during the Mayor's two years of office as chief magistrate they had given hint very little trouble. (Applause). His Wousuir, then addressed the meeting. Ile s mid he appeared there that evening with very great pleasm e be- cause he thought all friendly societies were doing a vast amount of good in the kingdom. He was given to under- stand that the Oddfellows in the Manchester Unity numbered over half a million, and of funds he was afraid to say how much they were possessed. That went to prove if men could combine together, and do what they were doing, to re- lieve the widow and orphan and those who were laid down with sickness, it was not charity, but it was the right of every individual who became a member of these lodges to receive what he ought to receive by paying so much per quarter or per annum. Thy should never forget that. H 2 always ranked friendly societies as standing second in order in the noble institutions in this country. The first in order, he thought they must say were the charitable institutions of this country—hospitals, &c. Charitable people said, and they all said charity was the chief of the honourable things which a man could have. Faith, hope, and charity, but be- yond all was charity. They were proud of their charitable institutions in this country. There was no country in the world, be believed, with such charitable institutions as we have. He thought next in order were the friendly societies by which men by paying so much per week provided for themselves in time of sickness and their widows and orphans in time of death. It was a very noble institution and one which had taken deep root in the soil of old England, and would succeed in doing good as it had done before. He had come with very great pleasure because he thougat one of the duties of the mayor, as chief magistrate of the borough, to use his influence to assist and patronise—if he could use the word not in a paying sense—these institutions, lie hoped the society would go on and prosper as it had hitherto; in fact, he thought it would. Its foundations were laid on a rock. They all helped themselves when they combined together to relieve widows and orphans, and those who were 'on the sick list. (Applause.) Brother FINNEY, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, expressed his regret that the society did not seem to be supported as it ought by the middle chars tradespeople, and other classes in Warrington. He felt that this and kindred societies ought to be supported for this reason: they were doing, as the Mayor said, a great amount of good. div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1881.

LEBONAH TO NABLOUS. As we rode along, Gerizim gradually stood out from the rest of his companions, and seemed to rear his head far above them all. Even Ebal, his twin brother, whose equal stature and similar features he had, until now greatly hidden, looked small in the distance. We arrived at the ever memorable well of Jacob exactly at noon. As the sun's rays poured down upon us we could very feelingly under- stand how Jesus. after toiling over the hard rugged hills in the scorching heat, should have " sat wearied by the well?' There was no circular stone wall on which to rest. The mouth of the well was covered over with an old ruined arch, around which were scattered the broken columns sad stones of some building, either an early Christian church or Nahomalan mosque, which bad been erected over it. We clambered down through an opening in the arch, and there indeed was the old well with but a comparatively small opening at the top. We "had nothing to draw with." It was clear, too, that there was plenty of water, and we -emealed to our never-failing dragman to provide a rope. Soon he (mina au Aral? NY.I.!? hag a hair roDe and a pitcher, which I I:ad the hot t loweringlnto the well with my own b.ahus. The rope was too short. After some delay a 1:Oog piece of hempen rope was found. Where it sprung from I could not imagine. I suppose, on mature considera- tion, it was " backsheesh" that found it. Having fastened the ropes together we soon had a p!entiful supply of clear, cool, and delicious water. We measured and found that the water was about 45 feet from the top. Our lunch was spread close to the well upon the ruins, and we drank I gratefully and reverently of the priceless beverage. The well stands quite outside the valley of Shechem. I sho old say there is not a finer parcel of ground in Palestine than the one which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Looking from it towards the valley, the twin mountains, Gerizitn and Ebal, form a grand entrance. What a scene it must have been when the blessings and curses of the law were read, the one from Gerizim, and the other from Ebal, and when the mighty "Amen "arose from thousands of voices and rolled its echoes along the valley to the Great Sea! Just at the entrance of the valley, to the right and at the vase of Ebal, is Joseph's tomb. If it be the actual site, a small square building of comparatively modern date is now raised upon it. Inside of the place is a still more modern mausoleum. I forget who they said had restored the tomb and ornamented the sarcophagus quite recently. At each end of the latter is a broken column, on which, being squared at the top, were the remains of recently burned sacrifices. As the Pashal feast of the Samaritans had just passed, and Joseph's tomb is held in great veneration by them, we concluded the sacri- fice had been offered by that strange people of whom I shall have more to say. Ins country like Samaria, in which the traditions of the people have, even to this day, been so fondly cherished, we can scarcely conceive of' the tomb of Joseph, the father of Ephraim, being allowed to pass out of recollection at any period of Jewish history, and it was a solemn thing to stand on the very spot to which the embalmed body had been brought amidst obsequies so in- posing, after it had rested for centuries in Egypt. Will the mummies of Jacob add Joseph ever see the light ? As we rode up the valley to Nablone, or Shechem, we were sur- prised to see such an abundant supply of water evidently issuing from the mountain, rustling aloui the water courses. We began to ask ourselves how it was that Jacob, with such' a supply at hand, should have been at the trouble and expense ot sinking a well more than NO feet deep and 8 feet in diameter. A probable solution was suggested by Mr. E. C. Carey, the Baptist missionary at Nablous, who accom- panied us to the top of Gerizim, as we sat on the reined tower looking down upon the plain. Ile thought the fact of Jacob being a stranger in the land, and rtquiring to water his numerous cattle at the same time and in the same place as the Cmaanites, would be a sufficient reason for digging a well on his own land. Nothing is more common in the East than violent quarrels in struggles for priority at the wells. A young pregnant woman was killed at the well at Nazareth two or three days before we got there. The danger of an alien coming into conflict must have been tenfold, especially in Shechem, whose people have always borne the name of being the most turbulent anti unruly in Palestine. As to the point of the woman coming to the Well witlt water so much newer to the city, he thought she might either ive come from the open plain to get the water for the use a the herdsmen, or she might have a reverential prefr -nee for water drawn from a well so rich in family associa. My opinion is that Sychar is not to he confounded ith ,Fbechem, ch lies two miles from the well, but that it

F RODSH AM. THE MEN'S INSTITUTE.—The first annual general meeting of the members of the Frodsham Institute was held on Mon- day, Mr. Charles E. LinakE r presiding. The report and balance sheet was read by the hon. sec., Mr. George Gleave, and adopted. After some discussion, a slight alteration was made in the rules, the principal change being in the amount of subscription, which was reduced. The following officers were appointed for the ensuing year, viz. :—President, Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar; vice-presidents, E. A. Wright; Esq., John Simpson, Esq., Charles Reynolds, Esq.. and Henry Linaker, Esq.; committee, Revs. J. M. Bamford (Wesleyan minister), Robert Trotter (Free Church minister), Messrs. C. E. Linaker, Samuel Davies, George Gleave, Peter Riley, J. E. Bate, and David loose; hon. sec. and treasurer, Mr. Henry They. HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE.--A special harvest thanksgiving service was held in the Iron Church, Frodsham, on Wednesday, when the service was corducted by the Revs. J. D. Havard, vicar of Helsby, and L. K. Kinder, curate. A sermon suitable for the occasion was preached by the Rev. E. W. Cory, senior curate of Warrington Parish Church. The church had been tastefully decorated with flowers, corn, and foliage intertwined, and numerous teats were prettily arranged in pleasing designs. The following ladies and gentlemen kindly undertook the decorations, VIZ.: --Mesdames C. Reynolds, J. Ashton; Misses F. Hilditch, S. and J. Crostield, E. Davies; Messrs. L. K. Kinder, 11. G. Linaker, J. Milner, and D. Ashton. REVISION OF VOTERS' LISTS—The cmrt for the annual revision of voters' lists for West Cheshire was held at the Bear's Paw Hotel, on Wednesday, by Mr. E. B. Wood. Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, Runcorn and Frodsham, repre- sented the Libel al party, and was successful in sustaining upwards of fifty new claims and seven out of nine objec- tions, including the names of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bat., and Mr. Peter Whitley. Votancrama Purzx SwoortNo.—The annual competition for prizes by the Frodsham volunteers took place on Satur- day, at the range on Frodsham score, after which a supper was partaken of at the Bull's Head, Overton, which had been kindly provided by Captain Robert Ashton, Mr. Har- greaves and Mr. Clarke. The prizes are to be distributed in , the Town Hall, Frodsham.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. On Tuesday evening the prizes and certificates in connec- tion with the Widnes Science and Art Classes were distribu- ted to the successful candidates, in the Volunteer Hall, by Dr. Oliver J. Lodge, of London, who has been appointed to one of the professorships in Liverpool College. Mr. John Brock, J.P., presided, and there were also present Messrs, S. A. Spoouer, Holden (Farnworth), Thomas Finegan, F. Gossage J.P.e, J. L. Muspratt, Sydney Muspratt, Hol- brook Gask'ell, jun., J.P. Major Cross, Eustace Carey, Dr. Hurter, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Joseph Morrison (secretary.) The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said his first duty was to call upon Mr. Joseph Morrison, the honorary secretary, to read the report.—Mr. MORRISON read the re- port of the committee for 1880-1, from which it appeared that during the session 119 individual students were under instruction. The entries to the classes were 158. Of these 112 came up for examination, and 66 passed. The only re- sult unsatisfactory was that of chemistry. The results in the other subjects were quite satisfactory, and the committee were glad to note a decided improvement in building and machine construction. The committee reported that although there were fewer students on the register than in the previous session, the attendance at the examinations was considerably better. With 21 less students, there had been earned from Government £22 10s. 6d. more than last year. In the City and Guilds of London Institute technolo- gical examinations Mr. George Treacy and Mr. R. J. Years- ley obtained certificates in " Alkali manufacture," and Mr. W. E. Oakden achieved the distinction of obtaining a first-class certificate (with the second prize of £5 and bronze medal) in the honours stage. The committee hoped that the time was not far distant when the local autholities would be in a positiou to see their way to establish, under the Public Libraries Act, a free public libray for Widnes. The financial position was exceedingly satisfactory. Not- withstanding the great depression in trade, the manufac- turers had supported the classes in the most handsome manner. After paying all expenses of the session there was a b dance in the bank of £23 17s. 7d. The classes had been in operation seven years, and during that time 476 students had been under instruction. The total expenditure from the commencement had been £1,534 10s. 2d.; of this amount £750 had been subscribed by the manufacturers, and the balance made up by students' fees and the Government grant. The CHAIRMAN called attention to several points in the report. It referred, he said, to the fact that while the num- ber of students on the register was less than last year, the number who had gone up for examination was considerably greater. This was a very important matter. The teachers depended for their remuneration upon the number of students who passed the examination. Another point mentioned in the report was the establishment of technological classes in connection with the City and Guilds of London leetitute. Unfortunately, in this country in past years there had been far too little attention paid to technological training. On the continent it had been otherwise, and artisans for a long series of years have had the benefit of technical training. It bad been his fortune to visit many industrial establishments on the Continent of Europe, and in America, and he had often been struck with the marked intelligence shown by the ordinary artisan, and especially by the overlooker and fore- man of departments in the work they had in hand. He observed that these workmen had certainly a very clear per- ception of the scientific principles involved in the work they were doing, and in their application to the particular indus- try in which they were engaged. On enquiry he generally found that this was to be traced to the fact that in their youth they had received a good technictl education. (Ap- plause.) If they in this country were to maintain their supremacy as a manufacturing nation, they must pay more attention to this subject than they had hitherto done. There could be no doubt that British artisans possessed all the necessary intelligence if they got an equal training, and he had no fear at all for our manufacturing supremacy if we only gave our artisans the best possible training we could. We had command of unlimited and the best appliances, un- bounded mineral wealth, and we had certainly the best cli- mate in the world for the prosecution of manufacting opera- tions. The committee told them they had decided to put on their shelves a number of the best technological works, and open one of their class rooms, on Saturday evenings, for the use of the students. Of course, from the nature of the case, this privilege could only he for the students and not for the general public. Now, he should like to ask them Iwhether something further than this was not needed in the town? Had not the time come when Widnes, like St. Helene and other places around, should have a public and free library of its own. (Loud applause.) He knew that ithis subject had been mooted at the Local Board meetings, ' and by some people it was considered a kind of bug bear, because it would certainly add to the rates. It would, how- ever, add very little to them, and he apprehended that the advantages accruing from having such an institution in their midst, would outweigh any disadvantages which they would feel in having to pay a slight additional rate. (Ap- plause.) He believed that the present rateable value of the town was about £102,000. New, the highest rate which the local authorities would be allowed to levy as a library and museum rate would be one penny in the £—that was the maximum. That amount of rate would realise in Widnes a 'little over £4OO, and about one half of that would be paid by the works and railways. Speaking as a manufacturer, he did not think that if there were any complaint at all about the rate, it would come from the manufacturers. (Applause.) He felt certain that if this matter were taken up with some spirit and moved in, they would very soon establish a free , library. It might not be known to many of them what were the steps which it was necessary to take in order to establish such an institution; but they were very simple and very few. To login with, they would have to put in motion the Local Board. He did not suppose that body would move in the matter until they were acted upon by outside influences, be- cause they would be afraid of being told that they were 1, doing that which would add to the rates; but if any ten rate- [payers would get up a petition to the Chairman of the Local Board, he would be bound to call a meeting of ratepayers, and if two-thirds of those present were agree able to the establishment of a free library, it would be sufficient. In St. [Helens they had a libriry numbering between 6,000 and 7,000 volumes, and it appeared from the report which had been published recently, that all which was required for the maintenance of the institution during the coning year was £2BO, which in the case of Widnes, would be little over a halfpenny in the £. He could not think that for so small a sum of money, the immense advantages which a public library would give them would be cast aside. He hoped that before very long they would see this movement heartily taken up by some of the ratepeyets, and that the Local Board would be memorialised to ;all a meeting at vvhich the question would be settled in the affirmative. (Hear, hear.) In the early part of his re-. marks he had said that, unfortnately for England, techno- logical training had not in the past been attended to as it oeght, but he was glad to report that we were making pro- gress, for If they looked at the elementary training in science and art which was now being carried on, they would observe I a very different state of things. The report of the Science and Art Department showed that ia 1870 there were 799 schools giving instruction in these branches, and 34,283 studerds under instruction, wlrilet last year there were 1,391 schools and 60,871 students. (Applause.) Now that state of things might be looked upon as substantial progress. At the same time it was only a eginning, and he trusted that during the next ten years they would find a very much larger proportionate progress made. He had now to intro- duce to them a gentleman who had volunteered to address them and deliver the prizes to the successful students—Dr. Lodge, who had come to Liverpool as the first professer of physics in the new University College. (Applause.) 'Therefore they might call him, at least by residence, a Lancashire man ; and lie trusted that he would receive from• them that evening a Lancashire welcome. Professor L6DGE, who was received with much enthu- siasm, then distri'auted the prizes to the successful cendi- dates, whose names have already appeared in The Examiner, after which he proceeded to give an address of considerable length. lie remarked that it was quite certain that, abstractly considered, a prize was by no m ass worthy of the labour and trouble which bad to be taken in order to acquire it, but the knowledge and discipline thus obtained were worth as much labour and perseverance as the stndents could bestow. ThVre was no doubt a tendency in , the present day to overdo examinations, and this was, pro- ' tbablr, the re icon why they were u. •aighed against. How- ever, as an indicator in regard to the studies of young men, examinations were most veluable, and it was very pleasant to have one's work recognized by a number of gentlemen acting as examiners, who looked over a variety of papers with absolute impartiality, and with great speed. Exatni- nations were really a great help and an incentive to methodical study. The way to pass an examination was not to think of nothing else but it. If they directly aimed ' at an examination, and thought of nothing else, they were very likely to fail. Let them work at the subjects for their own sake and the passing of the examination would natu- rally follow. He was very glad to hear that the results in connection with the Widnes classes had this year been more sitisfectory than they were last. He reminded the students that they surely could not imagine that the paltry fee they were called upon to pay was really sufficient to remunerate Ithe teacher, to provide a building, and meet all the expenses of apparatus and other materials incidental [to such classes. In fact, the classes were really free, as they were partly supported by local generosity on the part of the : manufacturers and others, and also very largely I,y grants , from the State. How were the Government to know whether the the classes were efficiently conducted P From the Government point of view, the examinations were merely a means of Age .rtaining how far the teaching was efficient and sound, and they made grants accordingly. A really important examination was often an important land mark in life, and often shaped a young man's future career. To these who had failed lie would soy don't rest content with your failure, as it is not the normal and healthy condition of life. It would take place sometimes, and, in moderation, it was a healthy experience and discipline, hut it wee one which should be taken in hommpathic (loses—(latighter) and no one shonld be satisfied with less than that they aimed at. In a few exceptional Cases there were hindrances which were beyond a man's control, but in the majority of cases a determination to succeed would infallibly in the end carry success with it. What, he wished to impress upon all of them WAS that the thing to do was to succeed, and not to give plausible excuses ror failure. For one man who SUC- ,eTer kaeriec nen,ennicohd Ceeded there were a thousand WI.) failed. It was riot due to es any accidental concatenation et circumstances that on man was able to oatstrip others in the race of life, but that he illldestor amt ie.purpose,a n d,,,e pc nsromees powereiali 3, of ,o e prrs so his sc nearly always g tlitorslhtads "oiy p not. WIDNES POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junior. A NIGHT ADVENTURE : THE END OF A NOSE LOST.— Felix Eavers, of Eleanor-street, a respectably dressed man, was charged with unlawfully wounding Francis Byrne, on the 10th inst. The Inspector of Police said the members of the force had made enquiries into the case, and they declined to take any part in it. Mr. Thomas Beasley appeared for the defence. Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, asked the complainant if he could identify the prisoner as the man who had assaulted him, for on the previous Wednesday he was unable to do so.—Complainant : I will swear that he is the man.—Mr. Beasley said the only reason why the charge was not entered upon on the previous Wednesday, was that the complainant could not identify the prisoner.—Com- plainant said he he did not do so on Wednesday because he was afraid the prisoner would do him some injury. Byrne then said he was a labourer, and on the evening of the 10th ult., about half past six, he left his work, and on his way home called at a publichouse about three minutes, and had a glass of beer. On coming out of the place he met two men, of whom the prisoner was one, but he did not know the other. As they passed him the second man addressed him in an insulting manner, and then struck him. Prisoner also tried to hit him, but he succeeded in warding off the blow. The second man ran away, and then Eavers put both his arms round his neck, and bit elf the " tip "of his nose. He felt the prisoner's teeth go through his nose, and it bled pro- fusely. He tried to detain the prisoner, but he managed to get away, leaving his bat behind him. He then went to Dr. Patterson, who dressed the wound.—The hat was sent for, and the prisoner put it on in court, but said it was too small for him.—Mr. Beasley, who had several witnesses who it is stated would have been called to prove a clear alibi, wished to call some of them, but was told it was not necessary.—Mr. Gaskell said he did not consider there was sufficient evidence to convict the prisoner, and he would, therefore, be discharged. If further evidenc'? were obtained, he might be brought up again.
THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaakell, junr.

SHOCKING KICKING CASE.—Thomas Mitchell, John Mit- chell, Timothy Mitchell, Joseph French, and Peter Heverty, all Irishmen living at Cuerdley, were charged, .on remand, with unlawfully wounding Daniel Plumpton.—Mr. Swift, senr., appeared for the defence.—Complainant said he was a labourer and lived at No. 6, Halton View. On Saturday night, the Ist instant, he was in the Castle Inn public-house, Warrington-road, up to nearly eleven o'clock at night, with his brother Abel. On leaving, he went towards his own , home, with his brother, and when near his (witness's) own house—about ten yards away—they heard a conversation in the middle of the road. The five prisoners passed at this time, and he said "A fine night, boys." One of the priso- ners said " Can I take anything out of you 2" when the gang bad got from seven to ten yards past. They knocked him down and kicked him. • Whilst lieverty was striking him lie heard some of the others encourage him by saying "Go in, Darby." John Mitchell and Timothy Mitchell were the prisoners who knocked him down, and Heverty and Thomas Mitchell kicked him on the head. The others joined in the assault, but he could only swear to the two men named as having kicked him. There was a gas lamp about four yards off, and he had a good view of the priso- ners, whom he had knoen for twelve months. The prisoners afterwards ran away towards Cuerdley. He was certainly a little dazed, but he knew very well what was taking place. Ile had five wounds on the head, one on the thigh, and another on the leg. In about an hour and a quarter after, lie saw Dr. Cooper, who attended him. He lost a consider- able quantity of blood. During the assault he lost the hat produced. On the following morning, the three Mitchells and Heverty were brought to his house, and he recognised the latter and Thomas Mitchell as having taken part in the assault. He was in bed two days, and this was the first time he had been out —ln cross-examination, witness said he did not believe that French struck him at all, and he had always known him as a harmless and inoffensive man.— Abel Plumpton, 73, Warrington-road, who said he was a wheelwright, gave corroborative evidence. D:tring the assault he triad to pull Thomas Mitchell off his brother, but he could not. He then ran to his brother's house, and on returning he saw Joseph French stooping over complainant. The other four prisoners ran away, but French did not. He asked French if he was one of the lot, and he said he was not. He then picked French's hat up from the ground, and enquired how it was that his hat was on the ground if he did not belong to the gang. He could not see whether the other men had knocked French's cap off, but "Ire rather ' thought they did." He had known French about 16 years, and he bad always considered him a harmless, inoffensive fellow. He did not believe that French had anything to do with hurting his brothen—Robert Dawson, labourer, Cuerdley, said that about eleven o'clock , on the night named, .he was returning home by way of , Warrington-road, when he saw Heverty and John Mitchell near to the complainant's house. Having gone about one hundred yards further he heard the noise of a struggle and some blows struck. Shortly after Heverty, John Mitchell, and some others ran past him.—Dr. Wm. Cooper said he examined the complainant after the assault, and found him snffering from five cuts on the head, a contusion of the upper part of the jaw bone a slight redness on one of his legs, near the knee joint, and he complained about his hip. All the wounds on the front of the head were contused, and !that at the back penetrated the scalp to the bone, about one ' inch in depth, and about one and a half in length. Whilst at the complainant's house, be saw • French there, and, ob- serving some blood upon one of his hands, he asked how it came there, on which "he believed" he replied that Plumpton's brother had given him a blow on the nose. He 11 examined French's nose, and he was of opinion that it had ' not been bleeding.—Sergeant Coutts proved apprehending ' the prisoners. Mr. Swift submitted that though there might be a case for the consideration of the Bench in regard to four of the prisoners, there was no evidence to prove that French had anything to do with injuring complainant.— Mr. Gaskell said there was no doubt that there had been a most gross assault committed; but with regard to French he considered that there was not sufficient evidence to com- mit him, and he would therefore be discharged. The other prisoners would be committed to take their trial at the Liverpool Assizes, and bail tef used,

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDI ANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDI ANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day, Mr. S. Marsh, presiding. There were also present the Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. T. Hall, Tyrer, Meadows, Fidler, Ranson, Lowe, Buckley, Jackson, Gerrard, Sadler, Harrison, Leigh, Dobell, and Syder ; with Mr. Hartley (clerk).

WORM-1017S1I MASTER'S REPORT. The MASTER reported 454 inmates in the Workhouse at the end of this week, as compared with 458 in thu previous week, and 418 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 147 boys and guts chargeable to the Union.—The bread was again unsatisfactory.

TILE "D—OUCEIIR " TO MESSRS. WEEKS AND HUGHES. The CLERK read the following letter dated September 30th, from Mr. Thomas Hoed, on behalf of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, respecting the "douceur" of 150 guineas which the Board had offered them in respect of their services in the preparation of plans of new schools :—"I have communi- cated with my clients on your letter of the 17th inst., and they decidedly will not accept the 150 guineas. They have the .advantage of a professional gentleman of good standing, having seen their detailed particulars, and is of opinion that my clients could easily recover the 200 guineas on a 'quantium val eat ' view, besides damages for the avoidance of contract, but acting under my advice, and solely with a view to save likation they will accept 173 guineas if paid to them within a week from this date. This letter is, of course, entirely without prejudice in the event of any advised offer not being accepted, and litigation must commence."—The CLERK read the letter which he had sent in reply, asking whether, if the Guardians paid the 175 guineas, that sum would be in full discharge of all claims and detnands of Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, and stating that he could assure him the Guanidine had no desire for litigation. They simply wished to do that which was right. In answer to that he had received the following :—" Absence from home has prevented me replying to your letter of the Ist instant before this. Without prejudice I will advise my clients to accept the 175 guineas in. full discharge on condition the cheque he sent to me within the time mentioned in my former letter."—The CLERK remarked that if the Guardians consented to that sum heingpaid, Messrs. Weeks and Hughes must be distinctly given to understand that they could not have any claim on the Guaidians if the latter: decided to build the schools hereafter.—ln the course of some discus- sion, Mr. MEADOR'S remarked that of course Messrs. Weeks and Hughes ought to be paid for what they had done, but his impression was that if they got the 150 guineas which had been offered to them they would be pretty well ptid. Ile did not think they could claim more legally as th matter stood at present.—Mr. FIDLER would rather the, Boa; paid the additional 25 guineas and have done with it.—Mr. Ranson thought the architects would take the 130 guineas. —Mr. MEADOWS: Yes, and jump at it. If they wait mucli longer they won't get anything at all. (Laughter).—Mr. hALL moved, and Mr. FIDLER seconded, that the sum of 175 guineas be paid to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes. architects, in full discharge of all claims and demands, whether pre- sent or future, arising out of their contract with the Guar- ians, and that a cheque for that amount be given. Ou being put to the meeting, however, the motion was lost by twelve votes to five.

About half way up the valley we passed the Tutkish barracks, outside of which were sitting a good many soldiers, then we rode on to Shechem. BY .k SOU 111-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SPEcter,.] No. XIX. ISETHEL TO SHILOH AND LEEONA.II. Ily nine a.m. on Tuesday, 21st of March, we were in the saddle and on the way to Shiloh. The road or beaten track (for there are no roads in Palestine such as we have in England) was very good for three or four miles. During this day's ride I was struck with the beautiful convexity of the mountains. They vary in shape from the almost exact half-circle to the semi-oval. Were it not for the intermin- able loose stones which lie scattered over their surface, the appearance of Judea's hills would be unique in the softness and variety of their outline. Where the terraces are pree served complete the effect is still 'charming. The olives rise in tiers, one above another, on the hill side, and their spirey leaves shine in the rays of the son with almost saitivt_eirlys brightness. The fig tree, also, although quite bare time, had not the miserable shivering look which our tree,s, have in the winter. "The time of figs was not yet , although the sun was pouring down with almost re fhurnh in heat, but its branches had a sort of delicate bloom, w the sun's rays threw quite a radiance down the mountain side. Before we had gone over Syria the leaves of the fig tree were all out, clothing their branches with a thick foliage of beautiful green. We had travelled about an hour when we began to descend a deep gorge, wchroascehlderdy bteonreraentht btehde, hteeltoofoser,twsot°oners'three miles. The sound bjesatdr eewf e de uwti thho trsoeus of eighty feet, shod with iron as only the Syrian can shoe them, travelling over big, dry, loose stones, and down hill for nearly an hour, became most painfully monotonous and nerve-trying. I can scarcely express the relief we felt as we issued from the ravine and passed along the narrow level valley which led up to the Robbers' Fountain, whose green- sward beneath the shadow of its great rock, made us feel how apt a similitude it was in that weary land of the bless- ings Christ brings in the gospel of salvation. Some fine clumps of the maiden-hair fern, growing in the crevices of the rock, made the contrast between the rugged ravine and our cool resting place still more delightful. About noon we reached the heights of Shiloh, and lunched beneath the shadow of an old mosque, having the scattered ruins of an old city spread over the hill immediately before us. The situation of Shiloh, environed with hills, and sitting in the midst of undulating valleys, must have been particularly favourable for the assembling of the tribes durieg the 400 years the ark remained here. Over these hills and valleys came the mother of Samuel every year with the little home- spun coat for the darling child she bad dedicated to the Lord. We saw many of these little coats, originally of many colours, worn by the shepherd boys of Palestine. Shiloh was greatly blessed through all the early history of God's chosen people; but now, as we wandered over its heaps and saw its ruins, we thought of the burning wrath that devoted a place so honoured as Shiloh to destruction and continued desolation. But in Jeremiah's day, long before its Grecian or Saracenic fragments had an existence, Shiloh was a by- word and reproach to the nation. After resting an hear or two we descended the course of the wady that leads to Lebonah, and in a few minutes we saw our tents in the far distance, at the head of a finely-cultivated valley, with u sitting on a hill to the right, and a noble back- greund of dark and fruitful terraces covering the mountain, at tbr foot of which our tents were spread. The next morn- ing, as we left the valley, it was quite lively with farming operations. Several oxen were plodding before the primitive ploughs, while the husbandmen, in their short tunics, were using the goal at almost every step, and calling upon the beasts to proceed. The goad is a long stick with a sharp nail stuck in at one end, and furnished with a scraper to clear the soil from the plougshare at the otherslT he goad is held with the left hand, and the plough with the right. Deep ploughing is unknown, and in Palestine unnecessary. Three or four inches is as deep as they need CO go, so that the plough can easily be lifted out of the soil with one hand when it meets with any obstruction or needs scraping. Mr. Nimmo and I were mounted, and quietly making our way through the valley, when we beard a great hubbub on the tenting ground. Some of the Arab muleteers had quartelled over a bit of rope, and got fighting most fiercely, trying in their peculiarly barbarous manner to seize each other by the throat, and when they could not do that began to throw stones. Mr. Hoelen, our conductor, and others of the party interfered, and before we fairly started the belligerent em- braced and kissed each other. So the cavalcade left in peace. After traversing the whole length of the beautiful e turned to the right and soon lost sight of Lebonah as we began to climb between the mountains on our way into Samaria. Up well-worn tracks whose ruts were some- times as many as 20 inchess deep, we ascended two steep mountain sides, one rismg above the other at a distance of r mile or two, an undulating valley lying between. As we reached the highest mountain peak the whole of Notthern Palestine burst upon our view. The far-reaching valleys lying between the two mountain ranges that run along the whole of Samaria, lay fair before us, while Hermon, with his snow clad peak, bounding the prospect on the far north sat, as it seemed to us, in the midst of the Galilean hills, a hoary patriarch surrounded by an innumerable family. In the near foreground, on the left, was Mount Gerizim. with his darker peak, a prince among the hills of Samaria. We no v dismounted and led our horses down the steep and rugged brow of the bill. The plain below, along whose border we travelled, had no hedges, but for miles its rich brown soil was divided into square patches, the young corn alternating and contrasting very beautifully with the newly turned soil. Of that forenoon I have a more vivid recollec- tion than of any other on the journey. The sun was very oppressive, and as I remembered how the Redeemer, with His few faithful followers, had trod the same mountain track, and along this same road, or. perhaps a more sultry day than this, I felt His presence more of a reality than I had done before. I thought of the sweetness, the lowliness, and the power of the man Christ Jesus as He trod those white, those heat-reflecting paths, and how He was now exalted and looking down from His glory, an interested spectator, as those who loved Him came from distant lands and islands of the sea to gaze upon the spot of earth made sacred by His presence, and seeking to use the impulse de- rived from contact with these holy :cones to His honour
and praise.

THE AUTUMN ASSIZES.—The opening of the autumn assizes at Carlisle, Manchester, and Liverpool, has been f xel for Monday, the 31st Oct., Thursday, 3rd Nov., and Satur day, the 12th Nov., respectively. AN IMPORTAINT, POINT AFFECTING SEA-SIDE RESI- DENTS.—‘I point was raised oh Tuesl iv, at the Chester Revision Court, which, if sustained, 'sill seriously affect many hundreds of persons residing in our sea-side towns. The Liberal agent objected to the votes of certiin residents in the coast villages of Cheshire who had let their houses to visitors during the summer months. It was pointed out that the borom,dt householder had the privilege of letting his qualifying property entirely for a period of not mare than three months without incurring the risk of disfranchise- ment, but that in the case of county voters the law wO5 more stringent, any such temporary evacuation of the pre- mises being a breach of the "continuous residence ' insisted upon by the statute. The objection thus raised was said to affect a considerable number of voters in the district, and, recognising its importance, the Revisin Barrister de- c, ferred giving a final opinion until he had more carefully con- sidered the law on the subject. An important noinl was decided at South:mt. Hitherto it has been customary for I°flging-houseS to be classed as business premises, thus affording votes to several persons for each house. It was. however. on Thursday decided that each lodging-houss suf- ficed to confer only one vote, the cons( quence being that a large number of persons are disfranchised.
